title: Introduction to IoT Systems
text:
Preface
This book teaches the Internet of Things the way IoT systems are actually built: one wire, one bus, one protocol layer at a time, on hardware you assemble yourself.
It was written for a ten-week, hands-on course in IoT software and systems. Every concept is paired with something you can run on a small ESP32 kit, so that the ideas in each chapter turn into working circuits, packets and devices before the week is over.

title: Introduction to IoT Systems
text:
Who this book is for
The book assumes you can program in C or C++ and have met basic computer organization and networking ideas. It does not assume any electronics background. Chapters that need circuit knowledge build it as they go, and the Lab Companion walks through soldering and wiring from first principles.

title: Introduction to IoT Systems
text:
How the book is organized
The book has two layers.

The core text (Parts I–VI) covers ideas that change slowly: how devices talk to sensors, how IoT networks are layered, how to make devices trustworthy, and how to build and test a complete system.
The Lab Companion (Part VII) covers the specific kit, pin assignments, starter code and lab procedures. It is updated every term as hardware and libraries change.

Each core chapter follows the same pattern: learning objectives, a motivating example, the concepts, a short exercise on your kit, design trade-offs, common pitfalls, review questions, and further reading.

title: Introduction to IoT Systems
text:
Two tracks
Every chapter has a core path that all readers should follow. Some chapters also contain Advanced track sections, marked with a distinct callout. These go deeper into standards, design reviews and engineering practice. They are optional on a first reading.

title: Introduction to IoT Systems
text:
Conventions

Code that runs on the kit is written for the Arduino framework on the ESP32, built with PlatformIO.
Course helper functions use the iot prefix (for example iotStartSerial()), and pin assignments live in iot_pins.h under the IoTPins:: namespace.
I²C addresses are written as 7-bit hexadecimal values, such as 0x68.

title: Introduction to IoT Systems
text:
Sources and originality
The text, figures and code in this book were written for it. Where the book follows an existing framework, taxonomy or teaching sequence, it says so in the text and cites the source. In particular:

The overall sequence of Parts I–IV, and several frameworks used in them (the IoT reference framework, the classification of sensors and actuators, the Observe–Decide–Act loop, IoT networking requirements, the layered IoT protocol stack and the three-domain view of IoT security), follow Rayes and Salam’s Internet of Things from Hype to Reality (Rayes and Salam 2022) and its security chapter by Dabbagh and Rayes (Dabbagh and Rayes 2017). These are used as frameworks with attribution; no text or figures are reproduced from them.
Facts, figures and standards are cited to their primary sources: datasheets, RFCs, specifications and official regulatory texts.
Code examples are original, or minimal uses of public library APIs written in the style of their documentation.
Product names and trademarks belong to their owners and are used only to identify products.

If you believe any passage is insufficiently attributed, please open an issue in the book’s repository; it will be corrected promptly.

title: 1  What Is the Internet of Things?
text:
1.1 Why it matters
In 2024 there were about 18.5 billion connected IoT devices in the world, more than two for every person. Analysts expected roughly 21 billion in 2025 and close to 40 billion by 2030 (IoT Analytics 2025). Most of them are not phones or laptops. They are thermostats, parking sensors, infusion pumps, irrigation valves, shipping-container trackers and factory motors.
Each of these devices is a small computer that senses something in the physical world, decides what it means, and either acts on it or reports it to someone who will. Building such devices well requires knowledge that usually lives in separate courses: electronics, embedded programming, networking, distributed systems and security. This book brings them together around one question: how do you build a small device that reliably senses, decides, communicates and acts?
crumbs: 1  What Is the Internet of Things?

title: 1  What Is the Internet of Things?
text:
1.2 Concepts

A working definition
There is no single official definition of the Internet of Things, but most definitions agree on four ingredients. An IoT system is a network of physical things that have:

Sensors, to collect information about the world;
Identifiers, so that every piece of data can be traced to the device that produced it;
Software, to process and interpret the data;
Connectivity, so that data and commands can travel between devices, people and services.

Putting these together, in a formulation close to that of Rayes and Salam (Rayes and Salam 2022):

The Internet of Things is the network of physical objects that are embedded with sensors, software and network connectivity, have a unique identity, and can collect and exchange data and act on the physical world.

Notice the last clause. Many IoT devices do not just observe; they also actuate: they open valves, lock doors, dim lights and move motors. A device that can change the physical world raises the stakes of every design decision, from how fast it responds to who is allowed to command it.


Related terms
You will meet several overlapping terms in the literature:







Term
Emphasis




M2M (machine-to-machine)
Devices talking directly to each other, often over cellular links, without a person in the loop. The older industrial term.


Wireless sensor networks
Large numbers of small, battery-powered sensing nodes; mostly research-driven.


Industrial IoT (IIoT)
Factories, energy and process control, where reliability and safety dominate.


Web of Things
Using web standards (HTTP, URLs, JSON) to expose devices as resources.


Internet of Everything
A marketing term that adds people, processes and data to the picture.


Cyber-physical systems
The academic term for tightly coupled computation and physical processes.



These are not competing technologies. They are different lenses on the same idea.


From the Internet of People to the Internet of Things
The internet has gone through several phases, each of which digitized something new (Evans 2011; Rayes and Salam 2022):

Connectivity digitized access to information: email, the web, search.
The networked economy digitized business: e-commerce, online banking, supply chains.
Immersive experiences digitized interaction: social media, video, mobile apps.
The Internet of Things digitizes the physical world itself.

The first three phases mostly connected people to applications. Almost every packet started or ended at a person looking at a screen. In the IoT, most traffic is between machines, and a person may never see the raw data at all. This changes the design priorities. A web page can take a second to load; a braking system cannot. A phone is recharged daily; a soil sensor may need to run for five years on one battery.
Connecting objects is not a goal in itself. The value comes from turning the data into better decisions (for example, scheduling maintenance before a pump fails) and delivering the right information to the right person or machine at the right time.


Three kinds of connection
It helps to classify IoT interactions by who is talking:

People to things. A person monitors or controls a device: checking a home camera, adjusting a thermostat, reading an ECG from a wearable.
Things to people. A device notifies a person: a leak alert, a low-battery warning, a door left open.
Things to things. Devices coordinate without a person: a motion sensor turns on a light, a traffic signal adapts to a queue of cars, a fleet of warehouse robots avoids collisions.

The third category grows fastest and is the hardest to get right, because no person is in the loop to notice when something goes wrong.


A reference architecture
Real IoT systems are built from many products made by different vendors. A reference architecture gives you a common vocabulary for where each part belongs. A widely used model, adapted here from Rayes and Salam (Rayes and Salam 2022), has four levels (Figure 1.1):






Figure 1.1: A four-level IoT reference architecture. Data generally flows upward; commands flow downward.




Device level. The things: sensors, actuators and the microcontrollers that run them. Your kit lives here.
Network level. Everything that moves data: radios, gateways, routers and switches, and the protocols they use. A gateway often translates between a local radio (Bluetooth, LoRa, Zigbee) and the internet.
Management and services platform level. Software that manages fleets of devices and their data: device registration and identity, configuration, firmware updates, data storage, rules engines and analytics. Cloud IoT platforms and MQTT brokers live here.
Application level. The applications people and businesses actually use: dashboards, mobile apps, alerting, and integration with business systems.

Two concerns cut across every level: security (who may read, send or change what) and management (how you find, configure, update and retire devices once they are deployed). Much of this book is organized around this picture. Parts I and II focus on the device level, Part III on the network level, Part IV on the cross-cutting concerns, and Parts V and VI on how the levels come together into a working system.


Application domains
IoT appears in almost every industry. A few domains recur throughout the book:

Smart homes and buildings: lighting, heating and cooling, locks, appliances and energy metering. Interoperability between brands is the central challenge (Chapter 13).
Smart cities: parking, street lighting, waste collection, air-quality monitoring and traffic management. Devices are spread over kilometers and must run for years, which favors long-range, low-power radios (Chapter 10).
Healthcare and wellness: wearables, remote patient monitoring and connected medical devices. Privacy, safety and regulation dominate.
Transportation and logistics: vehicle telematics, fleet tracking and cold-chain monitoring of goods in transit.
Industry and agriculture: predictive maintenance, process monitoring, irrigation control and livestock tracking.

Each domain weighs the same trade-offs differently. A smart-home light switch must respond in well under a second but can draw mains power. A soil-moisture sensor can report once an hour but must run on a battery for years.


The questions every IoT system must answer
The basic promise of IoT is to monitor and control things from anywhere. Delivering that promise raises a set of questions that this book takes up one at a time:







Question
Where it is covered




How does a device sense and act on the world?
Parts I and II


How does it reach the network, and the network reach it?
Part III


Who is allowed to monitor and control it, and how is that enforced?
Part IV


How do devices from different makers work together?
Chapter 13


How do we make it reliable when it is unattended for years?

How do we make it efficient in energy, bandwidth and cost?
Throughout

TipTry it on your kit: place the kit in the architecture

title: 1  What Is the Internet of Things?
text:
1.3 In depth (optional)






Optional, in-depth explanation. This section goes beyond the rest of the chapter into the math and physics behind it. Nothing later in the book depends on it; skip it on a first reading.




Back-of-the-envelope engineering
Most early IoT design questions are answered with two quick estimates: how long will the battery last, and how much data will the fleet produce. Both are simple averages, and both are worth doing before writing any code.
Average current. A device that is active for \(t_a\) seconds in every period \(T\) has a duty cycle \(D = t_a / T\). Its average current is
\[
I_\text{avg} = D \, I_\text{active} + (1 - D)\, I_\text{sleep}.
\]
For a sensor that wakes for 0.5 s every 10 minutes, draws 80 mA while awake (Wi-Fi on) and 10 µA asleep: \(D = 0.5/600 \approx 8.3\times10^{-4}\), so \(I_\text{avg} \approx 67\ \mu\text{A} + 10\ \mu\text{A} \approx 77\ \mu\text{A}\). Notice that the 10 µA sleep current is already 13% of the total: at low duty cycles, sleep current dominates.
Lifetime. A battery of capacity \(Q\) (in mAh) lasts roughly \(Q / I_\text{avg}\) hours. A 225 mAh coin cell would give \(225 / 0.077 \approx 2900\) h, about four months, on paper.
The physics the average hides. A battery is not an ideal voltage source; it has an internal resistance \(R_\text{int}\). The terminal voltage under load is \(V = V_\text{oc} - I R_\text{int}\). A coin cell’s internal resistance is typically 10–30 Ω and rises as it discharges, so an 80 mA pulse drops \(0.08 \times 15 = 1.2\) V: the 3 V cell sags to 1.8 V and the microcontroller resets. The average said four months; the peak says the design does not work at all. This is why Wi-Fi devices use AA or lithium-ion cells, and why coin-cell devices use BLE or LoRa, whose transmit current is far lower, often with a capacitor to supply the pulse.
Fleet data volume. If \(N\) devices each send \(b\) bytes every \(T\) seconds, the fleet produces \(N b / T\) bytes per second. One million smart meters sending 100 bytes every 15 minutes produce \(10^6 \times 100 / 900 \approx 111\) kB/s on average, or about 9.6 GB per day before protocol overhead (Chapter 8 shows the overhead can be many times the payload). The rate is modest; the challenge is the number of connections and the bursts when every meter reports at the same moment.
Exercise. Repeat the lifetime estimate for a device that reports every minute instead of every 10 minutes. Which term now dominates the average?
Sources for this section: (Espressif Systems, n.d.).

title: 1  What Is the Internet of Things?
text:
1.4 Design trade-offs
Every IoT design balances a small set of competing goals. It is worth naming them now, because they will reappear in every chapter:



Goal
Typically in tension with




Long battery life
Frequent sensing, fast response, high data rates


Long radio range
Data rate and energy per bit


Low unit cost
Security hardware, extra sensors, certification


Rich local processing
Power, cost and complexity of the device


Strong security
Usability, cost and development time


Openness and interoperability
Speed to market and vendor control



There is no universally right answer. A good IoT engineer can state which goals matter most for a given product and justify the trade-offs that follow.

title: 1  What Is the Internet of Things?
text:
1.5 Common pitfalls

Connecting things because you can. A device should be connected because the data or the remote control creates value, not because a radio is cheap.
Designing for the demo, not the deployment. A prototype on a desk has unlimited power, perfect Wi-Fi and a developer watching it. A deployed device has none of these.
Treating security as a feature to add later. Retrofitting identity, encryption and updates into deployed devices is expensive and sometimes impossible.
Ignoring the people involved. Someone installs, maintains and eventually discards every device. Their time and skills are part of the system.







NoteAdvanced track





Reference architectures in standards. The four-level model above is a simplified version of several formal architectures, including the ITU-T Y.2060 IoT reference model, the IEEE 2413 architectural framework and ISO/IEC 30141. They differ in naming and in how they divide responsibilities, but they all separate devices, networks, services and applications, and they all treat security and management as cross-cutting.
Exercise. Choose a commercial IoT product (for example a video doorbell, a connected car or a smart meter). Draw it on the four-level architecture, naming the actual products, protocols and companies at each level. Identify which party controls each level, and what happens to the product if that party goes out of business.

title: 2  Development Boards and the IoT Kit
text:
2.1 Why it matters
Every IoT device starts as a circuit on a bench. Before you can write code that senses or acts, you need to know how electricity reaches a component, how much of it the component can take, and how a microcontroller board fits into the circuit. Most “my code doesn’t work” problems in a first IoT course turn out to be circuit problems: an LED wired backwards, a missing ground, a component on the wrong breadboard row.
This chapter builds the smallest useful circuit, makes it blink, and then explains the development board that will run all the code in the rest of the book.
crumbs: 2  Development Boards and the IoT Kit

title: 2  Development Boards and the IoT Kit
text:
2.2 Concepts

Voltage, current and resistance
Three quantities describe what happens in a simple circuit:

Voltage (V, measured in volts) is the electrical “pressure” between two points. It is what pushes charge around a circuit. A USB port supplies 5 V; the ESP32’s pins work at 3.3 V.
Current (I, measured in amperes or milliamperes, mA) is the rate at which charge flows. Components are damaged by too much current, not by voltage alone.
Resistance (R, measured in ohms, Ω) opposes current.

They are related by Ohm’s law:
\[
V = I \times R
\]
Current only flows around a closed loop: from the supply, through the components, and back to ground (GND), the reference point that all voltages are measured from. If any part of the loop is open, nothing happens.


Lighting an LED safely
A light-emitting diode (LED) conducts in one direction only. Its longer leg, the anode, must face the positive supply; the shorter leg, the cathode, faces ground. Once it conducts, an LED holds a roughly fixed voltage across itself, called its forward voltage (\(V_f\)): about 2.0 V for a red LED, and around 3 V for blue or white ones.
An LED has almost no resistance of its own once it conducts. Connect it straight across a supply and the current rises until something burns out. A current-limiting resistor in series sets the current:
\[
R = \frac{V_{supply} - V_f}{I_{LED}}
\]
For a red LED driven from a 3.3 V ESP32 pin, aiming for 10 mA:
\[
R = \frac{3.3\ \text{V} - 2.0\ \text{V}}{0.010\ \text{A}} = 130\ \Omega
\]
Resistors come in standard values, and it is always safe to round up. The kit uses 220 Ω, which gives about 6 mA: plenty for an indicator LED, and gentle on the microcontroller pin.


Breadboards
A solderless breadboard lets you build and change circuits without soldering. Inside, metal clips connect groups of holes:

In the main area, each row of five holes is connected. The rows on either side of the central gap are not connected to each other. Chips and modules straddle this gap so that each pin gets its own row.
The long power rails along the edges run the length of the board. By convention, the red rail carries the supply voltage and the blue rail carries ground. On some boards the rails are split in the middle, so check before relying on them.

The kit uses two 830-point breadboards side by side, with the ESP32 bridging the seam. The rails carry 3.3 V and GND, except for one short rail section reserved for the servo’s 5 V supply (Lab 1).


From fixed circuits to microcontrollers
Suppose you want the LED to blink once per second. One classic solution is a 555 timer: a chip whose output switches on and off at a rate set by a resistor and a capacitor. It works, but changing the behavior means changing components. Making it blink twice and pause, or blink faster when a button is pressed, means designing a new circuit.
A microcontroller replaces the fixed circuit with software. It is a small computer on a single chip, with a processor, memory and input/output pins. The same chip can blink an LED, read a sensor or run a network stack, depending on the program you load:
void loop() {
  digitalWrite(LED_PIN, HIGH);
  delay(1000);
  digitalWrite(LED_PIN, LOW);
  delay(1000);
}
Microcontrollers are cheap (often well under a dollar for simple ones), so it is usually cheaper to use one than to design a custom circuit. This is a large part of why connected devices became affordable.


What a development board adds
A bare microcontroller chip is hard to use on a bench: its pins are tiny, it needs a stable power supply, and loading a program onto it requires special hardware. A development board wraps the chip with everything needed to experiment:

A power circuit: a voltage regulator that turns 5 V from USB into the 3.3 V the chip needs.
A programming interface: usually a USB-to-UART bridge chip (Chapter 5), so a laptop can upload programs and exchange text with the board.
Basic I/O: at least one LED and a reset button, often a second “boot” button.
Header pins: the chip’s I/O pins brought out at breadboard-friendly spacing.



Arduino and the ESP family
The Arduino project made microcontroller development accessible to people with no electronics background. It combined an inexpensive open-hardware board, the Arduino Uno based on an 8-bit AVR microcontroller, with a simple programming environment and a large library ecosystem. Its programming model (a setup() function and a loop() function, Chapter 3) is still the most common entry point to embedded programming.
The original Uno has no network connection. Adding Wi-Fi meant stacking an expansion board, called a shield, which added cost and size. The ESP8266 and later the ESP32, both from Espressif Systems, changed this by putting a capable processor and a Wi-Fi radio on the same inexpensive chip. A chip that combines a microcontroller with radios and other advanced peripherals is often called a system on a chip (SoC).

The ESP32 can still be programmed with the Arduino framework, so the simple programming model carries over unchanged.


The ESP32 DevKit V1
The kit uses the ESP32 DevKit V1, a widely cloned board built around the ESP32-WROOM-32 module. Its parts are:

The ESP32-WROOM-32 module (the metal can), which contains the ESP32 chip, its flash memory, a crystal and a printed antenna. Keep the antenna end clear of metal and wires.
A USB-to-UART bridge (typically a CP2102 or CH340 chip) for uploading and for the Serial Monitor. If your laptop does not recognize the board, the bridge’s driver is the usual culprit.
A 3.3 V regulator fed from USB or from the VIN pin.
Two buttons: EN resets the chip; BOOT (GPIO 0) puts it into upload mode if automatic upload fails.
A power LED and, on most versions, a blue LED on GPIO 2.

Not every pin is equally safe to use. These rules prevent most beginner problems:



Table 2.2: ESP32 DevKit V1 pin restrictions (ESP32 Series Datasheet, n.d.).









Pins
Restriction




GPIO 6–11
Connected to the module’s flash memory. Never use.


GPIO 34, 35, 36, 39
Input only, with no internal pull-up or pull-down resistors. Good for analog input (the kit’s potentiometer uses GPIO 34).


GPIO 0, 2, 5, 12, 15
Strapping pins, read at reset to choose the boot mode. Usable, but an external component holding them high or low can stop the board from booting or uploading.


GPIO 1, 3
UART0 TX and RX, used for uploading and the Serial Monitor.


ADC2 pins
Cannot be used for analog input while Wi-Fi is active. Use ADC1 pins (GPIO 32–39) for analog sensors.






Each pin can safely source or sink only a few tens of milliamperes. Drive LEDs through resistors, and never power motors directly from a GPIO pin.

Change the program so the LED blinks “SOS” in Morse code. What did changing the behavior cost you, compared with a 555 timer circuit?

A guided, step-by-step version for a lecture session is Activity 1.

title: 2  Development Boards and the IoT Kit
text:
2.3 In depth (optional)






Optional, in-depth explanation. This section goes beyond the rest of the chapter into the math and physics behind it. Nothing later in the book depends on it; skip it on a first reading.




Currents, resistors and heat on the kit
Sizing an LED resistor. A lit LED holds a roughly constant forward voltage \(V_f\) across itself. The resistor takes the rest of the supply, so by Ohm’s law
\[
I = \frac{V_\text{GPIO} - V_f}{R}.
\]
With a 3.3 V pin, a red LED (\(V_f \approx 2.0\) V) and 220 Ω, \(I = 1.3 / 220 \approx 5.9\) mA: bright enough to see, well within a pin’s limits. A green or blue LED (\(V_f\) from about 2.2 to 3.0 V) draws less, and appears dimmer, with the same resistor. The resistor dissipates \(P = I^2 R \approx 7.7\) mW, far below its ¼ W rating.
Without the resistor, the only thing limiting current is the pin driver’s own output resistance (tens of ohms) and the LED’s small dynamic resistance: the current can exceed the pin’s rating, and the pin or the LED can be damaged. The simulator in Activity 1 does not model this.
Pin limits add up. The ESP32 lets you set each pin’s drive strength; at the default setting a pin sources roughly 20 mA, and the absolute maximum is around 40 mA. What matters as much is the total drawn through the chip’s power pins. Use pins to signal, not to power things: anything over a few milliamperes deserves a transistor.
Pull-up resistors. With INPUT_PULLUP, an internal resistor of roughly 45 kΩ connects the pin to 3.3 V. When the button closes, the current is \(3.3 / 45\,000 \approx 73\ \mu\)A: negligible for an LED-sized budget, but not for a coin-cell device that holds a button down for hours.
The regulator gets warm. The DevKit’s linear regulator drops USB’s 5 V to 3.3 V and turns the difference into heat:
\[
P_\text{reg} = (V_\text{in} - V_\text{out})\, I_\text{load}.
\]
During Wi-Fi bursts of 250 mA, \(P = 1.7 \times 0.25 \approx 0.43\) W. A small regulator package rises in temperature by its thermal resistance \(\theta_{JA}\) times that power; at a typical 90 °C/W, about 38 °C above ambient. It works, but leaves little margin, which is one reason not to hang extra loads on 3V3.
Exercise. You want an LED current of 10 mA from a 3.3 V pin with a green LED of \(V_f = 2.2\) V. Which standard resistor value would you choose, and what current do you actually get?
Sources for this section: (ESP32 Series Datasheet, n.d.).

title: 2  Development Boards and the IoT Kit
text:
2.4 Design trade-offs







Choice
Consider




Development board vs. custom board
Development boards are ideal for prototypes and small runs. Products use a custom circuit board with only the parts they need, which lowers cost, size and power.


Module vs. bare chip
A pre-certified radio module (like the WROOM-32) avoids designing and certifying an antenna circuit yourself.


Arduino framework vs. vendor SDK (ESP-IDF)
Arduino is faster to learn and has many libraries. The vendor SDK gives full control of power modes, the RTOS and security features.


5 V vs. 3.3 V parts
Mixing them needs level shifting. Prefer 3.3 V parts with a 3.3 V microcontroller.

title: 2  Development Boards and the IoT Kit
text:
2.5 Common pitfalls

LED backwards. It simply stays dark. Flip it.
No resistor. The LED may glow briefly and fail, and the GPIO pin can be damaged.
Component in the wrong row. Both legs of a resistor in the same five-hole row connect it to nothing.
Split power rails. Half the board has no power.
Charge-only USB cables. The board powers up but the computer never sees it. Use a data cable.
Strapping pin held at the wrong level. The board refuses to upload or boot. Disconnect the component on that pin and try again.







NoteAdvanced track





Reading a datasheet. Beyond the ESP32. Newer Espressif chips use RISC-V cores (ESP32-C3, C6, H2) and add radios such as 802.15.4 for Thread and Zigbee. Other families popular in IoT include Nordic’s nRF52 and nRF54 (Bluetooth Low Energy), Silicon Labs’ EFR32 (multi-protocol) and the Raspberry Pi RP2040/RP2350 (no radio, but very low cost). title: 3  Programming the Device
text:
3.1 Why it matters
A push button looks like the simplest input imaginable: pressed or not pressed. Yet a naïve button handler on a microcontroller will often count one press as three, miss presses entirely, or freeze the rest of the program while it waits. Getting the basics of input, output and timing right is what separates a demo that works once from a device that works every time.
This chapter covers the programming model you will use for the rest of the book, and the handful of techniques that make simple I/O reliable.

title: 3  Programming the Device
3  Programming the Device
text:
3.3 In depth (optional)






Optional, in-depth explanation. This section goes beyond the rest of the chapter into the math and physics behind it. Nothing later in the book depends on it; skip it on a first reading.




Bounce, time and wrap-around
Why buttons bounce. A pushbutton is two springy metal contacts. When they close, they collide, separate and collide again several times before settling, typically for 1–10 ms. A pin sampled every microsecond sees each collision as a separate edge.
Hardware debouncing with an RC filter. A resistor \(R\) and capacitor \(C\) smooth the signal. When the button opens, the pull-up charges the capacitor:
\[
V(t) = V_{DD}\left(1 - e^{-t/RC}\right).
\]
The pin reads HIGH once \(V\) crosses its input threshold \(V_{IH}\), at time \(t = -RC \ln\left(1 - V_{IH}/V_{DD}\right)\). With \(R = 10\) kΩ, \(C = 1\) µF (\(RC = 10\) ms) and \(V_{IH} = 0.75\,V_{DD}\), that is \(10 \ln 4 \approx 14\) ms: long enough to ride out the bounce. A slow edge can make an ordinary input chatter as it crosses the threshold, which is why hardware debouncers often add a Schmitt-trigger input with two thresholds.
Software debouncing replaces the capacitor with a time window: accept an edge only if more than \(t_d\) has passed since the last accepted one. The window must be longer than the worst bounce and shorter than the fastest intentional double press (about 100 ms for a person).
Timer arithmetic. millis() counts milliseconds in an unsigned 32-bit integer, so it wraps to zero after \(2^{32}\) ms \(\approx 49.7\) days. The idiom
if (now - last >= interval) { ... }
still works across the wrap, because unsigned subtraction is arithmetic modulo \(2^{32}\): if last is just before the wrap and now just after, now - last is still the small, correct difference. The tempting alternative if (now >= last + interval) fails for the interval around the wrap. A device meant to run for months must get this right.
Hardware timers. The ESP32’s general-purpose timers count a clock (80 MHz by default) through a prescaler \(P\). One tick lasts \(P / 80\ \text{MHz}\); with \(P = 80\), one tick is 1 µs, and an alarm after \(N\) ticks fires every \(N\) µs. This is how micros() and periodic timer interrupts are built.
Exercise. A wearable samples a button every 5 ms and declares a press when it has seen k consecutive LOW samples. What is the smallest k that rejects bounces of up to 8 ms? What is the longest delay the user can notice?
Sources for this section: (ESP32 Technical Reference Manual, n.d.).

Choice
Prefer it when

The loop is fast, the event is slow, and simplicity matters


Interrupts
Events are short or rare, or the processor should sleep while waiting

Short wires and simple buttons


External pull-ups (e.g. 10 kΩ)

You need a true analog voltage (audio, a reference level)

Dimming LEDs, controlling motor speed or driving servos


delay()
Throwaway tests only

Anything that must stay responsive

title: 3  Programming the Device
text:
3.5 Common pitfalls

Floating inputs. An input with no pull resistor reads random values.
Forgetting active-low logic. With INPUT_PULLUP, pressed is LOW.
Long or blocking ISRs. Printing, delaying or using I²C inside an ISR crashes the ESP32 or causes watchdog resets.
Missing volatile. The main loop never notices that the ISR changed a variable.
Integer overflow and unsigned loops. for (uint8_t i = 255; i >= 0; i--) never ends, because an unsigned value is always ≥ 0.
ADC2 with Wi-Fi. Analog readings fail silently once Wi-Fi starts.
Unpinned platform versions. Code that compiled last week fails after a core update.







NoteAdvanced track





Hardware debouncing. A resistor and capacitor (an RC filter) on the button line, followed by a Schmitt-trigger input, removes bounce in hardware. Calculate an RC time constant that filters bounces of up to 5 ms, and discuss when hardware debouncing is worth the extra parts.
Atomic access. Copying a 32-bit counter on the ESP32 is atomic, but a 64-bit value or a structure is not: an interrupt can arrive halfway through the copy. On the ESP32, protect such data with portENTER_CRITICAL_ISR() / portEXIT_CRITICAL_ISR() and a portMUX_TYPE spinlock, or pass events through a FreeRTOS queue (Chapter 4).
Hardware timers. For precise periodic work, the ESP32 has hardware timers whose interrupts fire at exact intervals regardless of what the main loop is doing. The esp_timer API offers microsecond-resolution software timers built on them.

title: 4  Embedded Systems and Operating Systems
text:
4.1 Why it matters
Your laptop runs hundreds of programs at once, can be restarted when something hangs, and has gigabytes of memory to spare. An IoT device may run one program for ten years in a place no one can reach, with a few hundred kilobytes of memory and a battery that must last the whole time. It may also have to react to an event within milliseconds, every time.
Writing software for these conditions is different from writing desktop or web software. This chapter introduces the vocabulary of embedded systems and the two main ways to structure their software: a single loop, or a set of tasks managed by a real-time operating system.
crumbs: 4  Embedded Systems and Operating Systems

title: 4  Embedded Systems and Operating Systems
crumbs: 4  Embedded Systems and Operating Systems

title: 4  Embedded Systems and Operating Systems
text:
4.3 In depth (optional)






Optional, in-depth explanation. This section goes beyond the rest of the chapter into the math and physics behind it. Nothing later in the book depends on it; skip it on a first reading.




Will every task meet its deadline?
A real-time operating system schedules tasks by priority. For periodic tasks, there is a classic way to check, before running anything, that every task will finish before its next period starts.
Describe each task \(i\) by its worst-case execution time \(C_i\) and its period \(T_i\) (its deadline is the end of the period). Its utilization is \(U_i = C_i / T_i\), the fraction of the CPU it needs.
Necessary condition. The total utilization must not exceed 1: \(U = \sum_i C_i / T_i \le 1\).
A sufficient test for fixed priorities. With rate-monotonic priorities (shorter period, higher priority), Liu and Layland showed that \(n\) independent periodic tasks always meet their deadlines if
\[
U \le n\left(2^{1/n} - 1\right).
\]
The bound is 1.0 for one task, 0.828 for two, 0.780 for three, and approaches \(\ln 2 \approx 0.693\) as \(n\) grows.
Example. A kit runs three tasks: read the IMU every 10 ms (1 ms of work), update the OLED every 100 ms (25 ms), and publish to MQTT every 1000 ms (60 ms). Then \(U = 0.10 + 0.25 + 0.06 = 0.41 \le 0.780\): schedulable.
Response-time analysis gives an exact answer when the bound fails. The worst-case response time \(R_i\) of task \(i\) is the smallest solution of
\[
R_i = C_i + \sum_{j \in hp(i)} \left\lceil \frac{R_i}{T_j} \right\rceil C_j,
\]
where \(hp(i)\) are the tasks with higher priority. Solve it by iteration from \(R_i = C_i\). For the OLED task: \(R = 25 + \lceil 25/10 \rceil \cdot 1 = 28\), then \(25 + \lceil 28/10\rceil \cdot 1 = 28\): converged, well under 100 ms.
What breaks the model. Real tasks share resources. If a low-priority task holds a mutex that a high-priority task needs, while a medium-priority task runs, the high-priority task waits indefinitely: priority inversion. FreeRTOS mutexes use priority inheritance to bound it; binary semaphores do not. Interrupts, Wi-Fi stack activity on the other core, and flash writes also steal time that a simple \(C_i\) does not show, so leave margin.
Exercise. Add a fourth task that reads the BMP280 every 50 ms for 5 ms. Is the set still guaranteed schedulable by the utilization bound? If not, apply response-time analysis to the lowest-priority task.
Sources for this section: (Liu and Layland 1973; Barry 2016).

Every job waits for every other

Responsive to events, no kernel needed

Most simple products

title: 4  Embedded Systems and Operating Systems
text:
4.5 Common pitfalls

Stack overflow. A task with too small a stack corrupts memory or crashes. Start with generous stacks and measure with uxTaskGetStackHighWaterMark().
Starving tasks. A high-priority task that never blocks prevents all lower-priority tasks from running, and triggers the watchdog timer.
Using delay() instead of yielding. On the ESP32 delay() calls vTaskDelay(), but a busy-wait loop does not, and it starves other tasks.
Unprotected shared resources. Two tasks using the same I²C bus or Serial port at the same time interleave their messages. Protect them with a mutex.
Priority inversion. A low-priority task holding a mutex can block a high-priority task. Use mutexes (which support priority inheritance) rather than plain semaphores for shared resources.







NoteAdvanced track





Scheduling theory. In rate-monotonic scheduling, tasks with shorter periods get higher priorities. Liu and Layland showed that \(n\) periodic tasks are guaranteed to meet their deadlines under this policy if total processor utilization is at most \(n(2^{1/n} - 1)\), which approaches about 69% for large \(n\). Compute whether three tasks with execution times 1, 2 and 3 ms and periods 10, 20 and 40 ms are schedulable.
Watchdog timers. A watchdog is a hardware timer that resets the processor unless software “feeds” it regularly. The ESP32’s task watchdog fires when a task hogs a core. Design a watchdog strategy for a field device: what should be fed, by whom, and how do you avoid feeding it from a loop that is itself stuck?
Zephyr. The Zephyr RTOS, hosted by the Linux Foundation, has become a common choice for new IoT products because it includes networking, Bluetooth, security and update support in one project. Compare its configuration model (Kconfig and devicetree) with the Arduino approach.

title: 5  Serial Communication: UART, SPI and I²C
text:
5.1 Why it matters
Open almost any IoT device and you will find a microcontroller surrounded by smaller chips: a temperature sensor, a motion sensor, a display, a radio, a secure element. The microcontroller is the only part that runs your code. Everything the device senses, shows or transmits reaches it over a handful of wires.
Your kit is a good example. Its ESP32 talks to a computer, two sensors, a security chip, a display and a LoRa radio over about a dozen signal wires, most of them shared. It manages this because it uses three different serial protocols, each designed for a different job (Figure 5.1).
Choosing the wrong bus, or wiring the right one carelessly, is one of the most common reasons an IoT prototype does not work. This chapter gives you the vocabulary and the mental model to get it right.
crumbs: 5  Serial Communication: UART, SPI and I²C

title: 5  Serial Communication: UART, SPI and I²C
text: Figure 5.1: The kit uses all three buses covered in this chapter. UART connects the ESP32 to your laptop. SPI connects fast devices that each get their own chip-select wire. I²C connects slower devices that share two wires and are told apart by address.
crumbs: 5  Serial Communication: UART, SPI and I²C

title: 5  Serial Communication: UART, SPI and I²C
text:
5.2 Concepts

Protocols, parallel and serial
A communication protocol is an agreement between two or more parties about how information is exchanged: the syntax (how bits are grouped), the semantics (what they mean), and the synchronization (when each bit is valid). Protocols also say what happens when something goes wrong.
Suppose you want to move one byte from one ESP32 to another. The simplest approach is parallel communication: use eight wires, one per bit, and set them all at once. Parallel buses are fast and are still used inside computers, for example between a processor and its memory.
Parallel links do not scale well for small devices, though. Each extra bit costs a pin, a trace and a wire, and microcontrollers have few pins to spare. Over longer wires, the bits also stop arriving at exactly the same moment. Serial communication solves both problems by sending the bits one after another over a single data line, and adding just enough control information for the receiver to reassemble them.
Two properties describe any serial link:

Synchronization. In a synchronous link, one side drives a separate clock wire that tells the receiver exactly when to read each bit. In an asynchronous link there is no clock wire, so both sides must agree on the bit rate in advance and resynchronize on every frame.
Direction. A simplex link carries data one way only. A half-duplex link carries data both ways, but only one way at a time. A full-duplex link carries data both ways simultaneously.







NoteA note on terminology



Older documents describe bus roles as master and slave, and name SPI pins MOSI and MISO. Current specifications use controller and target for I²C (UM10204: I2C-bus Specification and User Manual 2021), and many vendors now use controller and peripheral for SPI, with pins named COPI (controller out, peripheral in) and CIPO. This book uses the modern terms. You will still see the older labels printed on modules and in the Arduino API, and they mean the same thing.




UART: asynchronous serial
A UART (Universal Asynchronous Receiver/Transmitter) is a hardware block, not a protocol in itself. It turns bytes into a timed stream of bits on a transmit (TX) wire, and turns the bit stream arriving on a receive (RX) wire back into bytes.

The frame
Because there is no clock wire, every byte is wrapped in a frame that the receiver can recognize on its own (Figure 5.2):

The line idles high.
A start bit pulls the line low for one bit time. This falling edge tells the receiver a byte is coming and where its bits begin.
Five to nine data bits follow, least-significant bit first. Eight is almost universal.
An optional parity bit allows simple error detection.
One or two stop bits return the line high, so the next start bit always produces a fresh falling edge.







Figure 5.2: One UART frame carrying the ASCII character ‘A’ (0x41) in the common 8N1 format.



A configuration is usually written in shorthand such as 8N1: 8 data bits, no parity, 1 stop bit. The receiver samples each bit near the middle of its time slot, which gives it some tolerance for timing error.


Baud rate and throughput
The baud rate is the number of bit times per second. Both sides must be set to the same value. Common rates are 9600 and 115200 baud.
The framing bits are overhead. In 8N1, each byte costs 10 bit times, so a link at 115200 baud moves at most
\[
\frac{115\,200 \text{ bits/s}}{10 \text{ bits/byte}} = 11\,520 \text{ bytes/s}.
\]
If the two sides disagree on the baud rate, the receiver samples at the wrong moments and the error accumulates across the frame. A mismatch of a few percent is enough to corrupt data. A large mismatch produces the familiar screen full of random characters in the Serial Monitor.


Wiring
A UART link is point-to-point between two devices:

Connect each device’s TX to the other’s RX, not TX to TX.
Connect the grounds. The receiver measures voltage relative to its own ground, so without a common reference the levels are meaningless.
Check the logic levels. The ESP32 uses 3.3 V signals. Connecting a 5 V device’s TX directly to an ESP32 input can damage it.



UART on the ESP32
The ESP32 has three UART controllers. On the DevKit V1, UART0 is wired to a USB-to-UART bridge chip on the board. That is the link you use every time you upload code or open the Serial Monitor, so avoid using its pins for anything else. The other two UARTs can be routed to almost any free GPIO pins through the ESP32’s pin multiplexer (ESP32 Technical Reference Manual, n.d.).
In the Arduino framework, each UART is a HardwareSerial object:
#include <Arduino.h>

constexpr int UART2_RX = 16;   // example pins; check your pin map first
constexpr int UART2_TX = 17;

void setup() {
  Serial.begin(115200);                                  // UART0 → USB → laptop
  Serial2.begin(9600, SERIAL_8N1, UART2_RX, UART2_TX);   // e.g., a GPS module
}

void loop() {
  if (Serial.available() > 0) {        // bytes waiting in the receive buffer?
    int b = Serial.read();             // take one byte
    Serial.printf("Received 0x%02X ('%c')\n", b, b);
  }
}
The course helper iotStartSerial() wraps Serial.begin(115200) and prints a banner, which is why the Serial Monitor in every activity is set to 115200 baud.


Strengths and limits
UART is simple, needs only two wires, and every microcontroller has one. That is why it remains the standard way to talk to a development board, and why modules such as GPS receivers and cellular modems still use it.
Its limits follow from its design. It connects only two devices. It spends 20% of the line on framing. Both sides must agree on the speed in advance. Inside devices, most chip-to-chip links have moved to SPI and I²C.



SPI: the fast synchronous bus
The Serial Peripheral Interface (SPI) is a synchronous bus introduced by Motorola in the 1980s (SPI Block Guide 2003). It has no formal standard, but it is supported by almost every microcontroller and by thousands of peripherals.

Signals and topology
One controller (the ESP32) drives the bus. Three wires are shared by every device:

SCK, the clock, always driven by the controller.
COPI (MOSI), data from controller to peripheral.
CIPO (MISO), data from peripheral to controller.

Each peripheral also gets its own chip select (CS) wire. CS is active low: the controller pulls one device’s CS low to talk to it, and keeps every other CS high. A deselected peripheral must ignore the clock and release CIPO, so devices do not fight over the shared line.
On every clock pulse, the controller shifts one bit out on COPI while the selected peripheral shifts one bit back on CIPO. SPI is therefore full duplex, and the hardware inside a simple peripheral can be little more than a shift register. Because the controller generates every clock edge, a peripheral can only send data while the controller is clocking. If the controller wants to read a reply, it must keep clocking (usually by sending dummy bytes) for as many bytes as it expects.


Clock modes
Devices disagree about which clock edge marks a valid bit. Two settings describe the convention:

CPOL (clock polarity): whether the clock idles low (0) or high (1).
CPHA (clock phase): whether data is sampled on the first (0) or second (1) clock edge of each bit.




Table 5.1: The four SPI modes. Mode 0 is the most common.





Mode
CPOL
CPHA

0
0

1

1

The controller must use the mode the peripheral expects, which is given in the peripheral’s datasheet. Most devices also send the most significant bit first.


Speed
SPI has no addressing overhead and no framing bits, and its push-pull outputs switch quickly. Clock rates of 10 MHz or more are routine, which makes SPI the usual choice for displays, radios, SD cards and flash memory. The practical limit is set by the slowest device on the bus and by the length of the wires.


SPI on the ESP32
The ESP32 has four SPI controllers. Two of them (SPI0 and SPI1) are reserved for the external flash chip that holds your program. The other two, HSPI and VSPI, are free for peripherals (ESP32 Technical Reference Manual, n.d.). The kit uses VSPI on its default pins: SCK on GPIO 18, COPI on GPIO 23 and CIPO on GPIO 19. Using a controller’s default pins gives the highest clock rates; routing SPI signals to other pins through the GPIO matrix works, but lowers the maximum speed.
The kit puts two devices on this bus (Figure 5.1):

The OLED display (CS on GPIO 5) only receives data, so it never uses CIPO. It has an extra D/C pin that tells it whether each byte is a command or pixel data.
The LoRa radio (CS on GPIO 14), added in Chapter 10, both receives commands and returns data, so it uses CIPO.

Because different devices may need different speeds and modes, the Arduino SPI library groups those settings into a transaction:
#include <SPI.h>

constexpr int LORA_CS = 14;

uint8_t readRadioRegister(uint8_t reg) {
  SPI.beginTransaction(SPISettings(8000000, MSBFIRST, SPI_MODE0));
  digitalWrite(LORA_CS, LOW);          // select the radio
  SPI.transfer(reg & 0x7F);            // send the register address (top bit 0 = read)
  uint8_t value = SPI.transfer(0x00);  // clock out a dummy byte, clock in the reply
  digitalWrite(LORA_CS, HIGH);         // release the bus
  SPI.endTransaction();
  return value;
}

void setup() {
  pinMode(LORA_CS, OUTPUT);
  digitalWrite(LORA_CS, HIGH);         // every CS starts deselected
  SPI.begin(18, 19, 23);               // SCK, CIPO (MISO), COPI (MOSI)
}
Notice that reading one byte takes two transfers: the first sends the register address, and the second exists only to generate eight clock pulses so the radio can answer.


Strengths and limits
SPI is fast, full duplex and simple to implement in hardware. Its costs are wiring and coordination. Every additional device needs another CS wire. There is no acknowledgment, so the controller cannot tell whether anyone is listening. Peripherals cannot start a conversation on their own, and they cannot talk to each other.
When there are more peripherals than spare pins, designers either add a decoder chip that turns a few pins into many chip selects, or daisy-chain devices so that data shifts through one into the next. Daisy-chaining suits output-only devices such as LED drivers.



I²C: two wires, many devices
I²C (Inter-Integrated Circuit, pronounced “I-squared-C”) was created by Philips in 1982 to connect many chips inside a television using as few wires as possible. Today it is the default bus for low-speed sensors and is defined by a published specification (UM10204: I2C-bus Specification and User Manual 2021).

Two wires and an address
Every device on an I²C bus shares just two lines:

SCL, the serial clock, driven by the controller.
SDA, serial data, driven by whichever side is sending.

Instead of chip-select wires, each target has a 7-bit address. The controller begins every transaction by sending an address, and only the target with that address responds. The kit’s three I²C devices sit on the same two wires at addresses 0x76 (BMP280), 0x68 (MPU-6050) and 0x60 (ATECC608A). A few addresses are reserved by the specification, so the usable range is 0x08 to 0x77.
Many breakout boards let you choose between two addresses with a pin or a jumper. The BMP280 answers at 0x76 or 0x77 depending on its SDO pin, and the MPU-6050 at 0x68 or 0x69 depending on its AD0 pin (BMP280 Digital Pressure Sensor Datasheet, n.d.; MPU-6000 and MPU-6050 Product Specification, n.d.). That is how two identical sensors can share a bus.


Open drain and pull-up resistors
I²C outputs are open drain: a device can pull a line low, but it can never drive it high. Instead, a pull-up resistor on each line returns it to the supply voltage whenever nobody is pulling down.
This design has two important consequences:

No device can short the bus. If one device holds the line low while another releases it, the line is simply low. This is what makes acknowledgments, arbitration and clock stretching (below) safe.
The pull-ups set the speed. The rising edge is only as fast as the resistor can charge the capacitance of the wires and inputs. Larger resistors save power but slow the edges; smaller ones allow faster edges but force each device to sink more current when it pulls low. Values between about 2.2 kΩ and 10 kΩ are typical.

Most sensor breakout boards include their own pull-up resistors. When several boards share a bus, their pull-ups act in parallel, so the effective resistance drops as you add boards. That is usually harmless with two or three boards, but worth checking as a bus grows.


Transactions, ACK and NACK
An I²C transaction is built from 9-bit units: eight data bits, most significant first, followed by one acknowledge bit (Figure 5.3).

The controller sends a START condition: SDA falls while SCL is high. Data never changes while SCL is high, so this pattern is unmistakable.
The controller sends the 7-bit address and a read/write bit (0 = write, 1 = read).
The addressed target pulls SDA low during the ninth clock to acknowledge (ACK). If no device has that address, SDA stays high: a NACK.
Data bytes follow, each acknowledged by the receiver.
The controller ends with a STOP condition: SDA rises while SCL is high.

Most sensors expose their data as numbered registers. To read a register, the controller first writes the register number, then uses a repeated START (a START without a STOP in between) to switch to reading without giving up the bus.






Figure 5.3: Reading the MPU-6050’s WHO_AM_I register (0x75). The chip answers 0x68, which identifies it as an MPU-6050.



#include <Wire.h>

constexpr uint8_t MPU6050_ADDR = 0x68;
constexpr uint8_t WHO_AM_I     = 0x75;

int readRegister(uint8_t addr, uint8_t reg) {
  Wire.beginTransmission(addr);
  Wire.write(reg);                          // which register we want
  if (Wire.endTransmission(false) != 0) {   // false = repeated START, keep the bus
    return -1;                              // NACK: nobody at this address
  }
  Wire.requestFrom(addr, (uint8_t)1);       // read one byte, then STOP
  return Wire.available() ? Wire.read() : -1;
}

void setup() {
  Serial.begin(115200);
  Wire.begin(21, 22);                       // SDA, SCL
  Serial.printf("WHO_AM_I = 0x%02X\n", readRegister(MPU6050_ADDR, WHO_AM_I));
}

void loop() {}


Scanning a bus
Because a missing device answers with a NACK, the controller can discover what is connected simply by addressing every possible target and noting which ones acknowledge. This bus scan is the first thing to run on any new I²C wiring.
#include <Wire.h>

void setup() {
  Serial.begin(115200);
  Wire.begin(21, 22);
  int found = 0;
  for (uint8_t addr = 0x08; addr <= 0x77; addr++) {
    Wire.beginTransmission(addr);
    if (Wire.endTransmission() == 0) {     // 0 = the address was acknowledged
      Serial.printf("Found device at 0x%02X\n", addr);
      found++;
    }
  }
  Serial.printf("%d device(s) found\n", found);
}

void loop() {}


Speed, clock stretching and multiple controllers
I²C runs at defined speeds: 100 kHz (Standard-mode), 400 kHz (Fast-mode) and 1 MHz (Fast-mode Plus), with faster modes defined for special hardware (UM10204: I2C-bus Specification and User Manual 2021). Address bytes, acknowledgments and the slow rising edges make it much slower than SPI in practice, which is acceptable for sensors that produce a few readings per second. On the ESP32, Wire.setClock(400000) selects Fast-mode.
Open-drain outputs also make two advanced features possible:

Clock stretching. A target that needs more time can hold SCL low after a byte. The controller waits until SCL is released.
Multiple controllers. Two controllers can share a bus. If both start at once, each watches SDA while sending; the first one to send a 1 while the line reads 0 knows it has lost arbitration and backs off.



Strengths and limits
I²C needs only two wires for up to dozens of devices, confirms that each byte was received, and lets software find devices by scanning. Its costs are speed and fragility: it is half duplex, slower than SPI, sensitive to pull-up values and wire length, and a single misbehaving device can hold the whole bus low.






TipTry it on your kit: map your buses



This exercise uses the kit wiring from Stage 2 of Lab 1, and corresponds to the I²C and SPI lecture activity.

Run the bus scanner above. You should find exactly three devices: 0x60, 0x68 and 0x76. Write down what you see before going on.
Unplug the USB cable, remove the MPU-6050’s SDA wire, and scan again. Which addresses remain? Why does removing one device not break the others?
Restore the wire and run the WHO_AM_I example. Confirm that it prints 0x68.
Set the Serial Monitor to 9600 baud while the code still uses 115200. Describe what you see, and explain it using Figure 5.2.
Write a line of your choice to the OLED. Which bus carried it, and which chip-select pin went low?

A guided, step-by-step version for a lecture session is Activity 3.

title: 5  Serial Communication: UART, SPI and I²C
text:
5.3 In depth (optional)






Optional, in-depth explanation. This section goes beyond the rest of the chapter into the math and physics behind it. Nothing later in the book depends on it; skip it on a first reading.




Bit budgets and bus electrics
UART efficiency. An 8N1 frame sends 10 bits (start, 8 data, stop) for every byte, so the useful byte rate is \(\text{baud}/10\): 11 520 bytes per second at 115 200 baud.
How much baud-rate error is tolerable? The receiver synchronizes on the start bit’s falling edge and samples each bit in its middle. If the two clocks differ by a fraction \(\varepsilon\), the sampling point drifts by \(\varepsilon\) bit-times per bit. By the stop bit, about 9.5 bit-times after the edge, the drift must stay under half a bit:
\[
9.5\,\varepsilon < 0.5 \quad\Rightarrow\quad \varepsilon < 5.3\%.
\]
That is the combined error of both ends, before any allowance for slow edges or noise, so designers aim for about 2% on each side. It explains why a 9600-baud monitor on a 115 200-baud stream produces garbage rather than a slowed-down message.
I²C pull-up resistors. I²C lines are open-drain: devices only pull them low, and a pull-up resistor \(R_p\) pulls them high through the bus capacitance \(C_b\) (wires plus pins). The rise is an RC charge, and the standard measures it from 30% to 70% of \(V_{DD}\):
\[
t_r = t_{70\%} - t_{30\%} = R_pC_b\left(\ln\frac{1}{0.3} - \ln\frac{1}{0.7}\right) = R_pC_b \ln\frac{7}{3} \approx 0.847\,R_p C_b .
\]
Fast mode (400 kHz) allows \(t_r \le 300\) ns, so \(R_p \le 300\ \text{ns} / (0.847\, C_b)\); for \(C_b = 100\) pF, \(R_p \le 3.5\) kΩ. The resistor also cannot be too small, or a device cannot pull the line low enough: with a 3 mA sink and a 0.4 V low level, \(R_p \ge (3.3 - 0.4)/0.003 \approx 970\) Ω. Breakout boards each add their own pull-ups (often 4.7 kΩ or 10 kΩ), and they combine in parallel, so three modules on one bus already give 1.6–3.3 kΩ.
Transfer time on each bus. An I²C byte takes 9 clock cycles (8 data bits plus acknowledge), so a 1024-byte display frame at 400 kHz takes at least
\[
\frac{1024 \times 9}{400\,000} \approx 23\ \text{ms},
\]
capping the refresh rate near 40 frames per second before any other work. On SPI at 8 MHz, with no acknowledge bit, the same frame takes \(1024 \times 8 / 8\,000\,000 \approx 1\) ms. That factor of twenty is why the kit’s display uses SPI.
Exercise. The MPU-6050 delivers 14 bytes per sample (accelerometer, temperature, gyroscope). At 400 kHz, counting the address and register bytes, what is the highest sample rate the bus could sustain? What does that leave for the BMP280?
Sources for this section: (UM10204: I2C-bus Specification and User Manual 2021; ESP32 Technical Reference Manual, n.d.).

A few rules of thumb follow from the table:

Talking to another computer or a module with its own processor (a laptop, GPS receiver or cellular modem): UART.
Moving a lot of data quickly (displays, radios, memory cards, cameras): SPI.
Reading many slow sensors with few pins: I²C.
Running out of pins: I²C for anything slow enough; a CS decoder or daisy-chain for SPI.
Long cables: none of these three. Use a differential standard such as RS-485 or CAN, or move to a network link (Chapter 10).

title: 5  Serial Communication: UART, SPI and I²C
text:
5.5 Common pitfalls

TX connected to TX. UART lines cross over: TX goes to RX.
No common ground. Two boards powered separately must share GND for any of these buses to work.
Baud-rate mismatch. Garbled characters almost always mean the two sides disagree on speed.
7-bit versus 8-bit addresses. Some datasheets give the address already shifted left with the read/write bit included. The ATECC608A, for example, is often listed as 0xC0, which is 0x60 in the 7-bit form the Arduino Wire library expects (ATECC608A CryptoAuthentication Device Summary Datasheet, n.d.).
Two devices with the same address. The scan shows one address, but the readings are nonsense. Move one device to its alternate address.
More than one CS low at once. Two SPI peripherals drive CIPO together and both replies are corrupted. Set every CS pin high in setup() before using the bus.
The wrong SPI mode. The device answers, but with shifted or meaningless bits. Check CPOL and CPHA in its datasheet.
Trusting the silkscreen. Many SPI display modules label their data input “SDA” even though it is SPI data, not I²C. The kit’s OLED is one of them: its “SDA” pin goes to the SPI COPI line (GPIO 23), not the I²C bus.
Using reserved pins. On the ESP32, GPIO 6 to 11 connect to the flash chip and must never be used.







NoteAdvanced track





Seeing the bits. A logic analyzer captures the actual voltages on each wire and decodes them as UART, SPI or I²C frames. Inexpensive USB analyzers, used with open-source software such as PulseView/sigrok, are the fastest way to answer “is the problem in my code or my wiring?” Capture a bus scan and identify every START, address, ACK and STOP.
Logic levels. The ESP32 uses 3.3 V logic. Many older sensors and Arduino shields use 5 V. Connecting them needs a level shifter. For I²C, a bidirectional MOSFET shifter works because the bus is open drain; for SPI, use a dedicated buffer.
Bus recovery. If a controller resets in the middle of a read, a target may still be holding SDA low, waiting for clock pulses that never come. The standard fix is to toggle SCL manually up to nine times until SDA is released, then send a STOP.
Beyond these three. RS-485 carries UART-style data over a differential pair for hundreds of meters. CAN, used in vehicles and factories, adds arbitration and error handling on a differential bus. I3C is a newer successor to I²C with higher speeds, in-band interrupts and dynamic addressing.
Design review question. Your product needs a display updated 30 times per second, four environmental sensors and a radio, and the microcontroller has 10 free GPIO pins. Assign each device to a bus, count the pins, and justify any choice a reviewer might challenge.

title: 6  Sensors
text:
6.1 Why it matters
A modern smartphone contains more than a dozen sensors. A fitness band carries an accelerometer, a gyroscope, an altimeter, an optical heart-rate sensor, skin-temperature and ambient-light sensors, and a satellite-positioning receiver. A modern car has well over a hundred: cameras, ultrasonic parking sensors, wheel-speed sensors, seat-occupancy sensors that tune the airbags, battery-temperature sensors, tire-pressure sensors and more.
Sensing is what puts the “things” into the Internet of Things. Every decision a device makes, and every chart on a dashboard, is only as good as the sensor readings behind it. This chapter explains how sensors work, how to read their specifications, and how to turn raw readings into numbers you can trust.

title: 6  Sensors
text:
6.2 Concepts

What a sensor does
A sensor detects a physical quantity, or a change in one, and produces a corresponding signal that another device can use. Sensors can measure almost anything: temperature, pressure, light, sound, motion, magnetic field, humidity, flow, distance, or chemical and biological properties.
The heart of every sensor is a transducer: an element whose electrical properties change with the quantity being measured. A thermistor’s resistance changes with temperature; a photodiode’s current changes with light; a tiny silicon structure flexes under acceleration and changes its capacitance.
Between the transducer and your code there is a signal chain (Figure 6.1):






Figure 6.1: The sensor signal chain. In a smart sensor, everything inside the dashed box is on one chip.




The transducer converts the physical quantity to an electrical quantity.
Conditioning circuits amplify and filter the signal and make it suitable for conversion.
An ADC converts it to a number (Chapter 3).
Processing applies calibration, compensation and filtering.
An interface (I²C, SPI or UART, Chapter 5) delivers the result to the microcontroller.



Smart sensors
In the simplest sensors, such as a potentiometer or a thermistor, the microcontroller’s own ADC does the conversion and your code does everything else. A smart sensor (Rayes and Salam 2022) integrates the whole chain on one small chip, with its own ADC, a small processor and a digital interface. Smart sensors bring several advantages:

Self-calibration. Factory calibration coefficients are stored in the chip, and the sensor or its driver applies them automatically.
Communication. The sensor reports over a digital bus, which is far less sensitive to noise than a small analog voltage on a long wire.
Local computation. Many smart sensors average, filter, detect events (a tap, a fall, a step) or raise an interrupt when a threshold is crossed, so the main processor can sleep.
Multi-sensing. Several sensing elements share one package. The kit’s MPU-6050 combines an accelerometer, a gyroscope and a temperature sensor.

Both of the kit’s environmental and motion sensors, the BMP280 and the MPU-6050, are smart sensors on the I²C bus.


Classifying sensors
Sensors can be grouped in several useful ways (Rayes and Salam 2022):








Dimension
Options
Example

Active (needs an external supply) or passive (generates its own signal)
A thermocouple is passive; an ultrasonic range finder is active


Intrusiveness
Invasive (part of the system it measures) or non-invasive
An implanted glucose sensor versus a camera


Contact
Contact or non-contact
A thermistor on a pipe versus an infrared thermometer


Reference
Absolute or relative (measured against a reference)
Absolute pressure versus differential pressure across a filter


Output
Analog or digital
A potentiometer versus the BMP280
