Most motion and pressure sensors today are MEMS (micro-electro-mechanical systems) devices: microscopic mechanical structures etched into silicon alongside their electronics. MEMS made precise motion sensing cheap enough for every phone and wearable.


Reading a sensor’s specifications
A datasheet describes a sensor with a handful of terms that are easy to confuse:

Range: the minimum and maximum values the sensor can measure. The BMP280 measures 300 to 1100 hPa.
Resolution: the smallest change the sensor can report. A 16-bit reading across a ±2 g range has a resolution of about 0.06 mg.
Accuracy: how close a reading is to the true value.
Precision (or repeatability): how close repeated readings of the same value are to each other.
Sensitivity: how much the output changes for a given change in the input, such as 16 384 counts per g.
Offset (bias): the reading when the true input is zero.
Drift: slow change of offset or sensitivity over time or temperature.
Noise: random variation in readings, often given as a noise density or an RMS value.
Response time and sampling rate: how quickly the sensor follows a change, and how often it can produce a reading.

A sensor can be precise but inaccurate (readings tightly clustered around the wrong value) or accurate on average but imprecise (readings scattered around the right value). High resolution does not imply high accuracy: a sensor can report many digits, all of them wrong.
Calibration measures a sensor’s offset and sensitivity against a known reference and corrects for them. Many smart sensors ship with factory calibration; others, such as gyroscopes, need a quick calibration at start-up, for example by averaging readings while the device is held still.


The kit’s sensors

BMP280: pressure and temperature
The Bosch BMP280 measures barometric pressure and temperature (BMP280 Digital Pressure Sensor Datasheet, n.d.). On the kit it sits on the I²C bus at address 0x76. Internally it produces raw readings that must be combined with factory calibration coefficients stored in the chip. The Adafruit library handles this:
#include <Wire.h>
#include <Adafruit_BMP280.h>

Adafruit_BMP280 bmp;

void setup() {
  Serial.begin(115200);
  Wire.begin(21, 22);
  if (!bmp.begin(0x76)) {
    Serial.println("BMP280 not found: check wiring and address");
    while (true) delay(1000);
  }
}

void loop() {
  float tempC = bmp.readTemperature();
  float hPa   = bmp.readPressure() / 100.0f;      // Pa → hPa
  float altM  = bmp.readAltitude(1013.25f);       // sea-level reference pressure
  Serial.printf("%.2f °C  %.2f hPa  %.1f m\n", tempC, hPa, altM);
  delay(1000);
}
Pressure falls by roughly 12 Pa for every meter of height near sea level, so a pressure sensor can estimate altitude:
\[
h \approx 44\,330 \left(1 - \left(\frac{p}{p_0}\right)^{1/5.255}\right)\ \text{m}
\]
where \(p_0\) is the pressure at sea level. Because weather changes \(p_0\) by tens of hectopascals, absolute altitude estimates are only rough unless you use the local sea-level pressure. Changes in altitude, such as climbing a flight of stairs, can be detected much more reliably, because the BMP280’s relative accuracy is about ±0.12 hPa, or around ±1 m.
The temperature reading reflects the temperature of the chip, which is warmed slightly by its neighbors on the breadboard. Expect it to read a little above room temperature.


MPU-6050: acceleration and rotation
The InvenSense MPU-6050 is an inertial measurement unit (IMU) with a three-axis accelerometer and a three-axis gyroscope (MPU-6000 and MPU-6050 Product Specification, n.d.). On the kit it is at I²C address 0x68.

The accelerometer measures acceleration, including gravity. Lying flat and still, it reads about +1 g on its Z axis and 0 g on X and Y. Its default range is ±2 g, with a sensitivity of 16 384 counts per g.
The gyroscope measures the rate of rotation around each axis. Its default range is ±250 °/s, with a sensitivity of 131 counts per °/s.

Reading the MPU-6050 directly shows how a register-based smart sensor works. It starts in sleep mode, so the first step is to wake it by writing 0 to its power-management register. Then all six motion readings, plus temperature, can be read in one 14-byte burst starting at register 0x3B:
#include <Wire.h>

constexpr uint8_t MPU = 0x68;

void writeReg(uint8_t reg, uint8_t value) {
  Wire.beginTransmission(MPU);
  Wire.write(reg);
  Wire.write(value);
  Wire.endTransmission();
}

void setup() {
  Serial.begin(115200);
  Wire.begin(21, 22);
  writeReg(0x6B, 0x00);                      // PWR_MGMT_1: wake up
}

void loop() {
  Wire.beginTransmission(MPU);
  Wire.write(0x3B);                          // ACCEL_XOUT_H
  Wire.endTransmission(false);               // repeated START
  Wire.requestFrom(MPU, (uint8_t)14);

  int16_t raw[7];                            // ax, ay, az, temp, gx, gy, gz
  for (int i = 0; i < 7; i++) {
    raw[i] = (Wire.read() << 8) | Wire.read();   // big-endian, two's complement
  }
  float ax = raw[0] / 16384.0f, ay = raw[1] / 16384.0f, az = raw[2] / 16384.0f;
  float gz = raw[6] / 131.0f;
  Serial.printf("a = (%.2f, %.2f, %.2f) g   gz = %.1f °/s\n", ax, ay, az, gz);
  delay(100);
}
From the accelerometer alone, the device’s tilt can be estimated whenever it is not otherwise accelerating, because gravity then points straight down:
\[
\text{pitch} = \operatorname{atan2}\left(-a_x,\ \sqrt{a_y^2 + a_z^2}\right),\qquad
\text{roll} = \operatorname{atan2}(a_y,\ a_z)
\]



Making readings trustworthy

Sampling
How often should you read a sensor? The Nyquist criterion says you must sample at more than twice the highest frequency present in the signal to capture it faithfully. Sampling too slowly causes aliasing: fast changes masquerade as slow ones. In practice, sample several times faster than the fastest change you care about. Room temperature changes over minutes; footsteps produce accelerations of a few hertz; machine vibration can reach kilohertz.
Sampling faster than necessary wastes energy and bandwidth, which matters for battery-powered devices.


Filtering
Real readings are noisy. Two simple filters cover most needs:

A moving average of the last \(N\) readings reduces random noise by about \(\sqrt{N}\), at the cost of delay.
An exponential moving average needs only one stored value:
\[
y_k = \alpha\, x_k + (1 - \alpha)\, y_{k-1},\qquad 0 < \alpha \le 1
\]
A small \(\alpha\) smooths heavily but responds slowly; a large \(\alpha\) follows changes quickly but passes more noise.

float ema(float x) {
  static float y = NAN;
  constexpr float ALPHA = 0.2f;
  y = isnan(y) ? x : ALPHA * x + (1 - ALPHA) * y;
  return y;
}


Sensor fusion
Different sensors have complementary weaknesses. A gyroscope gives smooth, fast rotation estimates but drifts over time when integrated. An accelerometer gives a drift-free tilt reference but is disturbed by every bump. Sensor fusion combines them. The simplest example is a complementary filter:
\[
\theta_k = \beta\,(\theta_{k-1} + \omega_k\,\Delta t) + (1 - \beta)\,\theta_{\text{accel},k},\qquad \beta \approx 0.98
\]
It trusts the gyroscope over short time scales and the accelerometer over long ones. Phones, drones and wearables use more sophisticated versions, such as Kalman filters, but the idea is the same.






TipTry it on your kit: from raw counts to physics



This exercise uses Stage 2 of the kit build.

Read the BMP280 for one minute and compute the mean and standard deviation of the pressure. Then lift the kit from the floor to a table. Can you see the change?
Read the MPU-6050 with the board flat and still. Which axis reads about 1 g? Compute the gyroscope’s offsets by averaging 200 samples, and subtract them from later readings.
Tilt the board and print pitch and roll from the accelerometer. Now shake it gently. What happens to the tilt estimate?
Apply an exponential moving average to the pitch with α = 0.1 and α = 0.5. Describe the trade-off you see.
Optional: implement the complementary filter and compare it with the accelerometer-only estimate while shaking the board.

title: 6  Sensors
text:
6.3 In depth (optional)






Optional, in-depth explanation. This section goes beyond the rest of the chapter into the math and physics behind it. Nothing later in the book depends on it; skip it on a first reading.




From voltage to physics
Quantization. An \(N\)-bit ADC with reference voltage \(V_\text{ref}\) divides the input range into \(2^N\) steps of one least significant bit, \(\text{LSB} = V_\text{ref}/2^N\). For the ESP32’s 12-bit ADC over roughly 3.3 V, one LSB is about 0.8 mV. Rounding to the nearest step adds an error spread uniformly over ±½ LSB, whose standard deviation is
\[
\sigma_q = \frac{\text{LSB}}{\sqrt{12}},
\]
which gives the ideal signal-to-quantization-noise ratio \(\text{SQNR} \approx 6.02N + 1.76\) dB (74 dB for 12 bits). Real converters add their own noise and non-linearity; the ESP32’s ADC behaves more like a 9- or 10-bit converter, its effective number of bits (ENOB).
Averaging. Averaging \(M\) independent readings reduces random noise by \(\sqrt{M}\): 16 samples give a factor of 4, two extra effective bits. It does not remove systematic errors such as offset or non-linearity; those need calibration.
The potentiometer is a voltage divider. With the wiper at fraction \(x\) of the track, \(V_\text{out} = x\,V_{DD}\) regardless of the total resistance, as long as the ADC draws negligible current. A 10 kΩ potentiometer has a worst-case source resistance of 2.5 kΩ (at mid-travel), low enough for the ADC to sample accurately.
Pressure to altitude. In the standard atmosphere, pressure falls with height. A widely used approximation for the lower atmosphere is
\[
h = 44\,330 \left[ 1 - \left(\frac{p}{p_0}\right)^{1/5.255} \right]\ \text{m},
\]
where \(p_0\) is the pressure at sea level (1013.25 hPa by default). Near sea level, pressure falls about 12 Pa per metre, so the BMP280’s resolution of a few pascals corresponds to tens of centimetres. Weather changes \(p_0\) by several hectopascals a day, however, so absolute altitude needs a local reference, while changes in altitude (a floor climbed) are measured well.
Tilt from an accelerometer. At rest, an accelerometer measures only gravity. With the MPU-6050 at ±2 g, 16 384 counts represent 1 g. Pitch and roll follow from the gravity vector’s components:
\[
\theta_\text{pitch} = \operatorname{atan2}\left(-a_x,\ \sqrt{a_y^2 + a_z^2}\right), \qquad
\phi_\text{roll} = \operatorname{atan2}(a_y,\ a_z).
\]
Fusing gyro and accelerometer. The accelerometer’s angle is correct on average but noisy; the gyroscope’s integrated rate is smooth but drifts. A complementary filter combines them:
\[
\theta_k = \alpha\left(\theta_{k-1} + \omega_k\,\Delta t\right) + (1-\alpha)\,\theta_{\text{acc},k},
\]
with \(\alpha\) close to 1 (for example 0.98 at 100 Hz). It is a high-pass filter on the gyroscope and a low-pass filter on the accelerometer, with a crossover time constant \(\tau = \alpha\,\Delta t/(1-\alpha) \approx 0.5\) s.
Exercise. You average 64 ADC readings of a still potentiometer whose single readings have a standard deviation of 8 LSB. What standard deviation do you expect for the average, and how many effective bits did you gain?
Sources for this section: (BMP280 Digital Pressure Sensor Datasheet, n.d.; MPU-6000 and MPU-6050 Product Specification, n.d.; Fraden 2016).

title: 6  Sensors
text:
6.4 Design trade-offs







Decision
Considerations




Analog vs. digital (smart) sensor
Analog sensors are cheap and simple but sensitive to noise and wiring; digital sensors are calibrated and robust but cost more and need a bus.


Sampling rate
Faster sampling captures more detail but costs energy, processing and bandwidth.


On-sensor vs. on-MCU processing
Event detection on the sensor lets the MCU sleep; processing on the MCU is more flexible.


Filtering
More smoothing means less noise but more delay.


Accuracy class
Better accuracy costs money and often power. Buy only the accuracy the application needs.

title: 6  Sensors
text:
6.5 Common pitfalls

Trusting the first reading. Many sensors need a short warm-up or settling time after power-up or after waking.
Forgetting to wake the sensor. The MPU-6050 starts in sleep mode and returns zeros until it is woken.
Wrong byte order or sign. The MPU-6050 sends 16-bit two’s-complement values, high byte first.
Confusing resolution with accuracy. Many digits do not mean a correct value.
Self-heating. A temperature sensor next to a voltage regulator or a radio measures the board, not the room.
Integrating gyroscope data without correction. The angle drifts without bound.
Unit mistakes. Pa versus hPa, g versus m/s², degrees versus radians.







NoteAdvanced track





Characterizing noise. Log 10 000 gyroscope samples with the board still and plot their histogram and the Allan deviation. The Allan deviation separates white noise (which averaging removes) from bias instability (which it does not), and is the standard way to compare inertial sensors.
Sensor-hub architectures. Phones and wearables offload continuous sensing to a low-power sensor hub or to the sensor itself, so that the main processor can sleep. Modern IMUs such as the Bosch BMI270 or the ST LSM6DSO include step counters, gesture detectors and even small machine-learning cores. Compare the energy cost of counting steps on the MCU with counting them on the sensor.
Calibration in the field. Magnetometers need hard-iron and soft-iron calibration after they are mounted, because nearby metal and currents distort the field they measure. Research how a phone guides you through “figure-eight” calibration and what it is estimating.

title: 7  Actuators and the Observe–Decide–Act Loop
text:
7.1 Why it matters
Sensors let a device observe the world. Actuators let it change the world: open a valve, move a robot arm, sound an alarm, light a warning, or display a message. An IoT system that only senses is a monitoring system. One that also acts becomes a control system, and with that comes responsibility. A misread temperature produces a wrong chart; a misfired actuator can flood a basement or unlock a door.
This chapter covers the main families of actuators, how to drive them without damaging the microcontroller, and the decision loop that connects sensing to action.

title: 7  Actuators and the Observe–Decide–Act Loop
crumbs: 7  Actuators and the Observe–Decide–Act Loop

title: 7  Actuators and the Observe–Decide–Act Loop
text:
7.3 In depth (optional)






Optional, in-depth explanation. This section goes beyond the rest of the chapter into the math and physics behind it. Nothing later in the book depends on it; skip it on a first reading.




PWM, inductors and capacitors
What PWM delivers. A PWM signal switching between 0 and \(V_{DD}\) with duty cycle \(D\) has an average value \(\bar V = D\,V_{DD}\). Loads that respond slowly compared with the period (an LED seen by an eye, a motor with inertia, a heater) respond to the average. A servo is different: it reads the width of each pulse as a position command, not the average.
Resolution versus frequency. The ESP32’s LEDC peripheral counts a source clock (80 MHz by default). With \(b\) bits of resolution, the counter wraps every \(2^b\) clock ticks, so
\[
f_\text{PWM,max} = \frac{f_\text{clk}}{2^b}.
\]
At 16 bits that is \(80\times10^6 / 65\,536 \approx 1.2\) kHz, comfortably above a servo’s 50 Hz. A 20 kHz motor drive (above the range of hearing) leaves only \(\log_2(80\times10^6/20\times10^3) \approx 12\) bits.
Why motors need flyback diodes. A motor or relay coil is an inductor, whose voltage is \(V = L\,di/dt\). Switching off 200 mA through 10 mH in 1 µs would demand \(10^{-2} \times 0.2/10^{-6} = 2000\) V; in practice the voltage spikes until something breaks down, often the transistor. A diode across the coil gives the current a path to decay slowly instead.
Sizing a reservoir capacitor. When the servo starts moving, it draws a current pulse faster than the USB supply and its cable can respond. A capacitor across the rail supplies that pulse. If it must supply current \(I\) for time \(\Delta t\) while the rail sags by at most \(\Delta V\),
\[
C \ge \frac{I\,\Delta t}{\Delta V}.
\]
A 0.5 A step that the supply takes 0.5 ms to catch up with, allowing 0.5 V of sag, needs \(0.5 \times 0.5\times10^{-3}/0.5 = 500\ \mu\)F, the order of the kit’s 470 µF. A stalled servo draws its high current for much longer; no practical capacitor covers that, which is why the servo has its own 5 V rail.
Hysteresis. An alarm that turns on above 150° and off below 150° chatters when noise straddles the threshold. Use two thresholds, on above \(\theta_\text{on}\) and off below \(\theta_\text{off} < \theta_\text{on}\). The gap should exceed the peak-to-peak noise; with ±2° of noise, a 5° gap is enough.
Exercise. Your PWM drives an LED at 1 kHz with 10-bit resolution. What is the smallest change in average current you can make, if full brightness is 6 mA? Why might the LED still look non-linear across the range?
Sources for this section: (ESP32 Technical Reference Manual, n.d.; Åström and Murray 2021).

title: 7  Actuators and the Observe–Decide–Act Loop
text:
7.4 Design trade-offs







Decision
Considerations




Servo vs. stepper vs. DC motor
Servos are simple for positions within 180°; steppers give precise open-loop positioning; DC motors give continuous rotation and speed.


Relay vs. MOSFET
Relays switch AC and isolate circuits but are slow, noisy and wear out; MOSFETs are fast, silent and efficient for DC loads.


Bistable vs. monostable
Bistable actuators save energy but have no natural fail-safe state on power loss.


Local vs. remote decisions
Local loops are fast and survive network failures; remote loops can use more data.


On/off vs. proportional control
On/off is simple and suits slow processes; proportional or PID control is needed for precise, fast processes.

title: 7  Actuators and the Observe–Decide–Act Loop
text:
7.5 Common pitfalls

Powering motors from a GPIO pin or the 3.3 V rail. The board browns out and resets whenever the motor moves.
No common ground between the motor supply and the microcontroller. The control signal has no reference.
No flyback diode on relays and solenoids.
Forgetting display() on the OLED: drawing commands only change the frame buffer.
PWM channel conflicts. tone() and the servo fighting over the same LEDC channel or timer produce erratic movement.
Chattering from on/off control without hysteresis.
No fail-safe state, so a crash leaves an actuator in its last, possibly dangerous, position.







NoteAdvanced track





Tuning a PID loop. Build a simple closed loop in which the servo should point at a target angle measured by the MPU-6050 mounted on the servo horn. Implement proportional control, observe the steady-state error, then add integral and derivative terms. Document how you tuned \(K_p\), \(K_i\) and \(K_d\), and what limited the loop’s speed.
Actuator safety standards. Functional-safety standards such as IEC 61508 (general) and ISO 26262 (automotive) require a hazard analysis, defined safe states and evidence that the system reaches them. Choose an IoT actuator (a smart lock, a connected oven, an insulin pump) and write a one-page hazard analysis: what can go wrong, what is the safe state, and how is it enforced?

title: 8  Communication Models: OSI and TCP/IP
text:
8.1 Why it matters
The serial buses in Chapter 5 connect chips a few centimeters apart, on one board, under one controller. They cannot scale to billions of devices made by thousands of companies, spread across the planet and connected by every kind of medium from fiber to radio.
The internet solves that problem with layering: each layer provides one well-defined service to the layer above, and hides how it is done. A temperature reading from your kit can travel over Wi-Fi, Ethernet, fiber and a cellular link without your code knowing or caring. Understanding the layers is what lets you reason about where a problem is when “the device can’t reach the server”, and what lets you choose the right protocols for an IoT system in the chapters that follow.
crumbs: 8  Communication Models: OSI and TCP/IP

title: 8  Communication Models: OSI and TCP/IP
text:
8.2 Concepts

Protocols and layers
A network protocol defines the format and order of the messages exchanged between two or more communicating entities, and the actions taken when a message is sent or received, or when some other event happens (such as no reply arriving in time).
Human protocols work the same way. Taking a plane trip involves a sequence of layered steps: you buy a ticket, check your bag, pass security and board the plane; on arrival the steps run in reverse. Each step relies on the one below it and serves the one above. The ticket counter does not care how the plane flies.
Network designers organize protocols the same way, into a protocol stack. Each layer:

offers a service to the layer above (for example, “deliver this message to that application”);
uses the service of the layer below;
talks, conceptually, to the same layer on the other device, using that layer’s protocol.

A layer can be implemented in hardware, in software, or in both.


The OSI reference model
In the late 1970s and early 1980s, the International Organization for Standardization (ISO) defined the Open Systems Interconnection (OSI) model: seven layers meant to describe any communication system, independent of technology (Table 8.1).



Table 8.1: The seven layers of the OSI model.












#
Layer
Responsibility
Data unit
Examples




7

Message
HTTP, MQTT, SMTP


6
Presentation
Translation, compression, encryption
Message
Character encoding, TLS (partly)


5
Session
Opening, managing and closing dialogs
Message
Session setup and checkpoints


4
Transport
Process-to-process delivery
Segment (TCP) / datagram (UDP)
TCP, UDP


3
Network
Host-to-host delivery across networks: logical addressing and routing
Packet

2
Data link
Hop-to-hop delivery: framing, physical addressing, access to a shared medium
Frame
Ethernet, Wi-Fi MAC, BLE link layer


1
Physical
Moving individual bits over a medium
Bit
Voltages, light pulses, radio modulation






Some details of each layer:

The physical layer defines connectors, cables, how bits are represented as signals, the data rate and the line configuration.
The data link layer moves frames from one node to the next. It adds hardware (MAC) addresses, detects errors, and controls access to a shared medium so that devices do not all talk at once.
The network layer delivers packets from the source host to the destination host, possibly across many networks. It provides logical addresses and routing.
The transport layer delivers messages from one process to another. It adds port numbers to identify the application, and may provide segmentation and reassembly, flow control, error control and connection management.
The session layer controls the dialog between two applications, keeping it open long enough to finish and closing it afterwards.
The presentation layer makes data understandable: it translates between data representations, compresses data, and encrypts it.
The application layer provides services that applications use directly, such as transferring web pages or publishing sensor readings.



Encapsulation
As data moves down the stack on the sender, each layer adds its own header (and sometimes a trailer) carrying the information its peer needs. This is encapsulation. On the receiver, each layer reads and removes its header and passes the rest up: decapsulation (Figure 8.1).






Figure 8.1: Encapsulation: each layer wraps the data from the layer above with its own header.



A useful end-to-end example: when you send an email, the application chooses a protocol (SMTP) and passes the message down; it is segmented by the transport layer, placed in packets by the network layer, framed by the data link layer and sent as bits by the physical layer. At every router along the way, the lower layers are unwrapped and rewrapped for the next link. At the destination, the layers are unwrapped in reverse until the message reaches the recipient’s email application.


TCP/IP: the internet that won
The OSI model was developed slowly, through committees that included large telephone companies and computer vendors. Meanwhile, researchers funded by the US Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency (DARPA) built a simpler, working protocol suite, TCP/IP, and released it freely. By the 1990s, TCP/IP had become the de facto standard, and “the Internet” meant the network of networks that runs it (Russell 2013).
OSI survives as a vocabulary: engineers still say “a layer-2 switch” or “a layer-7 load balancer”. The protocols in use, however, follow the four-layer TCP/IP model (Table 8.2).



Table 8.2: The TCP/IP model and its relationship to OSI.











TCP/IP layer
Corresponding OSI layers
Main protocols
Main device




Application
5, 6, 7
HTTP, MQTT, CoAP, DNS, TLS
End hosts


Transport
4
TCP, UDP
End hosts


Internet
3
IPv4, IPv6, ICMP
Routers


Link (network access)
1, 2
Ethernet, Wi-Fi, BLE, 802.15.4
Switches, access points






TCP/IP has no separate session or presentation layers. If an application needs those services, such as encryption or compression, the application (or a library it uses, like TLS) provides them.


Four kinds of address
TCP/IP uses four kinds of address, each solving a different problem:

Physical (MAC) addresses identify a network interface on one link, such as the ESP32’s Wi-Fi interface (for example 24:6F:28:AB:CD:EF). They are only meaningful on the local link, and change at every hop as a packet is re-framed.
Logical (IP) addresses identify a host on the internet, such as 192.168.0.17 (IPv4) or 2001:db8::17 (IPv6). They normally stay the same from source to destination.
Port numbers (16-bit, 0–65535) identify a process or service on a host. Process IDs cannot do this job: they are local to one machine, and two machines may use the same ones. Ports 0–1023 are reserved for well-known services: DNS on 53, HTTP on 80, HTTPS on 443. MQTT uses 1883, or 8883 with TLS.
Names, such as host names and URLs, are what people and configuration files use. The Domain Name System (DNS) translates names into IP addresses.

Why not use MAC addresses everywhere? MAC addresses are flat: they say nothing about where a device is. Routing on them would require every router to know the location of every device in the world. IP addresses are hierarchical: their prefix identifies a network, so a router only needs to know which way to send each network’s traffic.


How a device joins a network
When your ESP32 connects to Wi-Fi, three supporting protocols do work you never see:

DHCP (Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol) gives the device an IP address, a subnet mask, a default gateway and DNS servers when it joins the network.
ARP (Address Resolution Protocol) finds the MAC address that belongs to an IP address on the local network, so frames can be addressed. IPv6 uses Neighbor Discovery for the same job.
DNS turns a name such as broker.example.org into an IP address.



NAT
There are only about 4.3 billion IPv4 addresses, far fewer than the number of connected devices. Most homes and campuses therefore use private addresses inside their network (such as 192.168.x.x or 10.x.x.x) and a single public address on the router.
The router performs network address translation (NAT). When a device sends a packet out, the router replaces its private source address and port with the router’s public address and a new port, and records the mapping in a translation table. When a reply arrives at that public port, the router looks up the table and forwards it to the right device.
NAT has a major consequence for IoT: devices behind NAT can easily start connections outward, but nothing outside can start a connection to them. This is why most IoT devices connect out to a cloud service or broker and keep that connection open, rather than running a server that the outside world connects to. IPv6, with its vast address space, removes the need for NAT, although firewalls usually still block unsolicited inbound connections.


TCP and UDP
The transport layer offers two main services:



Table 8.3: Comparing the two main transport protocols.











TCP
UDP




Connection
Connection-oriented (a handshake first)
Connectionless


Delivery
Reliable, in order, with retransmission
Best effort: datagrams may be lost, duplicated or reordered


Flow and congestion control
Yes
No


Header size
20 bytes or more
8 bytes


Typical IoT uses
HTTP, MQTT, firmware downloads
DNS, CoAP, time sync (NTP), streaming






TCP’s reliability costs time and energy: a connection needs a three-way handshake before any data flows, and every segment must be acknowledged. For a sensor that sends one small reading every ten minutes, UDP (often with a lightweight application-level acknowledgment, as in CoAP, Chapter 12) can be far more efficient. For a firmware update, where every byte must arrive, TCP is the obvious choice.


TCP/IP on the ESP32
The ESP32’s Wi-Fi driver and the lwIP TCP/IP stack implement all four layers. From the Arduino framework, joining a network and making an HTTP request takes a few lines:
#include <WiFi.h>
#include <HTTPClient.h>
#include "secrets.h"                     // WIFI_SSID, WIFI_PASSWORD, SERVER_BASE_URL

void setup() {
  Serial.begin(115200);
  WiFi.mode(WIFI_STA);                   // station (client) mode
  WiFi.begin(WIFI_SSID, WIFI_PASSWORD);  // link layer: associate with the access point
  while (WiFi.status() != WL_CONNECTED) {
    delay(250);
    Serial.print('.');
  }
  // DHCP has now given us an IP address, gateway and DNS server
  Serial.printf("\nIP %s  gateway %s  MAC %s  RSSI %d dBm\n",
                WiFi.localIP().toString().c_str(),
                WiFi.gatewayIP().toString().c_str(),
                WiFi.macAddress().c_str(),
                WiFi.RSSI());

  HTTPClient http;                                   // application layer
  http.begin(String(SERVER_BASE_URL) + "/ping");     // DNS lookup, TCP connect
  int status = http.GET();
  Serial.printf("HTTP status %d: %s\n", status, http.getString().c_str());
  http.end();
}

void loop() {}
Keep credentials in a separate secrets.h file that is excluded from version control.






TipTry it on your kit: a classroom poll over HTTP



This exercise corresponds to the classroom-poll lecture activity. Your kit acts as an HTTP client and submits an answer to a poll server; the instructor’s dashboard shows everyone’s answers.

Connect to Wi-Fi and print your IP address, gateway, MAC address and signal strength. Which of these would change if you moved to a different building? Which would not?
Use the buttons to choose an answer and send it to the server with an HTTP POST. Show the server’s response on the OLED.
For one request, identify what each TCP/IP layer contributes: the link (Wi-Fi), internet (IP addresses), transport (ports) and application (HTTP method, path, body).
Your kit has a private IP address. Explain how the server’s reply finds its way back to it.

A guided, step-by-step version for a lecture session is Activity 5.

title: 8  Communication Models: OSI and TCP/IP
text:
8.3 In depth (optional)






Optional, in-depth explanation. This section goes beyond the rest of the chapter into the math and physics behind it. Nothing later in the book depends on it; skip it on a first reading.




Overhead and delay, counted
How much of a message is payload? Each layer adds its own header. Consider a 4-byte temperature reading sent in an HTTP POST over Wi-Fi with IPv4:



Layer
Bytes added (typical)




HTTP request line and headers
≈ 150


TCP header
20 (often 32 with options)


IPv4 header
20


802.11 MAC header, LLC/SNAP, FCS
≈ 36



The payload is 4 of roughly 230 bytes, an efficiency \(\eta = \text{payload}/\text{total}\) under 2%. Before it, TCP’s three-way handshake exchanged three more packets, and the response and connection teardown add more. For a 4-byte reading, protocol choice dominates the energy bill: Chapter 12 compares MQTT and CoAP, which shrink the application header to a few bytes and avoid a new connection per reading.
Where the delay comes from. The delay of one packet across one link is the sum of four parts:
\[
d = d_\text{proc} + d_\text{queue} + \underbrace{\frac{L}{R}}_{d_\text{trans}} + \underbrace{\frac{s}{v}}_{d_\text{prop}},
\]
where \(L\) is the packet length in bits, \(R\) the link rate, \(s\) the distance and \(v\) the signal speed (about \(2\times10^8\) m/s in cable). A 230-byte frame at 1 Mb/s takes 1.8 ms to transmit; it travels 300 m of air in 1 µs. On short links, transmission and queueing dominate; across continents, propagation does (about 40 ms each way across the United States in fibre).
Round trips set the floor. A new HTTPS request needs one round trip for TCP’s handshake, one for TLS 1.3’s, and one for the request itself: at least three round-trip times (RTT). With a 50 ms RTT to a cloud region, the minimum is 150 ms before the server even processes the reading. Keeping connections open, or using UDP-based protocols, removes most of it.
The bandwidth-delay product. A sender can only keep a link busy if it has \(R \times \text{RTT}\) bits in flight. At 10 Mb/s and 50 ms RTT that is 62.5 kB; a small device with a 4 kB TCP window gets at most \(4096 \times 8 / 0.05 \approx 655\) kb/s, whatever the link speed.
Exercise. In Activity 5’s extension you measured the POST round-trip time. Using the formula above, estimate how much of it is Wi-Fi transmission time, and suggest where the rest comes from.
Sources for this section: (Kurose and Ross 2021).

Decision
Considerations




TCP vs. UDP
Reliability and simplicity versus latency, overhead and energy


Device connects out vs. accepts connections
Outbound connections work through NAT and firewalls; inbound ones usually do not

title: 8  Communication Models: OSI and TCP/IP
text:
8.5 Common pitfalls

Confusing MAC and IP addresses. MAC addresses are local to a link; IP addresses are end to end.
Expecting to reach a device behind NAT from outside. Design for outbound connections.
Hard-coding IP addresses. Use names and DNS; addresses change.
Committing Wi-Fi passwords or API keys to a public repository.
Blocking forever on the network. Always set timeouts, and handle the case where Wi-Fi drops after it connected.
Enterprise Wi-Fi. Campus networks often use WPA2-Enterprise (802.1X) or captive portals, which small devices cannot easily join. A dedicated IoT network or a travel router is often needed.







NoteAdvanced track





Watching the layers. Run Wireshark on a laptop connected to the same access point (or on a mirrored port) while your kit makes an HTTP request. Identify the DHCP exchange, the ARP request, the DNS query, the TCP three-way handshake, the HTTP request and response, and the TCP connection teardown. How many packets and bytes did it take to send a single poll answer?
Overhead budget. A sensor sends 20 bytes of data. Estimate the total bytes on the air for that reading when sent (a) as an HTTP POST over a new TCP connection, (b) as an MQTT publish over an existing connection, and (c) as a single UDP datagram. What does that imply for battery life?

title: 9  IoT Network Requirements and the Protocol Stack
text:
9.1 Why it matters
The TCP/IP stack was designed for computers with plenty of memory, wired connections and a person waiting at a screen. It works well for laptops and phones, and for an ESP32 on campus Wi-Fi. But many IoT devices are much smaller: a battery-powered sensor with 10 KB of RAM, a radio that can send only a few hundred bytes per second, and a duty cycle of a fraction of a percent. Others sit in factories or vehicles, where a message that arrives a few milliseconds late is as bad as one that never arrives.
Following the analysis of Rayes and Salam (Rayes and Salam 2022), this chapter sets out what IoT asks of a network, and introduces the layered protocol stack that the rest of Part III fills in.
crumbs: 9  IoT Network Requirements and the Protocol Stack

title: 9  IoT Network Requirements and the Protocol Stack
text:
9.2 Concepts

Requirement 1: support for constrained devices
The traditional internet assumes hosts with fast processors, large memories and mains power. Many IoT devices have none of these. RFC 7228 defines three classes of constrained device by their memory (Bormann et al. 2014):



Table 9.1: Classes of constrained devices (Bormann et al. 2014).











Class
RAM (data)
Flash (code)
What it can run




Class 0 (C0)
≪ 10 KB
≪ 100 KB
Cannot run an IP stack securely; needs a gateway or proxy


Class 1 (C1)
≈ 10 KB
≈ 100 KB
A constrained IP stack with CoAP over UDP, but not HTTP and TLS comfortably


Class 2 (C2)
≈ 50 KB
≈ 250 KB
Most standard protocols, with care






The ESP32, with 520 KB of RAM and megabytes of flash, is well beyond Class 2. But the coin-cell sensors, smart locks and wireless switches that make up much of the IoT are Class 0 or 1.
Energy is often a tighter limit than memory. A radio typically uses far more power than the processor, so every byte sent, every acknowledgment and every second spent listening costs battery life. Constrained devices therefore need protocols with small headers, few round trips, and support for sleeping, since a device that is asleep cannot answer a packet.


Requirement 2: massive scalability
Tens of billions of devices stress the network in four ways.
Addressing. IPv4 has about 4.3 billion addresses, fewer than the number of IoT devices already deployed. Devices are hidden behind NAT and gateways (Chapter 8), which works but makes them hard to reach directly. IPv6, with 128-bit addresses, can give every device its own globally unique address.
Credentials and provisioning. Every device needs network credentials and an identity, and nobody can configure billions of devices by hand. Many devices have no keyboard or screen. IoT systems need zero-touch or low-touch provisioning: automated ways to get credentials onto a device and register it with a service. Common approaches for Wi-Fi devices include:

a temporary access point: the device starts its own Wi-Fi network and serves a configuration web page (the WiFiManager library does this on the ESP32);
BLE provisioning: a phone app sends the credentials over Bluetooth Low Energy (ESP-IDF includes this);
QR codes printed on the device, carrying a setup code that a phone app uses to commission it (Matter uses this, Chapter 13).

The control plane. Network protocols can be divided into the data plane, which carries the messages themselves, and the control plane, which discovers the topology, reports link health, sets up and tears down sessions, maintains quality of service and reacts to faults. When a network grows from hundreds to millions of devices, the control plane must scale with it, without flooding the network with management traffic.
Wireless spectrum. Most IoT devices are wireless, and the radio spectrum is finite and shared. As devices multiply, and each sends more data, the unlicensed bands, especially 2.4 GHz where Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, Zigbee and Thread all live, become crowded. Spectrum is sometimes called the most valuable real estate nobody can see. Protocols must coexist, retransmit gracefully and stay quiet when they have nothing to say.


Requirement 3: determinism
Many IoT applications only need data to arrive “soon”. Some need it to arrive within a guaranteed time. A motion-control loop in a factory, a vehicle’s braking system or a remote surgical robot fails if a packet is late.
A deterministic network is one where the worst-case latency and the jitter (variation in latency) of the messages that matter can be calculated in advance from a model of the network. Ordinary internet traffic is not deterministic: packets queue behind other traffic, and Wi-Fi devices wait for a quiet channel.
Achieving determinism requires precise time synchronization across devices, scheduled transmission slots, and quality-of-service reservations along the path. Standards such as IEEE Time-Sensitive Networking (TSN) for Ethernet and the IETF’s DetNet bring these properties to IP-based networks, and the scheduled channel-hopping mode of IEEE 802.15.4 (TSCH) does the same for low-power wireless.


Requirement 4: security and privacy
In 2016, the Mirai botnet scanned the internet for IoT devices, mostly cameras and video recorders running a stripped-down Linux, that still used factory-default usernames and passwords. It logged in, installed itself, and used hundreds of thousands of infected devices to launch distributed denial-of-service attacks. One attack on the DNS provider Dyn made many major websites unreachable for hours (Antonakakis et al. 2017).
Mirai used no clever exploit. It succeeded because the devices were exposed to the internet with default credentials and no way to update them. IoT networks need:

lightweight but strong cryptography that constrained devices can run: AES for encryption, SHA-2 for hashing, elliptic-curve cryptography for keys and signatures, and a good random number generator. The ESP32 has hardware accelerators for AES, SHA, RSA and big-number arithmetic, and a hardware random number generator;
authentication and authorization suited to devices without users;
privacy, because IoT data often reveals personal behavior: when someone is home, how they sleep, where they drive. Identity management should allow devices and data to be decoupled from their owner’s identity, while still letting the owner prove ownership.

Part IV covers these topics in depth.


Requirement 5: application interoperability
Two devices can share a network and still fail to understand each other. A light switch from one company and a bulb from another may both speak IP, but unless they agree on what “turn on” looks like, they cannot cooperate. IoT needs agreement not only on how bytes move but on what they mean. Chapter 13 is devoted to this problem.


The IoT protocol stack
To meet these requirements, the IoT uses a variant of the TCP/IP stack (Figure 9.1). Two changes stand out.






Figure 9.1: The IoT protocol stack compared with the TCP/IP stack. The chapter that covers each layer is shown on the right.




The lower layers gain constrained options. Alongside Wi-Fi and Ethernet, the link layer includes low-power radios such as Bluetooth Low Energy, IEEE 802.15.4 (used by Zigbee and Thread), LoRa and cellular IoT (LTE-M and NB-IoT). The internet layer adds adaptation layers such as 6LoWPAN, which compress IPv6 to fit small radio frames, and routing protocols designed for lossy networks, such as RPL.
The application layer splits in two.

Application protocols define how messages are exchanged: HTTP, CoAP, MQTT and others (Chapter 12).
Application services define what the messages mean: common data models, device descriptions and interaction patterns, so that devices from different makers interoperate (Chapter 13).


The IP layer in the middle acts as a normalization layer. As long as everything above and below speaks IP, any application protocol can run over any link technology, and each layer can evolve independently.
Not every IoT system uses IP end to end. Classic Bluetooth, LoRaWAN and Zigbee devices use their own stacks and reach the internet through a gateway that translates between them and IP. Newer standards, such as Thread, bring IPv6 all the way to the device.






TipTry it on your kit: provisioning without hard-coded credentials



Until now your Wi-Fi password has been compiled into the firmware in secrets.h.

List three problems with hard-coding credentials in a product shipped to thousands of customers.
Add the WiFiManager library to a project. On first boot, the kit should start an access point; connect to it with your phone and enter your network’s credentials. After a reset, it should reconnect automatically.
Where are the credentials stored now? Who could read them if they had the device in hand?
Add a “factory reset”: holding both buttons at power-up erases the stored credentials.

title: 9  IoT Network Requirements and the Protocol Stack
text:
9.3 In depth (optional)






Optional, in-depth explanation. This section goes beyond the rest of the chapter into the math and physics behind it. Nothing later in the book depends on it; skip it on a first reading.




The limits every radio lives within
Shannon’s capacity. No modulation scheme, however clever, can carry more than
\[
C = B \log_2\left(1 + \frac{S}{N}\right)\ \text{bits per second}
\]
over a channel of bandwidth \(B\) with signal-to-noise ratio \(S/N\) (as a ratio, not in dB). The formula explains the families in this chapter:

A 20 MHz Wi-Fi channel at 25 dB SNR (\(S/N \approx 316\)) is capped at \(20\times10^6 \log_2 317 \approx 166\) Mb/s. Wide channel, strong signal, high rate.
A 125 kHz LoRa channel at −10 dB SNR (\(S/N = 0.1\)) is capped at \(125\times10^3 \log_2 1.1 \approx 17\) kb/s. LoRa trades almost all of that capacity away to decode signals below the noise floor, which is what gives it range.

To get more bits, you can widen the channel (more spectrum, more noise collected, often a regulatory limit) or raise the SNR (more power, better antennas, shorter distance).
Noise floor. Thermal noise in a bandwidth \(B\) is \(N = kTB\); at room temperature that is \(-174\ \text{dBm/Hz} + 10\log_{10} B\). A 125 kHz channel has a floor of \(-174 + 51 = -123\) dBm, a 20 MHz channel \(-174 + 73 = -101\) dBm, before the receiver adds its own noise figure (typically 6 dB). Narrow channels hear weaker signals.
Energy per bit. For battery devices the useful metric is not the bit rate but the energy spent per delivered bit, \(E_b = P_\text{tx}/R\), plus the energy of waking up, joining and waiting. A radio at 100 mW and 1 Mb/s spends 100 nJ per bit; one at 50 mW and 5 kb/s spends 10 µJ per bit, 100 times more per bit, yet may still win for a 20-byte daily report because it needs no association, no IP stack and no keep-alive traffic.
Exercise. A 1 MHz channel offers 10 dB of SNR. What is its Shannon capacity? How much SNR would you need to double it, and what does that say about adding power as a way to buy throughput?
Sources for this section: (Shannon 1948).

title: 9  IoT Network Requirements and the Protocol Stack
text:
9.5 Common pitfalls

Assuming every device can run TLS and HTTP. Many cannot; choose protocols for the smallest device in the system.
Ignoring the cost of listening. A radio that listens continuously can drain a battery faster than one that transmits occasionally.
Treating the 2.4 GHz band as empty. In a dorm or office it is crowded; test in realistic conditions.
Shipping default passwords. Mirai is the textbook consequence.
Designing provisioning last. How a device gets its credentials shapes the whole user experience and much of its security.







NoteAdvanced track

title: 10  The Link Layer: Short and Long Range
text:
10.1 Why it matters
The link layer is where an IoT device meets the physical world of radio waves and wires, and it is usually where most of the device’s energy goes. Transmitting a packet over Wi-Fi can take more energy than a full second of computation; repairing lost transmissions with retries can account for most of the energy spent on communication.
There is no single best link technology. A wireless earbud, a smart lock, a soil sensor on a farm and a robot on a factory floor need very different combinations of range, data rate, latency, power and cost. This chapter surveys the main options and gives you a framework for choosing among them.
crumbs: 10  The Link Layer: Short and Long Range

title: 10  The Link Layer: Short and Long Range
text:
10.2 Concepts

What IoT asks of the link layer
Four groups of characteristics shape the choice of link technology (Rayes and Salam 2022):

Device characteristics. How much energy the device has, and how much processing and memory it can spend on the radio stack. For many devices, communication costs more energy than everything else combined, so low-power radios are essential.
Traffic characteristics. Some devices send short, occasional bursts (a door sensor); others send continuous streams (a camera). Some applications tolerate loss and delay (weather monitoring); others need guaranteed, bounded latency (engine control). The same device can face different requirements in different applications.
Access characteristics. Wired or wireless, mobile or stationary, short range or long range.
Scalability characteristics. Whether to build your own network (Wi-Fi, Zigbee, LoRa) or rent one (cellular), and whether to use a star topology, where every device talks to a central hub, or a mesh, where devices relay each other’s traffic. Meshes extend coverage but add forwarding delay, and they converge more slowly as they grow.



Energy and duty cycling
The ESP32 illustrates how much a radio costs and how sleep modes save it. Approximate figures for the ESP32 chip are (ESP32 Series Datasheet, n.d.):



Table 10.1: ESP32 power modes. Figures are for the chip; a development board’s USB bridge, regulator and LEDs add several milliamperes.





Mode
What is running
Approximate current




Active, Wi-Fi transmitting
CPU and radio
160–260 mA


Active, receiving or listening
CPU and radio
80–90 mA


Modem sleep
CPU on, radio off between beacons
≈ 3–20 mA


Light sleep
CPU paused (clock-gated), RAM kept
≈ 0.8 mA


Deep sleep
Only the RTC domain and its memory
≈ 10 µA


Hibernation
Only an RTC timer
≈ 2.5 µA






Light sleep uses clock gating: the clock is stopped to most of the chip, so its logic stops switching and stops consuming dynamic power, but its state is preserved. Deep sleep powers down the CPU, most of the RAM and the digital peripherals, leaving only the real-time-clock (RTC) controller, its peripherals and a small RTC memory. Waking from deep sleep is like a reset: setup() runs again. Variables marked RTC_DATA_ATTR survive.
RTC_DATA_ATTR uint32_t bootCount = 0;      // kept in RTC memory across deep sleep

void setup() {
  Serial.begin(115200);
  bootCount++;
  Serial.printf("Boot #%lu: measure, transmit, sleep\n", bootCount);
  // ... read the sensor and send the reading here ...
  esp_sleep_enable_timer_wakeup(60ULL * 1000000ULL);   // wake in 60 s
  esp_deep_sleep_start();                              // never returns
}

void loop() {}                                         // never reached
Battery life follows from the average current:
\[
\text{battery life} = \frac{\text{capacity}}{I_{avg}},\qquad
I_{avg} = \sum_i I_i \cdot \frac{t_i}{T}
\]
For a 1 300 mAh battery:

Always active at 250 mA: 1 300 / 250 ≈ 5.2 hours.
Modem sleep, active 50 ms of every second at 250 mA and in modem sleep (10 mA) the rest: \(I_{avg} = 250 \times 0.05 + 10 \times 0.95 = 22\) mA, so about 59 hours.
Hibernation, active 4 ms of every second at 250 mA and hibernating at 2.5 µA the rest: \(I_{avg} \approx 1.0\) mA, so roughly 54 days.

The lesson is that battery life is set almost entirely by how long the radio is on. Sending less often, sending less data, and reconnecting quickly matter far more than optimizing code.


IEEE 802.15.4: low-rate personal area networks
IEEE 802.15.4 defines the physical and MAC layers for low-rate wireless personal area networks: low cost, low power and low data rate, with battery lives of months to years. Its main features are:

operation in unlicensed bands: 868 MHz (Europe, one channel), 902–928 MHz (North America) and 2.4 GHz worldwide (16 channels at 250 kbit/s);
ranges from tens of meters indoors to around a kilometer outdoors with line of sight;
acknowledged frames for reliability, with frames of at most 127 bytes.

802.15.4 is the foundation for several complete stacks: Zigbee (widely used in lighting and home automation), Thread (an IPv6-based mesh used by Matter, Chapter 13), WirelessHART and ISA100.11a (industrial), and 6LoWPAN (Chapter 11).
An 802.15.4 network has three kinds of device:

a coordinator, the most capable node and the root of the network, which chooses the channel, assigns the network identifier and allocates addresses;
routers, which relay traffic and buffer messages for sleeping devices;
end devices, which know only enough to talk to their parent and can sleep most of the time.

These devices can be arranged in three topologies:



Table 10.2: 802.15.4 topologies.












Topology
Description
Strengths
Weaknesses
Typical use




Star
All devices talk to one coordinator
Simple and cheap; end devices can sleep
Single point of failure; range limited to one hop
Smart home, peripherals, health monitors


Mesh
Any device can relay for any other within range
Self-organizing and self-healing; multipath reliability
Forwarding delay; routers must stay awake
Agriculture, environmental monitoring, building automation


Cluster-tree
Hierarchical mesh; routers connect only through parents
Covers large areas with simple routing
Longer latency; less redundancy
Large sensor deployments






The TSCH (time-slotted channel hopping) mode, introduced in IEEE 802.15.4e, synchronizes all nodes to a shared schedule of time slots, and changes radio channel on every slot. Synchronization lets nodes sleep until their slot, which saves energy; channel hopping means interference on one frequency only affects some transmissions, which improves reliability. TSCH is the basis of deterministic low-power industrial networks.


Bluetooth
Bluetooth (originally IEEE 802.15.1, now maintained by the Bluetooth SIG) operates in the 2.4 GHz band between 2 402 and 2 480 MHz. It uses frequency hopping: devices change channel up to 1 600 times per second, which reduces the impact of interference from Wi-Fi, microwave ovens and other devices sharing the band.
Bluetooth Classic (BR/EDR) organizes devices into piconets: one central device (historically called the master) and up to seven active peripherals that share its clock and hopping sequence. Piconets can be linked into larger scatternets. Classic Bluetooth suits continuous streams such as audio, but discovery and connection maintenance keep the radio busy, which limits battery life.
Bluetooth Low Energy (BLE), introduced in Bluetooth 4.0, is a separate, much simpler protocol designed for low power. Its main concepts are:

Advertising. A device broadcasts short packets on three dedicated channels to announce itself. Beacons do nothing else; many sensors simply put their readings in their advertisements.
Connections. A central device (such as a phone) can connect to a peripheral. Both then wake only at agreed connection intervals, typically every 7.5 ms to 4 s, and sleep in between.
GATT. Connected devices exchange data through the Generic Attribute Profile. A peripheral exposes services, each containing characteristics (values with properties such as read, write and notify). Services and characteristics are identified by UUIDs; standard ones, such as the Heart Rate service, have short 16-bit UUIDs defined by the Bluetooth SIG.

Later versions added features important for IoT: Bluetooth 5 introduced a 2 Mbit/s mode and a long-range coded PHY; Bluetooth Mesh supports many-to-many networks; and Bluetooth 5.1 and later added direction finding and, more recently, channel sounding for distance measurement.
The original ESP32 supports Bluetooth 4.2, both Classic and BLE. A minimal BLE peripheral that exposes the potentiometer as a readable, notifying characteristic looks like this:
#include <BLEDevice.h>
#include <BLEServer.h>
#include <BLE2902.h>
#include "iot_pins.h"

#define SERVICE_UUID "6e400001-b5a3-f393-e0a9-e50e24dcca9e"   // example custom UUIDs
#define POT_UUID     "6e400002-b5a3-f393-e0a9-e50e24dcca9e"

BLECharacteristic* potChar;

void setup() {
  BLEDevice::init("IoT-Kit");
  BLEServer* server = BLEDevice::createServer();
  BLEService* service = server->createService(SERVICE_UUID);
  potChar = service->createCharacteristic(
      POT_UUID, BLECharacteristic::PROPERTY_READ | BLECharacteristic::PROPERTY_NOTIFY);
  potChar->addDescriptor(new BLE2902());          // lets clients enable notifications
  service->start();
  BLEDevice::getAdvertising()->addServiceUUID(SERVICE_UUID);
  BLEDevice::startAdvertising();
}

void loop() {
  uint16_t value = analogRead(IoTPins::POT_ADC);
  potChar->setValue(value);                       // 2 bytes, little-endian
  potChar->notify();
  delay(500);
}
A generic BLE explorer app on a phone (such as nRF Connect) can now discover the kit, connect and subscribe to the value. Lab 4 builds a BLE step counter on this foundation.


Wi-Fi
Wi-Fi (IEEE 802.11) offers high data rates and uses infrastructure that already exists in most buildings, which makes it the most common link for IoT devices with mains power (IoT Analytics 2025). Its drawbacks for battery-powered devices are high transmit power, the time needed to associate and obtain an address, and the need to wake regularly to hear the access point’s beacons.
Two variants address some of these drawbacks:

ESP-NOW is a connectionless protocol from Espressif that sends short packets (up to 250 bytes) directly between ESP devices using the Wi-Fi radio, with no access point. It supports encrypted and unencrypted peers and delivery callbacks. It is ideal for simple device-to-device control, such as a remote button that switches a light, but it is proprietary and limited to a small number of encrypted peers.
Wi-Fi HaLow (IEEE 802.11ah) moves Wi-Fi to the sub-GHz bands (902–928 MHz in the US) for longer range (around 1 km outdoors) and better penetration through walls. It supports thousands of stations per access point, longer sleep periods and smaller headers, with data rates from about 150 kbit/s to tens of Mbit/s.

Newer mainstream Wi-Fi standards also help IoT: Wi-Fi 6 (802.11ax) adds target wake time, which lets a device negotiate when it will next wake, so it can sleep through beacons.


Long range: LPWANs
Low-power wide-area networks (LPWANs) trade data rate for range and battery life. They can reach several kilometers in cities and further in open country, with batteries lasting years, but they carry only a few bytes per message and a limited number of messages per day.

LoRa and LoRaWAN
LoRa is a radio modulation (the physical layer) developed by Semtech. It uses chirp spread spectrum: each symbol is a frequency sweep, which can be decoded even below the noise floor. Its key parameter is the spreading factor (SF7 to SF12). Each step up roughly doubles the time on air and adds range; SF7 at 125 kHz bandwidth carries about 5.5 kbit/s, while SF12 carries under 300 bit/s. In North America LoRa uses the 902–928 MHz band (US915), and in Europe the 863–870 MHz band (EU868), where regulations limit each device to a small duty cycle.
LoRaWAN is the MAC and network protocol built on LoRa, maintained by the LoRa Alliance (LoRaWAN Specification, n.d.). Its main features are:

a star-of-stars topology: end devices transmit to any gateways in range; gateways are simple bridges that forward everything to a network server, which removes duplicates, manages devices and routes data to application servers. The intelligence is in the server, so devices stay simple;
device classes that trade latency for energy: Class A devices listen only briefly after each uplink (lowest power); Class B devices also open scheduled receive windows; Class C devices listen continuously (mains-powered actuators);
adaptive data rate, which picks the fastest spreading factor that reliably reaches a gateway;
built-in security, with separate network and application session keys derived when a device joins (typically over the air, with OTAA).

The kit’s RFM95W module (Semtech SX1276) speaks raw LoRa. Without a LoRaWAN network, two kits can talk directly, point to point:
#include <SPI.h>
#include <LoRa.h>          // arduino-LoRa library
#include "iot_pins.h"

void setup() {
  Serial.begin(115200);
  LoRa.setPins(IoTPins::LORA_CS, IoTPins::LORA_RST, IoTPins::LORA_G0);
  if (!LoRa.begin(915E6)) {                // US915 band
    Serial.println("LoRa init failed: check wiring");
    while (true) delay(1000);
  }
  LoRa.setSpreadingFactor(7);
  LoRa.setSyncWord(0x34);                  // pick a team-specific value to avoid crosstalk
}

void loop() {
  LoRa.beginPacket();
  LoRa.print("beacon team-07 ");
  LoRa.print(millis() / 1000);
  LoRa.endPacket();                        // blocks until sent

  int size = LoRa.parsePacket();           // anything received?
  if (size) {
    String msg;
    while (LoRa.available()) msg += (char)LoRa.read();
    Serial.printf("RX '%s' RSSI %d dBm SNR %.1f dB\n",
                  msg.c_str(), LoRa.packetRssi(), LoRa.packetSnr());
  }
  delay(5000);
}


Cellular IoT
Cellular networks offer wide coverage without building infrastructure, at the cost of a subscription and higher module prices. Two standards are designed for IoT:

LTE-M (LTE Cat-M1): up to about 1 Mbit/s, supports mobility and voice, suited to trackers and wearables.
NB-IoT (narrowband IoT): tens of kbit/s, excellent building penetration, very low power, suited to static meters and sensors.

Both support power saving mode (PSM) and extended discontinuous reception (eDRX), which let a device sleep for hours while remaining registered. Many older devices rely on 2G and 3G networks, which carriers are shutting down; new designs should use LTE-M, NB-IoT or 5G variants such as RedCap.


Other LPWANs
Sigfox offered an ultra-narrowband network with a very small daily message allowance, and is now operated by UnaBiz. Other options include Wi-SUN (used by utilities for smart meters), Wireless M-Bus (metering in Europe) and mioty.



Wired: time-sensitive networking
Not every IoT link is wireless. Factories and vehicles use Ethernet extended with IEEE Time-Sensitive Networking (TSN) standards. TSN combines:

precise time synchronization (IEEE 802.1AS, a profile of the Precision Time Protocol) to better than a microsecond;
scheduled and shaped forwarding (for example IEEE 802.1Qbv and 802.1Qav), so that time-critical traffic gets guaranteed, bounded latency even on links shared with video or file transfers;
stream reservation and redundant paths (IEEE 802.1CB) for reliability.

Targets in industrial automation reported in the literature (Rayes and Salam 2022) are on the order of microseconds of latency within a machine cell and around 100 µs across a factory.

title: 10  The Link Layer: Short and Long Range
text:
10.3 In depth (optional)






Optional, in-depth explanation. This section goes beyond the rest of the chapter into the math and physics behind it. Nothing later in the book depends on it; skip it on a first reading.




Link budgets and time on air
Free-space path loss. In free space, received power falls with the square of distance and with the square of frequency (for fixed-gain antennas). In decibels, with \(d\) in metres and \(f\) in hertz,
\[
\text{FSPL} = 20\log_{10} d + 20\log_{10} f - 147.55\ \text{dB}.
\]
At 915 MHz the loss over 1 km is \(60 + 179.2 - 147.6 \approx 91.7\) dB; at 2.4 GHz it is about 8.4 dB more. Real environments lose more, and a log-distance model captures it with an exponent \(n\) (2 in free space, roughly 2.7–3.5 in towns, 4–6 indoors through walls):
\[
PL(d) = PL(d_0) + 10\,n \log_{10}\frac{d}{d_0}.
\]
The link budget. A link works if
\[
P_\text{tx} + G_\text{tx} + G_\text{rx} - PL - L_\text{misc} \ge S_\text{rx},
\]
where \(S_\text{rx}\) is the receiver sensitivity. For an SX1276 at 14 dBm with unity-gain antennas, sensitivity is roughly −123 dBm at SF7 and −137 dBm at SF12 (125 kHz). The difference between transmit power and sensitivity, the maximum coupling loss, is 137 dB at SF7 and 151 dB at SF12. Every 6 dB of extra budget doubles the free-space range; with \(n = 3\), it multiplies range by \(10^{6/30} \approx 1.6\).
LoRa time on air. A chirp spread-spectrum symbol at spreading factor SF and bandwidth BW lasts \(T_s = 2^{SF}/BW\). Semtech’s formula for the number of payload symbols, for a payload of PL bytes, coding rate \(4/(4+CR)\), CRC on (\(\text{CRC} = 1\)), explicit header (\(IH = 0\)) and low-data-rate optimization off (\(DE = 0\)), is
\[
n_\text{payload} = 8 + \max\left(\left\lceil \frac{8PL - 4SF + 28 + 16\,\text{CRC} - 20\,IH}{4\,(SF - 2DE)} \right\rceil (CR + 4),\ 0\right),
\]
and the preamble of \(n_p\) symbols adds \((n_p + 4.25)\,T_s\).
For Activity 6’s 23-byte beacon at SF7, BW 125 kHz, CR = 1 (4/5) and an 8-symbol preamble: \(T_s = 1.024\) ms; the fraction is \(200/28 = 7.14\), rounded up to 8, times 5 gives 40, so \(n_\text{payload} = 48\). Time on air is \((12.25 + 48) \times 1.024 \approx 62\) ms. At SF12, \(T_s = 32.8\) ms, low-data-rate optimization becomes mandatory (\(DE = 1\)), and the same packet takes about 1.5 s: the range costs airtime, and airtime costs energy and channel capacity.
Duty-cycle arithmetic. In Europe’s 868 MHz bands many sub-bands limit each device to 1% of the time: 36 s per hour, or about 580 of these SF7 packets but only about 24 at SF12. North American rules for 902–928 MHz instead limit the dwell time on a channel (400 ms for many configurations), which an SF12 packet of this size already exceeds.
Exercise. Two kits are 300 m apart in a town (\(n = 3\), \(PL(1\,\text{m}) = 31.7\) dB at 915 MHz). Is SF7 enough? What margin do you have?
Sources for this section: (Friis 1946; SX1276/77/78/79 Datasheet: 137 MHz to 1020 MHz Low Power Long Range Transceiver, n.d.; LoRa Modem Designer’s Guide (AN1200.13) 2013).

10.4 Design trade-offs







Decision
Considerations




Range vs. data rate vs. power
You can usually have two of the three


Own network vs. carrier network
Building your own avoids subscription fees but requires deploying and maintaining gateways


Star vs. mesh
Stars are simple and let end devices sleep; meshes extend coverage but need always-on routers


Licensed vs. unlicensed spectrum
Licensed (cellular) bands are managed and predictable; unlicensed bands are free but shared


Standard vs. proprietary
Standards (BLE, Thread, LoRaWAN) bring interoperability; proprietary protocols (ESP-NOW) can be simpler but lock you in

title: 10  The Link Layer: Short and Long Range
text:
10.5 Common pitfalls

Estimating battery life from the chip’s datasheet only. Regulators, USB bridges, LEDs and sensors on the board often draw more than the chip in deep sleep.
Ignoring retransmissions. Lost packets cost energy twice.
Using a European LoRa frequency in the US, or vice versa. Hardware and frequency plans are regional.
Exceeding duty-cycle or dwell-time limits in unlicensed bands, which can make a device illegal to operate.
Operating a LoRa module without an antenna. It can damage the transmitter.
Relying on 2G/3G modules in new designs.
Testing radios only on a desk. Walls, people, metal and other radios change everything.







NoteAdvanced track





Link budget. A link works if transmit power plus antenna gains, minus path loss, exceeds the receiver’s sensitivity by a margin. With free-space path loss \(\text{FSPL(dB)} = 20\log_{10}(d) + 20\log_{10}(f) - 147.55\) (meters and hertz), compute the free-space range of a 915 MHz LoRa link with +14 dBm transmit power, 0 dBi antennas and −130 dBm sensitivity. Then explain why real-world range is far shorter.
LoRaWAN on campus. Community networks such as The Things Network provide free LoRaWAN gateways in many cities. Register a device, join it over the air with OTAA, and compare the effort and the result with the point-to-point exercise above. What do you gain from the network server?
Coexistence. Wi-Fi channel 1, BLE advertising channels and Thread channel 11 all overlap near 2.4 GHz. Design a test that measures BLE packet loss while a nearby laptop streams video over Wi-Fi, and propose mitigations.

title: 11  The Internet Layer: 6LoWPAN and RPL
text:
11.1 Why it matters
Early sensor networks and home-automation systems used proprietary protocols. Each vendor’s devices formed an island, reachable from the internet only through that vendor’s gateway, which translated every message. When the vendor changed its product line or went out of business, the island was stranded.
The alternative is to make IoT devices first-class citizens of the internet, with their own IP addresses, so that the same open, long-lived standards, tools and skills work everywhere. The obstacle is that IP was designed for links with large frames and reliable delivery, and for hosts that never sleep. This chapter shows how two IETF standards, 6LoWPAN and RPL, adapt IPv6 to the smallest and least reliable networks.
crumbs: 11  The Internet Layer: 6LoWPAN and RPL

title: 11  The Internet Layer: 6LoWPAN and RPL
text:
11.2 Concepts

Why IP for IoT?
Moving from proprietary protocols to IP-based connectivity brings:

Open, long-lived standards, maintained by the IETF and implemented by many vendors;
A familiar model with decades of tools, documentation and trained engineers;
Transparent internet integration: no protocol translation at the gateway, so end-to-end data flows and end-to-end security become possible;
Maintainability: the same diagnostic tools (ping, traceroute, packet capture) work everywhere;
Global scalability, given enough addresses, which means IPv6.



The internet layer, briefly
Recall from Chapter 8 that the internet layer delivers packets from a source host to a destination host across many networks. Routers forward each packet toward its destination using a routing table, and routing protocols build those tables by exchanging information about network links. On the wider internet, routing protocols such as OSPF (within an organization) and BGP (between organizations) do this job.


IPv6 in a nutshell
IPv6 uses 128-bit addresses, written as eight groups of four hexadecimal digits, with leading zeros dropped and one run of zero groups replaced by ::. For example, 2001:0db8:0000:0000:0000:0000:0000:0017 becomes 2001:db8::17.
Typically, the first 64 bits are a network prefix and the last 64 bits an interface identifier. Several features make IPv6 attractive for IoT:

Enough addresses for every device to have a globally unique one, without NAT.
Stateless address autoconfiguration (SLAAC): a device can build its own address from the prefix advertised by a router plus an interface identifier, with no DHCP server.
Link-local addresses (starting fe80::) that every interface creates automatically, so devices on the same link can talk with no configuration at all.
A simpler, fixed 40-byte header, with options moved into extension headers.
Neighbor Discovery, which replaces ARP, finds routers and detects duplicate addresses.



Low-power and lossy networks
Many IoT deployments form low-power and lossy networks (LLNs): networks of hundreds or thousands of constrained devices (Chapter 9) connected by links where packet loss is high and variable, such as 802.15.4, BLE or low-power Wi-Fi. LLNs appear in building automation (heating, lighting, access control and fire systems), connected homes, healthcare, environmental monitoring and urban networks such as smart grids.
LLNs pose five challenges for the internet layer (Rayes and Salam 2022):

Very little state. Nodes have tiny memories, so routing protocols must keep as little per-node state as possible. A protocol that stores a full map of the network on every node will not fit.
Sleeping nodes. Nodes save energy by sleeping for long periods, so from the network’s point of view the topology changes constantly.
Varied traffic patterns. Traffic can be point-to-point, point-to-multipoint (a controller commanding many lights) or multipoint-to-point (many sensors reporting to one collector), and both unicast and multicast must be supported.
Small frames. Link technologies such as 802.15.4 carry at most 127 bytes per frame, while IPv6 requires links to carry packets of at least 1 280 bytes.
Unreliable links, whose loss rates change over time with interference, weather and moving objects.



6LoWPAN: IPv6 over small frames
6LoWPAN (IPv6 over Low-Power Wireless Personal Area Networks) is an adaptation layer between the link layer and IPv6 (Montenegro et al. 2007; Hui and Thubert 2011). It was designed for 802.15.4 and later adapted to BLE, DECT ULE and other links.
The size problem is stark. Of the 127 bytes in an 802.15.4 frame, the MAC header can take up to 25 bytes and link-layer security up to 21, leaving about 81. An uncompressed IPv6 header takes 40 of those and a UDP header another 8, leaving only about 33 bytes for application data.
6LoWPAN provides three functions:

Header compression. Most IPv6 header fields are predictable in an LLN: the version is always 6, hop limits and traffic classes take common values, and the addresses can usually be derived from the link-layer addresses already in the frame. 6LoWPAN’s IPHC encoding replaces these fields with a few bits, compressing the 40-byte IPv6 header to as little as 2 bytes. The UDP header can be compressed similarly, to as little as 4 bytes.
Fragmentation and reassembly. When a packet does not fit in one frame, 6LoWPAN splits it into fragments with small headers and reassembles it at the other end, so that IPv6’s 1 280-byte minimum is met.
Forwarding across multiple hops. In mesh-under forwarding, the adaptation layer relays frames hop by hop, and the whole mesh looks like one IP link. In route-over forwarding, each hop is an IP router, and a routing protocol such as RPL decides the path.

A 6LoWPAN network connects to the rest of the internet through a border router (also called an edge router), which translates between compressed 6LoWPAN packets on the radio side and ordinary IPv6 packets on the Ethernet or Wi-Fi side. Because addresses and semantics are preserved, this is adaptation, not protocol translation: a server on the internet sees ordinary IPv6 packets from each sensor’s own address.


RPL: routing in lossy networks
RPL (pronounced “ripple”), the IPv6 Routing Protocol for Low-Power and Lossy Networks, is the IETF’s standard routing protocol for LLNs (Winter et al. 2012).
RPL is a distance-vector protocol. Unlike link-state protocols such as OSPF, which keep a database of the entire network on every node, a distance-vector node keeps only a little information about its neighbors and their distance to a destination. This fits the “very little state” constraint.
RPL organizes the network as a destination-oriented directed acyclic graph (DODAG): a tree-like structure rooted at the border router, in which every node points toward the root through one or more parents (Figure 11.1).






Figure 11.1: An RPL DODAG. Arrows point from each node toward its preferred parent; rank increases with distance from the root.



The DODAG is built with a few control messages:

The root broadcasts a DIO (DODAG Information Object), announcing the graph and its own rank (its position in the graph).
Each node that hears DIOs chooses a preferred parent using an objective function and computes its own rank, which must be greater than its parent’s. It then sends its own DIOs, so the graph spreads outward.
A new node can ask for DIOs with a DIS (DODAG Information Solicitation).
To make downward routes possible, nodes send DAO (Destination Advertisement Object) messages toward the root. In storing mode, intermediate routers remember downward routes; in non-storing mode, only the root does, and it places the full route in the packet header (source routing), which saves memory in the nodes.

The objective function defines what “best” means. Common choices minimize hop count (OF0) or the expected transmission count (ETX), the average number of transmissions needed to deliver a packet over each link (MRHOF). Other metrics include latency and remaining node energy.
Two properties make RPL suitable for lossy links:

It is proactive: it builds and maintains routes before they are needed, and nodes can keep backup parents, so alternative paths exist before a failure.
It is under-reactive: when a link fails, a node simply switches locally to another parent, instead of triggering a network-wide recomputation.

To keep control traffic low, RPL sends DIOs on a Trickle timer: frequently when the network is changing, and exponentially less often when it is stable.


Thread: putting it together
Thread is a complete IPv6 mesh networking stack for homes and buildings, maintained by the Thread Group. It runs on 802.15.4 radios, uses 6LoWPAN for adaptation, adds its own mesh routing and secure commissioning, and connects to Wi-Fi or Ethernet through border routers, which are often built into smart speakers, hubs and TVs. Thread is one of the main transports for Matter (Chapter 13).
The original ESP32 in your kit has no 802.15.4 radio, so it cannot join a 6LoWPAN or Thread network directly. Newer Espressif chips such as the ESP32-C6 and ESP32-H2 do have 802.15.4 radios and support Thread through the OpenThread stack, and dedicated 802.15.4 modules are also available.


Mobility and security at the internet layer

Mobility. When a device moves between networks, its IP address changes and its connections break. Mobile IPv6 lets a device keep a permanent home address while it roams, with a home agent forwarding traffic. In practice, most IoT systems avoid the problem by having devices reconnect and re-register with a cloud service from wherever they are.
Security. IPsec can protect traffic at the internet layer, but it is heavy for constrained nodes. LLNs usually rely on link-layer encryption (802.15.4 includes AES-CCM) combined with security at the transport or application layer, such as DTLS or OSCORE (Chapter 12, Chapter 14).







TipTry it on your kit: IPv6 on Wi-Fi



Although the kit cannot run 6LoWPAN, its Wi-Fi interface can run IPv6.

Enable IPv6 before connecting (WiFi.enableIpV6() in the Arduino-ESP32 2.x core; WiFi.enableIPv6() in 3.x) and print the link-local address after connecting. How was its interface identifier derived?
If your network advertises a global IPv6 prefix, print the global address as well. Is there a NAT between the kit and the internet now?
Calculate how many bytes of application payload remain in one 802.15.4 frame (a) without compression and (b) with IPv6 and UDP headers compressed to 2 and 4 bytes respectively, assuming a 25-byte MAC header and 21 bytes of security.
Sketch the DODAG that RPL would build for a building with sensors on three floors and a border router in the basement. Which nodes need to stay awake?
