title: 11  The Internet Layer: 6LoWPAN and RPL
text:
11.3 In depth (optional)






Optional, in-depth explanation. This section goes beyond the rest of the chapter into the math and physics behind it. Nothing later in the book depends on it; skip it on a first reading.




Fragments, links and routes
Address space. IPv6 addresses have 128 bits: \(2^{128} \approx 3.4\times10^{38}\) addresses. A single /64 subnet, the standard size for one link, holds \(2^{64}\) interface identifiers, as many as the entire IPv4 address space squared. Scarcity, and therefore NAT, disappears as a design constraint; reachability and firewalling become policy decisions instead.
Why 6LoWPAN must compress and fragment. IPv6 requires every link to carry packets of at least 1280 bytes. An IEEE 802.15.4 frame carries at most 127 bytes; after the MAC header, security and checksum, roughly 80–100 bytes remain. Two consequences follow:

Compression. The uncompressed IPv6 header (40 bytes) plus UDP (8) would eat half the frame. Header compression (IPHC) elides fields that can be derived from the link layer, such as addresses built from MAC addresses, and can shrink both to under 10 bytes.
Fragmentation. A full 1280-byte packet becomes about 14 fragments.

Fragmentation multiplies loss. If each frame is lost independently with probability \(p\), a packet split into \(k\) fragments arrives only if all fragments do:
\[
P_\text{deliver} = (1-p)^k.
\]
With \(p = 5\%\), a single-frame packet arrives 95% of the time, but a 14-fragment packet only \(0.95^{14} \approx 49\%\), and a lost fragment forces the whole packet to be resent. Hence the guidance to keep IoT application messages small enough for one frame.
Choosing routes by expected transmissions. RPL routes along the parent that minimizes a cost; a common one is ETX, the expected number of transmissions to deliver a frame and receive its acknowledgment across a link:
\[
\text{ETX} = \frac{1}{d_f \, d_r},
\]
where \(d_f\) and \(d_r\) are the forward and reverse delivery ratios. A link with 90% delivery each way has ETX ≈ 1.23; one with 60% has ETX ≈ 2.78. ETX adds along a path, so two good hops (2.46) beat one poor hop (2.78): the shortest route by hop count is not always the cheapest.
Exercise. A sensor is three hops from the border router, each with ETX 1.5, or two hops with ETX 1.2 and 2.0. Which path does RPL prefer under the ETX objective? What is the expected number of radio transmissions per delivered packet on each?
Sources for this section: (Hui and Thubert 2011; Winter et al. 2012; De Couto et al. 2003).

title: 11  The Internet Layer: 6LoWPAN and RPL
text:
11.4 Design trade-offs







Decision
Considerations




End-to-end IPv6 vs. gateway translation
IPv6 enables end-to-end flows and security; gateways allow simpler devices and proprietary radios


Mesh-under vs. route-over
Mesh-under hides the mesh from IP; route-over lets each hop make IP routing decisions


RPL storing vs. non-storing mode
Storing mode spends router memory to save header space; non-storing mode does the opposite


Hop count vs. ETX
Fewer hops is simple; ETX finds more reliable paths that may be longer


Thread vs. Zigbee
Thread is IP-native and part of Matter; Zigbee has a very large installed base

title: 11  The Internet Layer: 6LoWPAN and RPL
text:
11.5 Common pitfalls

Assuming 802.15.4 frames carry IPv6 directly. They cannot without 6LoWPAN.
Ignoring fragmentation costs. Losing one fragment loses the whole packet; keep application messages small enough to fit in one frame.
Forgetting the border router. An LLN without one is an island.
Expecting IPv4 tools to work unchanged. Many IoT IPv6 addresses are link-local and need a zone (interface) identifier, as in fe80::1%wlan0.
Assuming IP connectivity means interoperability. Devices must also agree on application protocols and data models (Chapter 12, Chapter 13).







NoteAdvanced track





Simulating an LLN. Contiki-NG and RIOT include 6LoWPAN and RPL implementations, and the Cooja simulator can run hundreds of virtual nodes. Simulate a 30-node RPL network, kill the root’s busiest child, and measure how long the network takes to reconverge and how many control messages it sends.
Reading IPHC. Using RFC 6282, decode the two-byte IPHC header 0x7A33. Which IPv6 fields are elided, which are carried inline after it, and where does the receiver get each elided value from? (Answer check: the traffic class, flow label, hop limit and both addresses are elided; only the next-header field is carried inline.)
Comparing routing. Thread does not use RPL; it uses its own distance-vector protocol with a small number of routers (up to 32) and a leader. Compare its design with RPL’s in terms of state, scale and behavior when a router fails.

title: 12  Application Protocols: HTTP, CoAP, MQTT and More
text:
12.1 Why it matters
Once a device has an IP address and a transport, it still needs a way to exchange meaningful messages with other devices and services. Should a thermostat wait to be asked for the temperature, or announce it whenever it changes? Should a light accept commands directly, or should commands pass through a central server? What happens to a command sent while the light’s radio is asleep?
Application protocols answer these questions, and the right choice affects battery life, latency, reliability and how easily the system scales. This chapter covers the three protocols you will meet most often in IoT, HTTP, CoAP and MQTT, and places the others in context.
crumbs: 12  Application Protocols: HTTP, CoAP, MQTT and More

title: 12  Application Protocols: HTTP, CoAP, MQTT and More
text:
12.2 Concepts

Two interaction patterns
Request/response. A client sends a request to a server and waits for a response. The web works this way. It is simple and familiar, but the client must know the server’s address, the server must be reachable, and getting updates means asking repeatedly (polling), which wastes energy and bandwidth when nothing has changed.
Publish/subscribe (pub/sub). Senders (publishers) send messages labeled with a topic to an intermediary, a broker. Receivers (subscribers) tell the broker which topics they want, and the broker forwards matching messages. Publishers and subscribers do not need to know about each other, do not need to be online at the same time (with the right settings), and can be added or removed freely. This decoupling suits IoT, where many sensors produce data for many consumers.


HTTP and REST
HTTP is the web’s application protocol, standardized by the IETF. It is text-based, request/response, and runs over TCP (or, in HTTP/3, over QUIC on UDP). Its design follows the REST (Representational State Transfer) architectural style, in which:

every resource has a URI, for example /devices/kit-07/temperature;
a small set of methods act on resources: GET (read), POST (create or submit), PUT (replace), PATCH (modify) and DELETE;
status codes report outcomes: 200 OK, 201 Created, 400 Bad Request, 401 Unauthorized, 404 Not Found, 500 Internal Server Error;
each request is self-contained (stateless), which makes servers easy to scale.

From the ESP32, posting a JSON reading takes a few lines:
#include <WiFiClientSecure.h>
#include <HTTPClient.h>

void postReading(float tempC) {
  WiFiClientSecure tls;
  tls.setCACert(ROOT_CA_PEM);                       // verify the server's certificate
  HTTPClient http;
  http.begin(tls, "https://api.example.org/v1/readings");
  http.addHeader("Content-Type", "application/json");
  String body = String("{\"device\":\"kit-07\",\"temp_c\":") + tempC + "}";
  int code = http.POST(body);
  Serial.printf("POST -> %d\n", code);
  http.end();
}
HTTP’s strengths are universality: every cloud service, programming language and firewall understands it. Its costs for constrained devices are:

verbose, text-based headers, often hundreds of bytes per request;
TCP and TLS handshakes before each new connection, which cost several round trips and significant energy;
no built-in way for a server to push data to a device, other than polling, long polling, WebSockets or server-sent events.

HTTP is a good fit for mains-powered devices, for occasional uploads, and for talking to cloud APIs. It is a poor fit for battery-powered sensors on lossy networks.


CoAP: REST for constrained devices
The IETF’s CoRE (Constrained RESTful Environments) working group designed the Constrained Application Protocol (CoAP) to bring the REST model to devices and networks that cannot afford HTTP (Shelby et al. 2014). CoAP keeps HTTP’s concepts (URIs, methods, response codes, content types) but changes almost everything underneath:

It runs over UDP (with DTLS for security), avoiding TCP’s connection setup.
Its binary header is only 4 bytes, followed by a token and compact options. A typical request fits in a few dozen bytes.
It supports multicast, for example to discover all lights on a network at once.
It is asynchronous: requests and responses are matched by a token, not by a connection.


Messages and reliability
Because UDP is unreliable, CoAP adds a thin messaging layer with four message types:

CON (confirmable): must be acknowledged; retransmitted with exponential back-off until an ACK arrives.
NON (non-confirmable): fire and forget, for frequent readings where a lost one does not matter.
ACK: acknowledges a CON message. A response can be piggybacked on the ACK if it is ready immediately; otherwise the server ACKs first and sends the response later in its own CON message.
RST (reset): “I received your message but cannot process it”.

A request is carried in a message, with a method code such as 0.01 GET, and the response carries a code such as 2.05 Content or 4.04 Not Found, mirroring HTTP’s 200 and 404.


Observe, block transfer and discovery
CoAP adds three extensions that matter for IoT:

Observe (Hartke 2015): a client registers interest in a resource with one GET, and the server sends a notification whenever the resource changes, a lightweight form of push.
Block-wise transfer: large payloads, such as firmware images, are split into blocks that fit in small packets.
Resource discovery: a GET to /.well-known/core returns a list of the device’s resources in CoRE Link Format.



Caching and proxies
CoAP responses can be cached. The Max-Age option says how long a response stays fresh, and the ETag option lets a client check whether its cached copy is still valid. Proxies use caching to answer on behalf of sleeping devices and to reduce traffic on constrained networks. Because CoAP mirrors HTTP’s model, a proxy can also translate between the two, letting a web application GET a sensor value over HTTP while the proxy fetches it over CoAP.
CoAP is not a replacement for HTTP, nor a compression of it, nor separate from the web. It is a specialized web protocol for machine-to-machine use on constrained networks. It is used in LwM2M device management, in Thread-based products and in smart-metering and water networks.



MQTT: publish/subscribe telemetry
MQTT is a lightweight publish/subscribe protocol originally developed at IBM for monitoring oil pipelines over satellite links, and now an OASIS standard (MQTT Version 5.0 2019). (The name once stood for “MQ Telemetry Transport”; despite the “MQ”, MQTT has no message queues in the traditional sense.) It runs over TCP, usually with TLS, and has a very small code footprint.

Architecture
An MQTT system has two kinds of component (Figure 12.1):

Clients connect to a broker and publish messages to topics, subscribe to topics, or both. Your kit, a phone app and a cloud service can all be clients.
The broker receives all messages and forwards each one to the clients subscribed to its topic. Popular brokers include Eclipse Mosquitto, EMQX and HiveMQ; brokers can also be bridged together.







Figure 12.1: MQTT publish/subscribe. Publishers and subscribers only know the broker and the topic names.



Because every client connects out to the broker, MQTT works well with NAT and firewalls (Chapter 8).


Topics and wildcards
Topics are hierarchical strings separated by /, such as uci/iot/kit-07/temperature. Subscribers can use two wildcards:

+ matches exactly one level: uci/iot/+/temperature matches every kit’s temperature.
# matches any number of levels, and must come last: uci/iot/kit-07/# matches everything from kit 7.

Messages are opaque bytes: text, JSON, binary or images. MQTT does not care.


Quality of service
Each publication and subscription chooses a quality-of-service (QoS) level:



Table 12.1: MQTT quality-of-service levels.











QoS
Guarantee
Mechanism
Use




0
At most once
Send and forget; no acknowledgment
Frequent readings where loss is acceptable


1
At least once
PUBLISH → PUBACK; retransmit until acknowledged; duplicates possible
Most commands and events


2
Exactly once
Four-step handshake: PUBLISH → PUBREC → PUBREL → PUBCOMP
Billing, counters, anything where duplicates cause harm






Higher QoS levels cost more messages, more memory and more time. The effective QoS of a delivery is the lower of the publisher’s and subscriber’s levels.


Sessions, retained messages and wills
MQTT includes features for devices that come and go:

Persistent sessions. A client that connects with a clean start (clean session) flag of 0 asks the broker to remember its subscriptions and to queue QoS 1 and 2 messages while it is offline.
Retained messages. A message published with the retain flag is stored by the broker and sent immediately to any new subscriber. This gives late joiners the last known state, such as the current position of a switch.
Last will and testament. When connecting, a client can register a message for the broker to publish on its behalf if it disconnects unexpectedly, for example status = offline.
Keep-alive. Clients send small pings when idle, so both sides can detect a dead connection.

MQTT 5, the current version, adds reason codes, message expiry, shared subscriptions for load balancing, topic aliases to shorten repeated topics, and user properties. MQTT-SN is a variant for non-TCP networks such as Zigbee and UDP.


MQTT on the ESP32
The PubSubClient library is a simple MQTT 3.1.1 client. Connecting securely to a cloud broker (such as an EMQX Serverless deployment) looks like this:
#include <WiFiClientSecure.h>
#include <PubSubClient.h>
#include "secrets.h"     // WIFI_*, MQTT_HOST, MQTT_USER, MQTT_PASS, ROOT_CA_PEM
#include "iot_pins.h"

WiFiClientSecure tls;
PubSubClient mqtt(tls);
const char* CMD_TOPIC    = "uci/iot/kit-07/cmd";
const char* STATUS_TOPIC = "uci/iot/kit-07/status";

void onMessage(char* topic, byte* payload, unsigned int len) {
  String msg((char*)payload, len);
  if (msg == "led_on")  digitalWrite(IoTPins::LED_1, HIGH);
  if (msg == "led_off") digitalWrite(IoTPins::LED_1, LOW);
}

void ensureConnected() {
  while (!mqtt.connected()) {
    // client ID, user, password, will topic, will QoS, will retain, will message
    if (mqtt.connect("kit-07", MQTT_USER, MQTT_PASS, STATUS_TOPIC, 1, true, "offline")) {
      mqtt.publish(STATUS_TOPIC, "online", true);      // retained
      mqtt.subscribe(CMD_TOPIC, 1);
    } else {
      delay(2000);
    }
  }
}

void setup() {
  pinMode(IoTPins::LED_1, OUTPUT);
  // ... connect Wi-Fi as in Chapter 8 ...
  tls.setCACert(ROOT_CA_PEM);
  mqtt.setServer(MQTT_HOST, 8883);                       // MQTT over TLS
  mqtt.setCallback(onMessage);
  mqtt.setBufferSize(512);                               // default is small
}

void loop() {
  ensureConnected();
  mqtt.loop();                                           // process incoming packets
  static uint32_t last = 0;
  if (millis() - last > 10000) {
    last = millis();
    char buf[64];
    snprintf(buf, sizeof buf, "{\"pot\":%d}", analogRead(IoTPins::POT_ADC));
    mqtt.publish("uci/iot/kit-07/telemetry", buf);       // QoS 0
  }
}
PubSubClient publishes only at QoS 0 and subscribes at QoS 0 or 1. Libraries such as the ESP-IDF MQTT client support all three levels and MQTT 5.



Other application protocols



Table 12.2: Other application protocols used in IoT.











Protocol
Standard
Model
Notes




XMPP
IETF
Messaging and presence over XML streams
Originally for chat (Jabber); federated servers; presence (“online/away”) is useful for devices. Verbose for constrained devices.


AMQP
OASIS, ISO/IEC 19464
Message queuing over TCP
From the financial sector; rich routing, delivery guarantees and token-based flow control; common between back-end services.


DDS / RTPS
OMG
Data-centric pub/sub, brokerless
Automatic discovery, very rich QoS (deadlines, durability, reliability); used in robotics (ROS 2), defense and vehicles.


SIP
IETF
Session setup
Negotiates voice, video and messaging sessions; used in intercoms and video doorbells.


IEEE 1888
IEEE
Time-series read/write over SOAP and XML
Facility and energy management.


LwM2M
OMA SpecWorks
Device management over CoAP
Standard objects for firmware update, connectivity monitoring and configuration.








Payload formats
The protocol moves bytes; the payload format gives them structure:

JSON is human-readable and universal, but verbose.
CBOR (Concise Binary Object Representation) is a binary encoding of the same data model as JSON, often half the size, and is the natural partner of CoAP.
Protocol Buffers and similar schema-based formats are compact and strongly typed, at the cost of a shared schema.
Custom binary structs are the smallest, and the hardest to evolve and debug.



Choosing a protocol



Table 12.3: Comparing the three main IoT application protocols.












HTTP
CoAP
MQTT




Pattern
Request/response
Request/response + observe
Publish/subscribe via broker


Transport
TCP (+TLS) or QUIC
UDP (+DTLS/OSCORE)
TCP (+TLS)


Header size
Hundreds of bytes
4 bytes + options
2 bytes + topic


Reliability
From TCP
CON messages
QoS 0, 1, 2


Push to device
Polling, WebSockets
Observe
Native


Works through NAT
Device as client: yes
Needs care
Yes (clients connect out)


Best for
Cloud APIs, mains-powered devices
Constrained, low-power, LLNs
Telemetry and commands, many-to-many












TipTry it on your kit: MQTT command center



This exercise corresponds to the MQTT lecture activity and to Lab 5.

Connect the kit to the course broker. Publish the potentiometer reading every 2 s and subscribe to a command topic that controls the LEDs and the buzzer.
Use a desktop MQTT client (such as MQTT Explorer) to watch all kits with a wildcard subscription and to send commands to yours.
Register a last will. Unplug your kit and observe what other subscribers see.
Publish your LED state as a retained message. Restart the desktop client: what does it see immediately?
Pick the QoS: for each message type (telemetry, an emergency alarm, a “dispense medication” command, a firmware-available notice), choose QoS 0, 1 or 2 and justify your choice. What would duplicates or losses cost in each case?

A guided, step-by-step version for a lecture session is Activity 7.

title: 12  Application Protocols: HTTP, CoAP, MQTT and More
text:
12.3 In depth (optional)






Optional, in-depth explanation. This section goes beyond the rest of the chapter into the math and physics behind it. Nothing later in the book depends on it; skip it on a first reading.




Reliability and overhead, quantified
Header sizes. For a small reading, the application header is a large share of the message:

Application-layer header sizes.







Protocol
Fixed header
Plus




MQTT PUBLISH
2 bytes
2-byte topic length + topic; 2-byte packet ID at QoS 1–2


CoAP
4 bytes
Token (0–8) and options, often 10–20 bytes in all


HTTP/1.1
Text request line
Text headers, typically 100–300 bytes



A 4-byte reading published at QoS 0 to topic iot/t07/temp (12 characters) is \(2 + 2 + 12 + 4 = 20\) bytes of MQTT, against roughly 200 bytes of HTTP. Short topic names matter.
What QoS 1 buys. Suppose each MQTT packet is lost with probability \(p\) (after TCP gives up, or across a broker restart). A QoS 1 exchange succeeds when both the PUBLISH and the PUBACK arrive, with probability \(s = (1-p)^2\). With up to \(r\) attempts, the message is delivered unless every attempt fails:
\[
P_\text{lost} = (1 - s)^r ,\qquad E[\text{attempts}] \approx \frac{1}{s}.
\]
If \(p = 10\%\), \(s = 0.81\); three attempts leave \(0.19^3 \approx 0.7\%\) lost, at an average cost of about 1.23 exchanges. But a PUBACK that is lost after the PUBLISH arrived causes a resend the receiver already has: duplicates occur with probability up to \(p(1-p)\) per exchange, which is why QoS 1 receivers must be idempotent (or deduplicate by packet ID). QoS 2 removes the duplicates with a four-packet exchange: twice the messages, and state at both ends.
CoAP’s retransmission schedule. Confirmable CoAP messages are resent with exponential back-off. RFC 7252’s defaults are an initial timeout chosen randomly between ACK_TIMEOUT = 2 s and \(1.5\times\) that, doubled after each try, for up to MAX_RETRANSMIT = 4 retries. The longest time from first transmission to last retransmission is the MAX_TRANSMIT_SPAN:
\[
T_\text{span} = T_0 \left(2^{R} - 1\right) F = 2\ \text{s} \times 15 \times 1.5 = 45\ \text{s},
\]
where \(T_0\) is ACK_TIMEOUT, \(R\) is MAX_RETRANSMIT and \(F\) is ACK_RANDOM_FACTOR.
A sender that hears nothing for 45 s plus the time it waits for the last reply knows the message almost certainly failed. Randomizing the timeout prevents a room of devices from retrying in lockstep.
Exercise. A telemetry stream sends one reading per second at QoS 0 over a link that loses 2% of packets. How many readings are lost per day? Would QoS 1 be worth it if each reading replaces the previous one on the dashboard?
Sources for this section: (MQTT Version 5.0 2019; Shelby et al. 2014).

Decision
Considerations




Request/response vs. pub/sub
Direct, simple interactions versus decoupled many-to-many distribution

A broker simplifies NAT traversal and fan-out but is a central dependency and a target


Higher QoS

title: 12  Application Protocols: HTTP, CoAP, MQTT and More
text:
12.5 Common pitfalls

Polling over HTTP from a battery device. Each poll costs a full TCP and TLS setup.
Using one global MQTT topic. Design a hierarchy that supports fine-grained access control and wildcards.
Duplicate client IDs. Two clients with the same ID keep disconnecting each other.
Assuming QoS 1 means “exactly once”. Make command handlers idempotent: processing a duplicate should do no harm.
Forgetting mqtt.loop(). Incoming messages are never processed and the connection times out.
Skipping TLS certificate verification with setInsecure() outside the lab.
Messages larger than the client’s buffer, which are silently dropped.







NoteAdvanced track





Measuring overhead. Send the same 20-byte reading 100 times by HTTP POST (new connection each time), HTTP with keep-alive, MQTT QoS 0 and MQTT QoS 1, and capture the traffic with Wireshark. Report bytes on the air and elapsed time per reading, and relate them to battery life.
Securing CoAP. DTLS secures a whole CoAP connection hop by hop; OSCORE (RFC 8613) protects individual CoAP messages end to end, even through proxies. Explain why that difference matters when a proxy caches responses for sleeping devices.
Topic design for access control. Design an MQTT topic hierarchy and broker access-control list for a building with 200 rooms, in which each room’s devices may publish only their own telemetry, the building manager’s dashboard may read everything, and only the HVAC controller may send commands to thermostats.

title: 13  Interoperability and Standards
text:
13.1 Why it matters
In UCI’s SIMHome project, a smart-home testbed built with Southern California Edison, one of the hardest problems was not any single device. It was making sensors, actuators, networks and computers from different companies and research teams work together, when each used its own protocols (sometimes ad hoc), hardware, operating system (sometimes none at all) and data conventions.
Every IoT system that grows beyond a single vendor meets the same problem. Two devices can share a network and an application protocol and still be unable to cooperate, because they disagree on what their messages mean. This chapter explains the levels at which devices must agree, and the standards that help them do so.

title: 13  Interoperability and Standards
text:
13.2 Concepts

What interoperability means
Interoperability is the ability of a system or device to exchange information with another, and to understand and use the information exchanged. The second half is the hard part.
The Levels of Conceptual Interoperability Model (Tolk and Muguira 2003), adopted in IoT by organizations such as the Industrial Internet Consortium, describes interoperability as a stack of levels. Each depends on the ones below:



Table 13.1: Levels of interoperability.











Level
Question
Concerned with
Examples




Technical
Can the bytes get there?
Hardware, operating systems, communication protocols and infrastructure
Both devices speak IPv6 over Thread; both support MQTT


Syntactic
Can the receiver parse them?
Data formats and encodings
JSON, CBOR, XML, ASN.1, a fixed binary layout


Semantic
Does the receiver understand them?
The meaning of the content: units, names, relationships
“temp” is air temperature in °C, measured in the living room


Organizational
Do the organizations cooperate?
Business processes, agreements, policies across organizations, regions and cultures
A utility, a thermostat maker and a homeowner agree on a demand-response program






The protocols in the earlier chapters of Part III solve technical interoperability. Syntactic interoperability needs agreed formats. Semantic interoperability is the subject of most of this chapter: two devices may both send {"temp": 21}, yet one means degrees Celsius of the water in a boiler and the other means degrees Fahrenheit of a room, or a target rather than a measurement.
In healthcare, for example, standards such as HL7 (and its modern form, FHIR) define the meaning of clinical information exchanged between hospital systems, while the ISO/IEEE 11073 family (X73) covers personal health devices across several layers of the stack, so that a blood-pressure cuff from one maker can report to a hub from another.


From silos to horizontal platforms
Machine-to-machine (M2M) systems have existed for decades: remote meter reading, fleet tracking, alarm panels. They were typically built as vertical silos: one application, one type of device, one proprietary communication stack, tightly coupled end to end. A smart-metering system and a street-lighting system in the same city shared nothing, even when they used the same cellular network.
This fragmentation slowed the market. Every new application required building a new stack from the devices up. The response, in the phrase used by ETSI and by Rayes and Salam (Rayes and Salam 2022), was to invert the pipes: replace vertical silos with horizontal layers that many applications share. Devices connect through a common network (IP plus mobile infrastructure), and applications use a common application services layer that provides the functions every IoT application needs.


The application services layer
The key gap, in this view, is an abstraction layer offering a common set of services, so that an application can work with potentially any device without knowing its internals in advance. The value of IoT is in the data, not in how it is transported or which hardware produced it.
An application services layer typically provides:

network-agnostic message routing, synchronous and asynchronous;
a subscribe/notify model, with buffering so that devices are not overloaded with requests;
a uniform data storage model and resource naming;
a uniform API independent of programming language;
registration and discovery of devices and applications;
group management, to address many devices at once;
security: authentication, authorization and access control;
device management, such as configuration and firmware updates;
location information.

There are two broad routes to this layer:

Middleware: software that sits between devices and applications and translates each device-specific language into a common internal model. Middleware works with existing devices but must be updated for every new device type.
Standards: devices and applications agree on common interfaces and data models in advance. Standards scale better but require industry agreement and take time.

Real systems usually combine both.


Standards for the application services layer

ETSI M2M and oneM2M
In 2012 the European Telecommunications Standards Institute (ETSI) published a service-layer standard for M2M. Its central idea was a Service Capabilities Layer (SCL) present in devices, gateways and network servers, exposing common functions (registration, data transfer, identification, group management, security, device management and location) through a RESTful API in which all data, device information and access rights are represented as resources.
Later in 2012, seven standards organizations from the US, Europe, Japan, China and Korea, including ETSI, launched oneM2M to develop a single global standard for the IoT service layer, and transferred their own overlapping work to it (oneM2M, n.d.). oneM2M defines a common service layer that can run over HTTP, CoAP, MQTT or WebSockets, and is used mainly in smart-city and telecom-operator platforms.


LwM2M
Lightweight M2M (LwM2M), from OMA SpecWorks, focuses on device management for constrained devices. It runs over CoAP (and also over MQTT and HTTP in recent versions) and defines a registry of standard objects: Device, Firmware Update, Connectivity Monitoring, Location, Temperature and many more, each with numbered resources. A server can update firmware or read battery level on any compliant device, regardless of maker.


The W3C Web of Things
Rather than replace existing protocols, the W3C Web of Things (WoT) describes them (Web of Things (WoT) Thing Description 1.1 2023). Its central artifact is the Thing Description (TD): a JSON-LD document that lists a device’s properties (values that can be read or observed), actions (operations that can be invoked) and events (notifications), and for each one the protocol binding needed to use it (an HTTP URL, a CoAP resource, an MQTT topic):
{
  "@context": "https://www.w3.org/2022/wot/td/v1.1",
  "id": "urn:uuid:5f1b0c3e-iot-kit-07",
  "title": "IoT@UCI kit 07",
  "securityDefinitions": { "basic_sc": { "scheme": "basic" } },
  "security": "basic_sc",
  "properties": {
    "temperature": {
      "type": "number",
      "unit": "degree Celsius",
      "readOnly": true,
      "observable": true,
      "forms": [{ "href": "mqtts://broker.example.org/uci/iot/kit-07/temperature",
                  "op": ["readproperty", "observeproperty"] }]
    }
  },
  "actions": {
    "beep": {
      "input": { "type": "integer", "minimum": 50, "maximum": 2000, "description": "duration in ms" },
      "forms": [{ "href": "mqtts://broker.example.org/uci/iot/kit-07/cmd" }]
    }
  }
}
A generic client that understands Thing Descriptions can use any described device without device-specific code.


Semantic models and ontologies
Units, names and relationships can be pinned down further with shared ontologies: formal vocabularies that define concepts and how they relate. Examples include the W3C SOSA/SSN ontology for sensors and observations, SAREF (ETSI’s Smart Applications REFerence ontology) for appliances and energy, and Brick and Project Haystack for buildings. Linking a TD’s temperature property to saref:Temperature with a unit from a standard units vocabulary removes the ambiguity in {"temp": 21}.



Matter: interoperability in the smart home
For years, smart-home buyers had to check whether a product worked with Amazon Alexa, Apple Home, Google Home or Samsung SmartThings. Matter, developed by the Connectivity Standards Alliance with those companies and hundreds of others, addresses all four levels of interoperability at once (Matter Specification, n.d.):

Technical: Matter runs over IPv6 on Wi-Fi, Ethernet or Thread (Chapter 11), with BLE used for setup.
Syntactic and semantic: a single data model. A device has numbered endpoints; each endpoint implements standard clusters (On/Off, Level Control, Color Control, Door Lock, Thermostat, and so on); each cluster defines attributes, commands and events with precise meanings and units. A “dimmable light” is defined the same way by every maker.
Security and onboarding: every device carries a certificate chain proving it is a genuine, certified product; it is commissioned by scanning a QR code or entering a setup code; and all communication is encrypted.
Organizational: certification by the Alliance, and multi-admin support, which lets the same device be controlled by several ecosystems at once.

Matter has grown steadily since its first release in 2022. Version 1.5 (late 2025) added cameras, and version 1.6 (mid-2026) added NFC-based commissioning and better support for sharing devices across ecosystems, along with a product-security specification. Thermostats, locks, lights, plugs, sensors, appliances and energy-management devices are all covered.
Matter is a good example of the “standards” route: devices interoperate because they implement the same data model, not because a middleware translates for them. Its cost is that every device must implement the full stack and pass certification, which is why the ESP32 family is popular for Matter products: Espressif provides a certified SDK.






TipTry it on your kit: describe your device




Write a Thing Description for your kit that exposes the potentiometer, the BMP280’s temperature and pressure, and the LEDs, with the MQTT topics you used in Chapter 12. Validate it with an online TD playground.
Identify every piece of information in your TD that addresses semantic, rather than syntactic, interoperability.
Exchange TDs with another team. Without looking at their code, write a short program on your laptop that reads their kit’s temperature and turns on their LED. What was missing or ambiguous in their TD?
Which Matter clusters would your kit implement if it were a Matter device? Which kit features have no standard cluster?

title: 13  Interoperability and Standards
text:
13.3 In depth (optional)






Optional, in-depth explanation. This section goes beyond the rest of the chapter into the math and physics behind it. Nothing later in the book depends on it; skip it on a first reading.




Why common models scale, and what encodings cost
The translation problem. If \(N\) systems each speak their own data model and every pair must interoperate, you need a translator for each ordered pair: \(N(N-1)\) translators, or \(N(N-1)/2\) if each is bidirectional. Ten systems need 45 bidirectional translators. If they all map to one shared model, you need only \(N\) mappings (to and from the common model): 10 instead of 45. The gap grows quadratically, which is the economic argument for standards such as Matter’s data model, OPC UA information models, or W3C Thing Descriptions.
The argument has a cost: each mapping to a common model can lose information that the model does not represent. Two translations (A → common → B) can lose more than one direct translation. Good common models therefore include extension points.
Encoding size. The same reading, {"t":23.5,"h":41}, is 17 bytes as compact JSON. In CBOR (RFC 8949), a binary encoding with the same data model as JSON, it is 10 bytes:

The reading in CBOR.


Bytes
Meaning




A2
map with 2 pairs


61 74
text string of length 1: “t”


F9 4D E0
half-precision float 23.5


61 68
text string “h”


18 29
unsigned integer 41



The value 23.5 fits a 16-bit half-precision float exactly: \(23.5 = 1.46875 \times 2^4\), so the sign is 0, the biased exponent is \(4 + 15 = 19 = 10011_2\), and the 10-bit fraction is \(0.46875 \times 1024 = 480 = 0111100000_2\), giving 0 10011 0111100000 = 0x4DE0. With integer keys instead of text keys (as in many IoT profiles), the message shrinks to 8 bytes.
Smaller is not free: binary encodings need a decoder to be read by a person, and every party must agree on the key numbering. That agreement is exactly what a shared data model provides.
Exercise. Encode {"t":-4,"h":100} in CBOR by hand. (Negative integers use major type 1 and encode \(-1-n\); integers 24–255 need one extra byte.) How many bytes is it, and how many in JSON?
Sources for this section: (Bormann and Hoffman 2020; Web of Things (WoT) Thing Description 1.1 2023).

title: 13  Interoperability and Standards
text:
13.4 Design trade-offs







Decision
Considerations




Middleware vs. standards
Middleware integrates existing devices; standards scale but need agreement and certification


Rich semantics vs. simplicity
Ontologies remove ambiguity but add complexity that small teams may not need


Ecosystem standard (Matter) vs. open platform
A standard gives consumer reach; a custom platform gives freedom and differentiation


Describing vs. replacing protocols
WoT describes existing devices; Matter and oneM2M ask devices to adopt a new stack

title: 13  Interoperability and Standards
text:
13.5 Common pitfalls

Assuming technical interoperability is enough. Agreeing on MQTT does not mean agreeing on what a message means.
Missing units and reference frames. Always state units, coordinate frames and whether a value is a measurement or a set point.
Ad hoc field names. temp, t, temperature_c and Temp across one fleet make every consumer fragile.
Undocumented payloads. If the only specification is the firmware source, nobody else can integrate.
Ignoring the organizational level. Data sharing between organizations needs agreements on ownership, privacy and responsibility, not just formats.







NoteAdvanced track





Mapping between models. Map your kit’s Thing Description onto LwM2M objects (for example IPSO Temperature, object 3303) and onto Matter clusters. Which concepts map cleanly, which need extensions, and what is lost in each mapping?
Standards as strategy. Interoperability standards are shaped by companies with commercial interests. Read about the history of Zigbee, Z-Wave, Thread and Matter, and write a short analysis of why earlier smart-home standards did not unify the market and what Matter did differently, organizationally as much as technically.

title: 14  Security and Privacy
text:
14.1 Why it matters
When a web service is breached, data leaks. When an IoT system is breached, the damage can be physical. Researchers have shown that cars can be controlled remotely through their entertainment systems, and that implanted medical devices can be reprogrammed wirelessly. Doctors disabled the wireless features of a pacemaker implanted in a former US vice president because of exactly that concern. Botnets built from insecure cameras and routers have taken down major internet services (Chapter 9).
IoT also raises privacy concerns that traditional computing rarely did. Smart-home sensors, wearables and cameras record intimate details of daily life: when people are home, when they sleep, how they move, even their heartbeats. Facial, speech and activity recognition amplify what raw sensor data can reveal, and combining metadata from several devices can expose far more than any one of them. UCI’s TIPPERS project, an IoT testbed for privacy-preserving smart buildings, studied exactly these risks.
Security and privacy are not features to add at the end. They shape every layer of the design.

title: 14  Security and Privacy
text:
14.2 Concepts

Why IoT is hard to secure



Table 14.1: Why IoT security is difficult.









Challenge
Why it matters




Multiple technologies
An IoT system chains radios, gateways, cloud services, mobile apps and virtualization, each with its own vulnerabilities. Security is set by the weakest link.


Multiple verticals
eHealth, industry, smart homes and smart cities have very different requirements; one solution does not fit all.


Scale
Billions of devices make centralized, manual defenses impossible.


Big data
Each device produces streams of data that must be protected in transit and at rest.


Availability
Many systems must run continuously, sometimes to “five nines” (99.999%, about five minutes of downtime per year). Defenses must not take the system down.


Resource limits
Constrained devices are easy targets for denial of service, and expensive cryptography may not fit.


Remote locations
Unattended devices can be physically tampered with.


Mobility
Devices move between networks and owners’ infrastructure.


Delay sensitivity
Security mechanisms must not break real-time deadlines.


Long lifetimes
Devices may stay in service for 10–20 years, far longer than many vendors support them.








Security requirements
Following Dabbagh and Rayes (Dabbagh and Rayes 2017), a secure IoT system must provide:

Confidentiality: only the intended parties can understand exchanged messages.
Integrity: messages cannot be altered without detection.
Availability: the service keeps working. Denial-of-service attacks target this.
Authentication: every party is who it claims to be: devices, users, servers.
Authorization: every party may perform only the operations it is permitted to.
Freshness: data is current. Replay attacks resend an old, valid message, such as “unlock”, to drive a device back into an old state.
Non-repudiation: a party cannot deny an action it performed.
Forward secrecy (in the group-membership sense): a device that leaves the network cannot understand communications exchanged after it leaves.
Backward secrecy: a device that joins cannot understand communications exchanged before it joined.



Threat modeling with STRIDE
Before choosing defenses, identify what can go wrong. Threat modeling systematically asks how each part of a system could be attacked. Microsoft’s STRIDE mnemonic names six threat categories, each violating one security property:



Table 14.2: STRIDE threats in IoT.










Threat
Violates
IoT example




Spoofing
Authentication
A fake sensor reports false readings; a fake server sends commands


Tampering
Integrity
A message changing “set 21 °C” to “set 35 °C” in transit; modified firmware


Repudiation
Non-repudiation
A user denies sending the “unlock” command; no logs exist


Information disclosure
Confidentiality
Unencrypted MQTT reveals when a house is empty


Denial of service
Availability
Jamming the radio; flooding a device until it crashes or drains its battery


Elevation of privilege
Authorization
A guest’s phone app gains administrator control of a lock






A simple process: draw the system’s data flows (devices, gateways, brokers, cloud services, apps), mark the trust boundaries where data crosses from one party’s control to another’s, and for each element and flow ask which STRIDE threats apply. Then rank threats by likelihood and impact, and choose mitigations for the important ones.


A three-domain view of IoT security
It helps to divide an IoT system into three domains, each with its own attacks. The taxonomy below follows Dabbagh and Rayes (Dabbagh and Rayes 2017):

the cloud domain, which performs heavy computation and storage;
the fog domain (the edge), which aggregates, preprocesses and stores data close to the devices (Chapter 18);
the sensing domain, the smart objects themselves and their networks.


Cloud domain
Cloud IoT applications run in virtual machines (VMs) or containers that share physical servers, managed by a hypervisor. Sharing creates attack opportunities:



Table 14.3: Cloud-domain attacks.










Attack
How it works
Countermeasures




Side-channel (hidden-channel)
A malicious VM placed on the same server infers a victim’s secrets from shared hardware, for example by timing cache accesses
Hard isolation (dedicated caches or servers), co-residency allow-lists, cache flushing on switch


VM migration attacks
Attackers flood migration requests, advertise false capacity to attract VMs, or sniff and intercept VM memory in transit
Mutual authentication of servers, signed and encrypted control messages, sequence numbers, authenticated ARP


Theft of service
A VM games the scheduler to obtain more than its share of resources
Fair, precise scheduling and accounting


VM escape
A software bug lets a VM break out of the hypervisor and control the host
Patching, minimal hypervisors, nested isolation layers


Insider attacks
A data-center administrator accesses sensitive data
Encryption with keys the provider never sees; homomorphic encryption or secret-sharing storage for sensitive workloads








Fog domain
Fog devices virtualize computing resources close to the objects, so they inherit all cloud-domain attacks, and add some of their own:

Authentication and trust. Fog devices may be owned by many, less well-known parties, and a mobile device may hop between them. Devices must authenticate the fog node and decide whether to trust its owner; reputation systems can help.
Migration over the internet. VMs that follow mobile users move between fog nodes over the public internet, not a private data-center network, so migrations must be encrypted and authenticated.
Denial of service. Lower computing capacity makes fog nodes easier to overwhelm.
Privacy. A fog node can infer the location and habits of every connected device. Even wireless signals alone can reveal people’s presence, location and breathing; signal obfuscation can make such inference harder.
Containers. Lightweight containers share the operating system kernel as well as the hardware, which creates more opportunities for leakage and hijacking than full virtualization.



Sensing domain
The sensing domain faces attacks on its radios, its batteries and its routing:



Table 14.4: Sensing-domain attacks.










Attack
How it works
Countermeasures




Jamming
A transmitter interferes with legitimate signals at the receiver, or makes senders think the channel is busy. Jammers may be constant, deceptive (mimicking real frames), reactive (only when others transmit) or random.
Frequency hopping, spread spectrum, directional antennas, jamming detection (from signal strength and corrupted-packet ratios)


Vampire attacks
Drain batteries: denial of sleep (keeping devices awake, even with replayed encrypted control messages), flooding, and routing tricks such as carousel (looping source routes) and stretch (needlessly long routes)
Timestamps and freshness checks on control messages, rate limiting, path checks, disabling source routing


Selective forwarding
A malicious relay drops some packets (or all of them: a black hole)
Direct links where possible, path redundancy, trusted checkpoint nodes that acknowledge


Sinkhole
A node advertises a falsely short route to attract traffic, then reads or drops it
Intrusion detection using neighbor reports; authenticated routing






Physical access adds further risks: reading secrets from flash memory, attaching a debugger, or replacing firmware. Chapter 15 and Chapter 16 cover the hardware defenses.



Cryptographic building blocks
You do not need to design cryptography, and you never should. You do need to pick the right building block for each job:



Table 14.5: Cryptographic building blocks.










Goal
Building block
Common algorithms




Detect accidental corruption
Checksum / CRC
CRC-32 (not a security mechanism)


Fingerprint data
Cryptographic hash
SHA-256


Integrity + authenticity with a shared key
Message authentication code (MAC)
HMAC-SHA-256, AES-CMAC


Confidentiality with a shared key
Symmetric encryption
AES


Confidentiality + integrity together
Authenticated encryption (AEAD)
AES-GCM, AES-CCM, ChaCha20-Poly1305


Agree on a key over an open channel
Key exchange
ECDH (X25519, P-256)


Integrity + authenticity + non-repudiation
Digital signature
ECDSA (P-256), Ed25519


All of the above for a connection
Secure transport
TLS 1.3, DTLS 1.3






Three rules prevent most mistakes:

Use standard, well-reviewed libraries (mbedTLS on the ESP32) and standard protocols (TLS) rather than inventing your own.
Encryption is not integrity. An encrypted message can still be modified in ways that change its meaning unless it is also authenticated. Use AEAD or add a MAC.
Integrity is not freshness. A correctly signed “unlock” message can be replayed. Include a counter, a timestamp or a nonce, and reject messages that are old or repeated.


Signing messages on the kit
The ESP32 includes mbedTLS with hardware-accelerated SHA and AES. The following sketch attaches an HMAC and a monotonic counter to each command, so the receiver can detect both tampering and replay:
#include <mbedtls/md.h>

// Shared secret: provisioned per device, never hard-coded in a real product
static const uint8_t KEY[32] = { /* 32 random bytes */ };

String hmacHex(const String& msg) {
  uint8_t mac[32];
  const mbedtls_md_info_t* sha256 = mbedtls_md_info_from_type(MBEDTLS_MD_SHA256);
  mbedtls_md_hmac(sha256, KEY, sizeof KEY,
                  (const uint8_t*)msg.c_str(), msg.length(), mac);
  char hex[65];
  for (int i = 0; i < 32; i++) sprintf(hex + 2 * i, "%02x", mac[i]);
  return String(hex);
}

// Sender: "counter|command|mac"
String signCommand(uint32_t counter, const String& cmd) {
  String body = String(counter) + "|" + cmd;
  return body + "|" + hmacHex(body);
}

// Receiver: accept only authentic messages with a counter it has not seen
bool verifyCommand(const String& msg, String& cmdOut) {
  static uint32_t lastCounter = 0;              // persist this in flash in practice
  int a = msg.indexOf('|'), b = msg.lastIndexOf('|');
  if (a < 0 || b <= a) return false;
  String body = msg.substring(0, b);
  String mac  = msg.substring(b + 1);
  if (hmacHex(body) != mac) return false;       // tampered or wrong key
  uint32_t counter = msg.substring(0, a).toInt();
  if (counter <= lastCounter) return false;     // replayed or out of date
  lastCounter = counter;
  cmdOut = msg.substring(a + 1, b);
  return true;
}
In production code, compare MACs in constant time (so that timing does not reveal how many characters matched), store the counter in non-volatile memory so a reboot does not reset it, and keep the key in protected storage (Chapter 15). With a shared key, any device holding the key can also forge messages; digital signatures, where only the sender holds the private key, remove that limitation and also provide non-repudiation.



Privacy by design
Security protects data from attackers; privacy protects people, including from the system’s own operators. Practical principles include:

Data minimization: collect only what the application needs, at the coarsest resolution that works.
Local processing: compute on the device or at the edge, and send results instead of raw data (Chapter 18).
Purpose limitation and retention limits: use data only for the stated purpose, and delete it when it is no longer needed.
Transparency and control: tell people what is collected, and let them see, export and delete it.
Separation of identity: decouple device identifiers and data from the owner’s identity where possible, while still allowing the owner to prove ownership.

Many of these principles are also legal requirements (Chapter 17).






TipTry it on your kit: signed messages and STRIDE



This exercise corresponds to the security lecture activity.

Draw a data-flow diagram of the MQTT command center from Chapter 12: kits, broker, laptop client. Mark the trust boundaries.
Apply STRIDE to each element and flow. List at least one threat per category and rank the top three.
Add the HMAC scheme above to the command topic. Show that a command with a modified payload is rejected, and that replaying a captured valid command is also rejected.
Reboot the receiving kit and replay an old command. Does it succeed? Fix the problem.
Which STRIDE threats does your HMAC scheme not address?

A guided, step-by-step version for a lecture session is Activity 8.

title: 14  Security and Privacy
text:
14.3 In depth (optional)






Optional, in-depth explanation. This section goes beyond the rest of the chapter into the math and physics behind it. Nothing later in the book depends on it; skip it on a first reading.




How strong is strong enough?
Brute force and key length. A secret chosen uniformly from \(2^k\) possibilities takes, on average, \(2^{k-1}\) guesses to find. An attacker testing \(10^{12}\) keys per second needs about \(2^{55}/10^{12} \approx 10\) hours for a 56-bit key and \(2^{127}/10^{12} \approx 5\times10^{18}\) years for a 128-bit key. The difference is not 2.3 times but \(2^{72}\) times. Hence 128 bits as the modern floor for symmetric keys.
Human-chosen secrets are much weaker. A 6-digit PIN has \(10^6 \approx 2^{20}\) values; an 8-character password of lowercase letters \(26^8 \approx 2^{37.6}\). Default passwords shared by a whole product line have, effectively, zero bits. Rate limiting and lockout help online, but not against an attacker who has captured a hash and guesses offline.
Truncated authentication tags. A message authentication code (such as HMAC-SHA-256) is often truncated to save bytes on constrained links. An attacker who forges a message without the key succeeds with probability \(2^{-t}\) per attempt for a \(t\)-bit tag. A 32-bit tag gives one success in about 4 billion attempts: acceptable on a LoRa link limited to a few hundred messages per hour, unacceptable on a fast network that allows millions of attempts.
Nonces and the birthday bound. Many encryption modes need a nonce that never repeats under the same key. If nonces are chosen randomly from \(2^b\) values, the probability that \(n\) messages contain at least one repeat is approximately
\[
P_\text{collision} \approx 1 - e^{-n^2/2^{b+1}} \approx \frac{n^2}{2^{b+1}} .
\]
With 96-bit random nonces (the AES-GCM standard size), \(n = 2^{32}\) messages give \(P \approx 2^{-33}\): safe. With a 32-bit random nonce, collisions become likely after about \(2^{16} = 65\,536\) messages, a few days of a sensor reporting every few seconds. A counter avoids collisions entirely, provided it survives reboots (see Activity 8’s extension).
Risk as likelihood times impact. Threat modeling often scores each threat as
\[
\text{risk} = \text{likelihood} \times \text{impact},
\]
on simple 1–5 scales. The product is crude, but it forces two separate judgments and makes the ranking discussable. A cheap attack with small impact (reading one room’s temperature) can rank above an expensive attack with large impact (extracting a key from silicon), and that ranking is a design decision, not a fact.
Exercise. A command channel uses HMAC tags truncated to 24 bits and accepts up to 10 commands per second. How long would an attacker need, on average, to get one forged command accepted? What would you change?
Sources for this section: (Shostack 2014).

title: 14  Security and Privacy
text:
14.4 Design trade-offs







Decision
Considerations




Shared keys vs. public-key cryptography
Shared keys are fast and small but any key holder can impersonate others; public keys cost more computation but scale and give non-repudiation


Hop-by-hop vs. end-to-end security
Hop-by-hop (TLS to a broker) is simple but exposes data at each intermediary; end-to-end protects data through brokers and proxies


Security vs. availability
Locking out a device after failed checks can itself become a denial-of-service vector


Data collection vs. privacy
More data enables more features and more harm

title: 14  Security and Privacy
text:
14.5 Common pitfalls

Default or shared passwords across all units.
Disabling certificate verification to “make TLS work”.
Rolling your own cryptography or using outdated algorithms (MD5, SHA-1, DES, RC4).
No replay protection on commands.
Secrets in source code or firmware images, readable by anyone with the binary.
Debug interfaces left enabled in production (serial consoles, JTAG, open telnet).
Logging sensitive data in plain text.
Treating privacy as a policy document rather than as design decisions about what data exists.







NoteAdvanced track





Red-team review. Exchange your project’s architecture and repository with another team. Perform a structured security code review: threat-model their system with STRIDE, review their code for the pitfalls above, and write a short report with findings ranked by severity and concrete fixes. Chapter 22 describes the method in detail.
Lightweight cryptography. In 2023 NIST selected the Ascon family as its standard for lightweight cryptography, aimed at devices too constrained for AES-GCM. Read the NIST announcement and compare Ascon’s code size and performance with AES-GCM on a microcontroller.
Post-quantum readiness. Devices deployed today may still be in service when large quantum computers can break ECC and RSA. NIST published its first post-quantum standards (ML-KEM and ML-DSA) in 2024. What would it take to support them on an ESP32-class device, and why does this matter most for firmware-signing keys?

title: 14  Security and Privacy
text:
14.6 Check your understanding

Give two examples of IoT security failures with physical consequences.
Why does combining metadata from several devices threaten privacy more than any single device?
Explain the difference between integrity and freshness, with an example attack that violates freshness but not integrity.
What are forward and backward secrecy in a group of devices?
Apply STRIDE to a smart door lock with a phone app. Give one threat per category.
How does a denial-of-sleep attack work, even when control messages are encrypted? How do you defend against it?
What is a sinkhole attack, and why is it specific to multi-hop networks?
Why is encryption alone not enough to protect a command message?

title: 14  Security and Privacy
text:
14.7 Further reading

M. Dabbagh and A. Rayes, “Internet of Things Security and Privacy” (Dabbagh and Rayes 2017), the source of the three-domain attack taxonomy used in this chapter.
OWASP, IoT Top 10 (OWASP Foundation 2018), a list of the most common IoT security weaknesses.
V. Hassija et al., “A survey on IoT security: application areas, security threats, and solution architectures” (Hassija et al. 2019).
A. Shostack, Threat Modeling: Designing for Security (Shostack 2014).

title: 15  Device Identity and Secure Elements
text:
15.1 Why it matters
Almost every security property in Chapter 14 rests on one question: is this really the device it claims to be? A server that cannot tell a genuine thermostat from an impostor cannot trust its readings or decide who may send it commands. A device that cannot tell the genuine update server from an attacker will install whatever it is given.
Identity on the web is mostly about people, who can type passwords and answer second-factor prompts. Devices cannot. Their identity must be built in, unique to each unit, and protected even from someone who holds the device in their hands. This chapter explains how that is done, using the secure element in your kit as an example.
crumbs: 15  Device Identity and Secure Elements

title: 15  Device Identity and Secure Elements
text:
15.2 Concepts

Identifiers and credentials
Two things are easily confused:

An identifier names a device: a serial number, a MAC address, a UUID, a client ID. Identifiers are not secret. Anyone can read a MAC address from the air.
A credential proves the device is entitled to that name: a password, a shared key, or a private key with a certificate. Credentials must be secret, or at least their private part must be.

A device that authenticates with only its identifier (“I am kit-07”) is not authenticated at all.
Credentials must also be unique per device. If every unit shares the same key or password, compromising one device, for example by reading its flash memory, compromises the whole fleet. The Mirai botnet (Chapter 9) and many later attacks exploited exactly this.


Shared secrets and public keys
There are two broad ways for a device to prove its identity:

Shared secrets. The device and the server both know a key, and the device proves it knows the key, for example by computing an HMAC over a random challenge from the server. This is cheap, but the server must store every device’s secret, and anything that holds the secret can impersonate the device.
Public-key cryptography. The device holds a private key that never leaves it, and the server knows the matching public key. The device proves its identity by signing a challenge; anyone with the public key can verify the signature, but only the private key could have produced it. The server stores nothing secret about the device.

Elliptic-curve cryptography (ECC) makes public-key operations practical on small devices: a 256-bit ECC key (such as on the NIST P-256 curve) offers security comparable to a 3 072-bit RSA key, with much smaller keys and signatures and much less computation.


Certificates and PKI
How does a server know which public key belongs to which device, without a list of every device in advance? With a certificate: a signed statement, in the standard X.509 format, that binds a public key to an identity (“this public key belongs to device kit-07, made by IoT@UCI”). The statement is signed by a certificate authority (CA).
A public-key infrastructure (PKI) is the system of CAs, certificates and policies that makes this work. It forms a chain of trust:

A root CA certificate, whose key is kept offline and highly protected, is trusted in advance by the server.
The root signs an intermediate CA certificate, used day to day, for example at the factory.
The intermediate signs each device certificate.

To authenticate, the device presents its certificate and the intermediate certificate, and signs a challenge. The server checks each signature in the chain up to the root it trusts, then checks the device’s signature with the public key in the device certificate.
The same structure protects the other direction. When your kit connects to a broker with TLS, it verifies the server’s certificate chain against a root CA certificate stored in the firmware (setCACert() in Chapter 12). When both sides present certificates, the connection uses mutual TLS (mTLS), the standard way for devices to authenticate to cloud IoT platforms such as AWS IoT Core and Azure IoT Hub.
Certificates also carry validity periods, and CAs can revoke compromised certificates. Devices that run for years need a plan for both, including a way to check the current time securely.


Protecting the private key
A private key stored in ordinary flash memory can be read by anyone who can attach a programmer to the chip or extract the firmware image. Protecting it is the job of a hardware root of trust: hardware that stores keys and performs cryptographic operations so that the key itself is never exposed, even to the device’s own software.

Secure elements
A secure element is a small, dedicated chip designed to store keys and use them without revealing them, and to resist physical attacks: probing, glitching the power supply, and measuring power consumption or timing to infer secrets.
The kit’s Microchip ATECC608A is a typical example (ATECC608A CryptoAuthentication Device Summary Datasheet, n.d.). Connected to the I²C bus at address 0x60 (often listed as 0xC0 in its 8-bit form), it provides:

16 key slots for private keys, public keys, certificates and other data, each with configurable access rules;
ECC P-256 key generation inside the chip, ECDSA signing and verification, and ECDH key agreement;
SHA-256 and HMAC;
a hardware random number generator;
monotonic counters, useful for replay protection and limiting key use;
a unique 72-bit serial number.

A private key generated inside the ATECC608A never leaves the chip. Software asks the chip to sign a digest, and the chip returns only the signature. Even if an attacker dumps the ESP32’s entire flash, the device’s identity remains safe.


Configuration and locking
A new ATECC608A has two zones that must be locked before it can be used for real cryptography:

the configuration zone, which defines what each slot may hold and how it may be used;
the data zone, which holds keys and certificates.

Locking is permanent. Once the configuration zone is locked, it can never be changed. Until it is locked, some functions are restricted: for example, the random number generator returns a fixed test pattern rather than random data. In the course, kits are provisioned and locked by the teaching staff; do not run locking examples on your own kit.


Using the secure element
Libraries such as SparkFun’s ATECCX08A library or Microchip’s CryptoAuthLib wrap the chip’s command set. Reading the chip’s identity and generating random numbers on a provisioned kit looks like this:
#include <Wire.h>
#include <SparkFun_ATECCX08a_Arduino_Library.h>

ATECCX08A atecc;

void setup() {
  Serial.begin(115200);
  Wire.begin(21, 22);
  if (!atecc.begin(0x60)) {                      // 7-bit address
    Serial.println("ATECC608A not found");
    while (true) delay(1000);
  }
  atecc.readConfigZone(false);                   // reads serial number and lock bits
  Serial.print("Serial: ");
  for (int i = 0; i < 9; i++) Serial.printf("%02X", atecc.serialNumber[i]);
  Serial.printf("\nConfig locked: %s  Data locked: %s\n",
                atecc.configLockStatus ? "yes" : "no",
                atecc.dataOTPLockStatus ? "yes" : "no");

  if (atecc.configLockStatus) {
    Serial.printf("Random: %lu\n", atecc.getRandomLong());   // true hardware randomness
  }
}

void loop() {}
With a key in slot 0, signing a 32-byte message digest is a single call (atecc.createSignature(digest, 0) in the SparkFun library), and the matching public key can be read out and placed in a certificate.


Other roots of trust



Table 15.1: Hardware roots of trust.










Mechanism
What it is
Examples




Secure element
Separate tamper-resistant chip with its own key storage and crypto
ATECC608A, NXP SE050, Infineon OPTIGA Trust M


eFuses
One-time-programmable bits inside the MCU, readable only by hardware
ESP32 keys for secure boot and flash encryption (Chapter 16)


Digital signature peripheral
MCU block that signs with a key the CPU cannot read
ESP32-S2, S3, C3, C6 (not the original ESP32)


Trusted Platform Module
Standardized secure chip, common in PCs and gateways
TPM 2.0


Trusted execution environment
Isolated region of the main processor
Arm TrustZone-M, ESP-TEE


eSIM / iSIM
SIM functions, including identity, built into the module or chip
Cellular IoT devices






Certification schemes such as PSA Certified and SESIP evaluate how well a chip or device protects its roots of trust.



Provisioning: giving a device its identity
Provisioning is the process of giving each device its identity and credentials. It usually happens in two phases.
At manufacturing, each device:

generates a key pair inside its secure element (or has one injected in a secure facility);
has its public key signed by the manufacturer’s intermediate CA, producing a unique device certificate;
stores the certificate in the secure element or flash;
is registered (or its certificate chain is registered) with the cloud service.

Secure-element vendors offer pre-provisioned parts, with keys and certificates loaded in the factory, so that even small companies can ship unique device identities without building their own secure facility.
At onboarding (or commissioning), the owner claims the device and connects it to their network and account. Examples include scanning a QR code with a phone app, as in Matter, or just-in-time registration, where a cloud platform automatically accepts any device whose certificate chains to a registered CA. Matter combines both phases: every certified device carries a device attestation certificate proving it is a genuine, certified product, and commissioning adds operational credentials for the owner’s network.


Identity beyond authentication
A strong device identity enables much more than logging in:

authorization policies that refer to specific devices or groups;
audit logs that tie every action to a device, supporting non-repudiation;
secure updates, where devices verify the identity of the update server and the signer of the firmware (Chapter 16);
revocation: disabling a stolen or compromised device without affecting the rest of the fleet;
ownership transfer: re-provisioning a device when it is sold, without letting the previous owner retain access.







TipTry it on your kit: who are you?




Read and print your kit’s ATECC608A serial number and lock status. Compare serial numbers with another team: are they really unique?
Compare the ESP32’s MAC address (WiFi.macAddress()) with the secure element’s serial number. Which one is a credential? Which could an attacker copy?
If your kit is provisioned, generate 10 random numbers with the secure element and 10 with esp_random(). Why might a product prefer one over the other?
Design a challenge–response protocol in which the course server verifies that a message really came from your kit’s secure element. Which parts must be secret, and where does each live?

title: 15  Device Identity and Secure Elements
text:
15.3 In depth (optional)






Optional, in-depth explanation. This section goes beyond the rest of the chapter into the math and physics behind it. Nothing later in the book depends on it; skip it on a first reading.




Inside an ECDSA signature
The ATECC608A signs with ECDSA over the NIST P-256 curve. The arithmetic is worth seeing once, because it explains both why the scheme is secure and how it fails.
The setting. Points \((x, y)\) satisfying \(y^2 = x^3 - 3x + b \pmod p\), for a fixed 256-bit prime \(p\) and constant \(b\), form a group under a geometric “addition” rule. A fixed generator point \(G\) has a large prime order \(n\): adding \(G\) to itself \(n\) times returns to the identity. Computing \(Q = dG\) (adding \(G\) to itself \(d\) times, done efficiently by doubling and adding) is fast; recovering \(d\) from \(Q\) is the elliptic-curve discrete logarithm problem, believed to take about \(2^{128}\) operations for P-256.

Private key: a random integer \(d\) with \(1 \le d < n\), generated inside the chip.
Public key: the point \(Q = dG\) (64 bytes: \(x\) and \(y\)).

Signing a message \(m\), with \(z\) = the leftmost 256 bits of \(\text{SHA-256}(m)\):

Choose a fresh secret random \(k\) in \([1, n-1]\).
Compute \((x_1, y_1) = kG\) and \(r = x_1 \bmod n\).
Compute \(s = k^{-1}(z + r\,d) \bmod n\).
The signature is \((r, s)\): two 32-byte integers, the 64 bytes in Activity 8.

Verifying with the public key \(Q\):

Compute \(w = s^{-1} \bmod n\), \(u_1 = z w \bmod n\), \(u_2 = r w \bmod n\).
Compute \((x_2, y_2) = u_1 G + u_2 Q\), and accept if \(x_2 \equiv r \pmod n\).

It works because \(u_1 G + u_2 Q = w(z + r d)\,G = w\,s\,k\,G = kG\).
Why the nonce must never repeat. If two signatures \((r, s_1)\) and \((r, s_2)\) on hashes \(z_1 \ne z_2\) use the same \(k\) (visible because \(r\) is equal), subtracting the two signing equations gives
\[
k = \frac{z_1 - z_2}{s_1 - s_2} \bmod n, \qquad d = \frac{s_1 k - z_1}{r} \bmod n .
\]
Two signatures reveal the private key. Even a slightly biased \(k\) leaks it, given enough signatures. Generating \(k\) inside a secure element with a hardware random-number generator, or deterministically from the key and message (RFC 6979), removes this failure mode.
Why a signature proves so little about time. Nothing in \((r, s)\) depends on when it was made. A valid signature proves who signed which bytes; freshness must be inside the signed bytes (a counter, timestamp or challenge), as Activity 8 shows.
Exercise. Verification needs two scalar multiplications, signing one. On a microcontroller where a P-256 scalar multiplication takes 50 ms in software, how many signatures per second can a gateway verify? What changes if the gateway uses a secure element that verifies in 60 ms?
Sources for this section: (National Institute of Standards and Technology 2023; Pornin 2013; ATECC608A CryptoAuthentication Device Summary Datasheet, n.d.).

title: 15  Device Identity and Secure Elements
text:
15.4 Design trade-offs







Decision
Considerations




Shared secrets vs. certificates
Shared secrets are simple and cheap; certificates scale, keep servers free of secrets and support revocation


Software keys vs. secure element
A secure element costs about a dollar per unit and a little complexity, and protects keys against physical extraction


Own PKI vs. pre-provisioned parts
Running a CA requires secure processes; pre-provisioned parts outsource them


Long-lived vs. short-lived certificates
Long-lived certificates avoid renewal in the field; short-lived ones limit damage from compromise
crumbs: 15  Device Identity and Secure Elements

title: 15  Device Identity and Secure Elements
text:
15.5 Common pitfalls

Using a MAC address or serial number as a credential. Identifiers are public.
The same key in every device. One extraction compromises the fleet.
Private keys in firmware images or source repositories.
Locking a secure element with the wrong configuration. It is irreversible.
Never planning for revocation or renewal. Certificates expire, and some devices will be compromised.
Accepting any certificate. Disabling verification makes TLS useless against impersonation.







NoteAdvanced track





Build a mini-PKI. With OpenSSL on your laptop, create a root CA, an intermediate CA and a device certificate for your kit’s public key. Configure a local Mosquitto broker to require client certificates, and connect the kit with mutual TLS. Then revoke the device certificate and show that the broker rejects it.
Side channels. Software ECC implementations can leak private keys through timing or power consumption. Read about the “Minerva” and “TPM-Fail” timing attacks, and explain which properties of a secure element are designed to resist them.
Ownership transfer. Design the process for reselling a used smart lock: what the seller does, what the buyer does, what the cloud service does, and how you guarantee that the seller can no longer open the door.
