title: 16  Over-the-Air Updates and the Device Lifecycle
text:
16.1 Why it matters
Every non-trivial program has bugs, and some of them are security vulnerabilities. For a laptop or phone, the fix arrives as an update the next week. For an IoT device, someone has to build an update mechanism into the product before it ships, or the bug is permanent. Recalling devices or sending technicians to thousands of sites is rarely possible.
A broken update mechanism is worse than none. An update that fails halfway through, or that installs firmware that crashes, can turn every device in the field into a “brick”. An update mechanism that accepts unsigned firmware hands attackers a way to install their own code on the whole fleet. Getting updates right, and securing the boot process that runs them, is one of the most important engineering tasks in IoT.
crumbs: 16  Over-the-Air Updates and the Device Lifecycle

title: 16  Over-the-Air Updates and the Device Lifecycle
text:
16.2 Concepts

The device lifecycle
An IoT device passes through several stages, and security must be considered in each:



Table 16.1: The IoT device lifecycle.










Stage
Activities
Security concerns




Design
Architecture, component choice, threat modeling
Choosing hardware with a root of trust; planning for updates


Manufacture
Building and testing; flashing firmware
Protecting signing keys; injecting unique identities (Chapter 15)


Provisioning and onboarding
Registering the device and connecting it to an owner
Proving genuineness; claiming ownership securely


Operation
Normal use, monitoring, remote configuration
Detecting faults and attacks; protecting data


Update
Fixing bugs and vulnerabilities, adding features
Authentic, reliable updates; recovering from failures


Transfer
Resale or change of owner
Removing the previous owner’s access and data


Decommissioning
Retirement and disposal
Wiping data and credentials; revoking identities






Embedded programmers must assume a deployed device is physically unreachable (Chapter 4). The update mechanism is therefore the only way to change a device’s behavior for the rest of its life.


Over-the-air updates
An over-the-air (OTA) update delivers new software to a device through its network connection: directly over Wi-Fi or cellular, or through a gateway that relays it over a local link such as Bluetooth. OTA updates are routine in phones and cars, where they update everything from infotainment screens to engine and brake control software.
To reduce download time and cost, updates are often sent as a delta: only the differences between the old and new image, which the device applies to its current firmware. The delta, together with metadata and security credentials (the signature, version numbers, target hardware), forms an update package.
A complete OTA system has two halves:



Table 16.2: Requirements of an OTA update system.









Server side
Device side




Management of users, devices and groups
Agnostic to the network used to deliver the image


Scalable, highly available distribution (often a CDN)
Small enough to fit in flash alongside the application


Authentication and authorization for publishing updates
Verifies authenticity and integrity before installing


An API for devices to check for and fetch updates
Survives power loss at any moment during the update


Delta generation and compression
Supports rollback and recovery from bad images


Staged rollout, monitoring and analytics
Integrates with secure boot and the device’s identity








A/B partitions on the ESP32
The ESP32 stores its firmware in external flash, divided into partitions described by a partition table. An OTA-capable layout includes:

otadata: a small partition recording which application slot to boot;
ota_0 and ota_1: two application slots;
optionally a factory slot with a known-good image;
nvs for settings and other data partitions.

The device always runs from one slot and downloads updates into the other (Figure 16.1). Only when the new image has been completely written and verified does it update otadata to point at the new slot and reboot. If power fails during the download, the old image is untouched and still marked as the one to boot. This A/B (dual-bank) scheme is the core of reliable updates.






Figure 16.1: A/B updates: the new image is written to the inactive slot, verified, and only then selected for the next boot.




Rollback
A new image can be complete and correctly signed, yet still fail: it crashes on start-up, cannot connect to the network, or cannot reach the update server, which would make it impossible to fix with another update. With rollback enabled, the bootloader marks a newly installed image as pending verification. The new firmware must run its self-tests and then confirm that it is healthy; if it reboots before confirming, the bootloader returns to the previous image.
#include <esp_ota_ops.h>

void confirmFirmwareIfHealthy() {
  const esp_partition_t* running = esp_ota_get_running_partition();
  esp_ota_img_states_t state;
  if (esp_ota_get_state_partition(running, &state) == ESP_OK &&
      state == ESP_OTA_IMG_PENDING_VERIFY) {
    bool ok = connectWiFi() && reachUpdateServer() && sensorsRespond();  // your checks
    if (ok) esp_ota_mark_app_valid_cancel_rollback();
    else    esp_ota_mark_app_invalid_rollback_and_reboot();
  }
}
(Rollback must be enabled when the bootloader is built, which the default Arduino-ESP32 configuration does not do; it is available with ESP-IDF, or with PlatformIO using the ESP-IDF framework or custom configuration.)



Fetching updates
The Arduino-ESP32 core offers two update paths:

ArduinoOTA lets a developer push new firmware from PlatformIO over the local network instead of over USB. It is convenient during development but does not scale to a fleet.
HTTP(S) update lets a device pull an image from a server:

#include <WiFiClientSecure.h>
#include <HTTPUpdate.h>

void checkForUpdate() {
  WiFiClientSecure tls;
  tls.setCACert(ROOT_CA_PEM);                     // authenticate the update server
  httpUpdate.rebootOnUpdate(true);
  t_httpUpdate_return r = httpUpdate.update(
      tls, "https://updates.example.org/kit/firmware.bin", FIRMWARE_VERSION);
  switch (r) {
    case HTTP_UPDATE_NO_UPDATES: Serial.println("Up to date"); break;
    case HTTP_UPDATE_FAILED:
      Serial.printf("Update failed: %s\n", httpUpdate.getLastErrorString().c_str());
      break;
    case HTTP_UPDATE_OK: break;                   // not reached: the device reboots
  }
}
TLS authenticates the server and protects the image in transit. That is necessary but not sufficient: if the update server itself is compromised, it can serve malicious firmware over a perfectly valid TLS connection. The image itself must be signed by the developer, and the device must verify the signature before installing or booting it. That is the job of secure boot.


Secure boot and the chain of trust
Secure boot ensures that a device runs only software signed by its legitimate developer. It builds a chain of trust in which each stage verifies the next before handing over control:

Key generation. The developer creates a signing key pair and keeps the private key in a secure location, ideally a hardware security module.
Signing. Each firmware image is hashed, and the digest is signed with the private key. The signature is attached to the image.
Verification at boot.

The ROM bootloader runs first. It is in mask ROM inside the chip, so it cannot be modified and is trusted by definition.
The ROM reads the public key attached to the second-stage bootloader, hashes it, and compares the hash with a digest stored in eFuses (below). If they match, it verifies the bootloader’s signature with that key.
The verified bootloader repeats the process for the application image, before running it and before accepting an OTA image.


Why store only a hash of the public key in the eFuses rather than the key itself? eFuse space is scarce (a 3 072-bit RSA key would not fit in a 256-bit block), and a hash is enough to confirm that the key presented with the image is the right one.
On the ESP32, Secure Boot V2 (available on chip revision 3 and later) uses RSA-3072 signatures with the scheme above; newer Espressif chips also support ECDSA. The original Secure Boot V1 used a symmetric scheme and is now deprecated.


eFuses
The ESP32 contains 1 024 bits of eFuse memory: one-time-programmable bits, organized in four 256-bit blocks, that are burned by a high current and can never be reset. They hold:

the flash-encryption key and the secure-boot key digest, in blocks that can be made read-protected, so that only the hardware can use them and no software (including the device’s own firmware) can read them;
configuration bits that permanently enable secure boot and flash encryption, and permanently disable features an attacker could abuse, such as JTAG debugging and the UART download mode used to flash new firmware over USB.

Because eFuses are permanent, enabling secure boot or flash encryption on a production device is a one-way decision. Mistakes can brick the chip, so these features are practiced on spare boards, never on a kit you need.


Flash encryption
Secure boot stops a device from running unauthorized code, but it does not stop someone from reading the flash chip to extract firmware, Wi-Fi passwords or keys stored in software. Flash encryption protects the contents of the external flash with AES:

Firmware is flashed as plain text, and encrypted in place on the first boot.
From then on, all memory-mapped reads from flash are decrypted transparently by hardware as code runs, and writes are encrypted, using the key in the eFuses.
Someone who removes and reads the flash chip sees only ciphertext.

Secure boot and flash encryption are designed to be used together, with JTAG and UART download disabled, for production devices.


Operating a fleet
Shipping an update mechanism is only the start. Running it safely across thousands of devices requires:

Version management: every device reports its firmware version, and the server knows which versions exist where.
Staged rollouts: release to a small percentage of devices first, watch crash rates and health metrics, then expand. Halt automatically if failures rise.
Anti-rollback: prevent attackers from installing an older, validly signed but vulnerable version, using a security version number checked against an eFuse or secure-element counter.
Monitoring and logging: health reports, crash dumps and connectivity statistics, so problems are visible before customers report them.
Remote configuration: changing parameters without a full firmware update.
A software bill of materials (SBOM): a list of all software components and versions in each image, so that when a vulnerability is announced in a library, you know which devices are affected.
A support period: a published commitment to how long security updates will be provided, increasingly a legal requirement (Chapter 17).
End of life: when support ends, devices should fail safe, and owners should be able to wipe them.







TipTry it on your kit: a safe update



Use a spare board or the Wokwi simulator for steps that change eFuses; never burn eFuses on a kit you need.

Print the running partition’s label and the firmware version at boot. Use PlatformIO’s partition table option to select a layout with two OTA slots.
Host two firmware versions on a laptop web server and update the kit over HTTP, then HTTPS. Confirm that the running slot changes.
Pull the USB cable in the middle of an update. What does the kit run when power returns, and why?
Write the health checks your project firmware should run before confirming a new image.
Write a short plan (one page) for updating 500 deployed kits: rollout stages, metrics, halt criteria and rollback.

title: 16  Over-the-Air Updates and the Device Lifecycle
text:
16.3 In depth (optional)






Optional, in-depth explanation. This section goes beyond the rest of the chapter into the math and physics behind it. Nothing later in the book depends on it; skip it on a first reading.




The numbers behind a safe rollout
How long does an update take to download? Time is size divided by effective throughput:
\[
t = \frac{8\,S}{R_\text{eff}} .
\]
A 1.2 MB firmware image over Wi-Fi at an effective 2 Mb/s takes about 5 s. Over LoRa at SF7 the raw rate is about 5.5 kb/s, but a 1% duty-cycle limit leaves 55 b/s on average: \(8 \times 1.2\times10^6 / 55 \approx 1.7\times10^5\) s, almost two days, before counting lost packets. Hence delta updates (send only the changed bytes), compression, and firmware-update-over-the-air schemes for LPWANs that multicast fragments with forward error correction.
Canary rollouts catch rare failures. Suppose a new version bricks a fraction \(p\) of devices in some unusual configuration. Updating a random canary group of \(n\) devices first reveals the problem with probability
\[
P_\text{detect} = 1 - (1-p)^n .
\]
For \(p = 1\%\) and \(n = 300\), \(P \approx 1 - e^{-3} \approx 95\%\). To catch a 0.1% failure with the same confidence you need about 3000 canaries. The rule of thumb \(n \approx 3/p\) for 95% confidence comes from \(e^{-np} \approx (1-p)^n = 0.05\).
Why A/B partitions matter. If a power cut during an in-place update bricks the device with probability \(q\) per update, and the fleet does \(u\) updates per year, the expected number of bricked devices per year is \(N u q\). For 100 000 devices, four updates a year and \(q = 10^{-4}\), that is 40 truck rolls per year. A/B partitions (Figure 16.1) make \(q\) effectively zero for power loss: the old image is untouched until the new one has booted and confirmed itself.
Flash wear. NOR flash sectors survive on the order of \(10^5\) erase cycles. A full image rewrite once a week uses 52 cycles a year, harmless. Logging a sensor reading to the same sector every second would exhaust it in about a day, which is why logs use wear-leveling file systems or rotate across many sectors.
Exercise. Your fleet has 20 000 devices. You want 95% confidence of catching a defect affecting 0.5% of devices before more than 5% of the fleet is updated. Is that possible? How many stages would you use?
Sources for this section: (Moran et al. 2021; Espressif Systems, n.d.-a).

Decision
Considerations




Full images vs. deltas
Deltas save bandwidth but need the exact old image and more complex tooling


Push vs. pull
Pull (device checks periodically) works through NAT; push (server notifies) gives faster response


Automatic vs. user-approved updates
Automatic updates patch faster; user approval respects control but leaves devices unpatched

Strong protection, at the cost of irreversible configuration and harder debugging


Factory image
A known-good fallback costs flash space

title: 16  Over-the-Air Updates and the Device Lifecycle
text:
16.5 Common pitfalls

One firmware slot. A failed update bricks the device.
TLS without image signing. A compromised server can push malicious firmware.
No health check before confirming. A new image that cannot reach the update server can never be fixed.
Signing keys on a developer laptop or in a CI system without protection.
Updating the whole fleet at once.
No anti-rollback, allowing downgrade attacks.
Burning eFuses on development boards by accident.
Forgetting the end of life. Unsupported devices stay on networks for years.







NoteAdvanced track





Update frameworks. Compare the ESP-IDF OTA APIs with general-purpose update frameworks such as Mender, SWUpdate, RAUC, and MCUboot (used with Zephyr). The IETF SUIT working group defines a standard manifest format for IoT firmware updates; read its architecture document (RFC 9019) and map its concepts onto the ESP32.
The Uptane framework. Vehicle updates use Uptane, which separates the roles of image repository and director, and uses multiple keys with different privileges, so that compromising one server is not enough to install malicious firmware. Explain how this design defends against a compromised update server.

title: 17  Compliance and Regulation
text:
17.1 Why it matters
A prototype on a lab bench is not a product. Before a connected device can be sold, it must usually show that its radio stays within its assigned frequencies and power, that it will not electrocute or burn anyone, that it does not contain banned substances, and, increasingly, that it meets minimum cybersecurity standards. Selling in another country often means another set of rules.
For a long time, cybersecurity was voluntary. That has changed. The European Union’s Cyber Resilience Act makes security requirements mandatory for almost all products with digital elements sold in the EU, and its first obligations took effect in September 2026. The UK already bans default passwords. Asking “does it ship in the EU?” now changes design decisions from the first week of a project: whether the device has unique credentials, whether it can be updated, and how long the company will support it.

title: 17  Compliance and Regulation
text:
17.2 Concepts

Why connected products are regulated
Regulation protects people and shared resources from harms that individual buyers cannot judge for themselves:

Radio spectrum is shared; one badly designed transmitter can disrupt many other users, including emergency services.
Electrical safety and fire risks are invisible until something fails.
Hazardous substances and electronic waste harm the environment.
Insecure devices harm not only their owners but everyone else, as botnets such as Mirai showed (Chapter 9).
Personal data collected by devices can be misused.

Regulation typically works through conformity assessment: the manufacturer (or an independent test lab) shows that the product meets the relevant requirements, documents the evidence in a technical file, and marks the product accordingly.


Radio and electromagnetic compatibility
Every device that transmits radio waves, or that unintentionally emits radio-frequency noise, is regulated:

United States. The FCC regulates radio devices. Most IoT radios operate in unlicensed bands under Part 15 of the FCC rules, which limits transmit power, bandwidth, and, in some bands, how long a device may occupy a channel. Products need FCC equipment authorization and display an FCC ID.
European Union. The Radio Equipment Directive (RED) covers radio products. A manufacturer who shows compliance affixes the CE mark. In the EU’s 868 MHz band, devices must respect strict duty-cycle limits, often 1% of the time.

Testing a radio product costs time and money. Pre-certified modules, such as the ESP32-WROOM-32 or the RFM95W, have already passed radio testing. A product that uses one, without changing its antenna or RF design, can often rely on the module’s certification for the radio part (in the US, under the modular approval rules), and only needs testing for unintentional emissions and the complete product. This is a major reason products use modules rather than bare radio chips.
Hardware is also regional: a LoRa radio built for the US 902–928 MHz band must not be operated in Europe, and vice versa (Chapter 10).


Safety and environmental rules

Electrical safety standards such as IEC/UL 62368-1 cover audio, video and IT equipment, including most IoT devices; battery-powered products also face battery-safety and transport rules for lithium cells.
RoHS restricts hazardous substances such as lead, mercury and cadmium in electronics sold in the EU, and similar rules apply in other regions.
WEEE requires producers in the EU to finance the collection and recycling of electronic waste, which is why products carry a crossed-out wheelie-bin symbol.



Cybersecurity regulation

A common baseline
Most IoT cybersecurity rules draw on the same baseline. The European standard ETSI EN 303 645 (ETSI EN 303 645: Cyber Security for Consumer Internet of Things: Baseline Requirements 2020) and the US NIST IR 8259 series (Fagan et al. 2020) are the most influential sources. Their key provisions are:

No universal default passwords. Each device must have a unique credential or require the user to set one.
A vulnerability disclosure policy. A public way for researchers to report vulnerabilities, and a process to act on reports.
Software updates. Devices must be securely updatable, and the manufacturer must state how long updates will be provided.
Secure storage of credentials and sensitive data.
Secure communication, using current cryptography.
Minimized attack surface: unused ports, services and debug interfaces disabled.
Software integrity: verifying software before it runs.
Protection of personal data.
Resilience to outages of networks and power.
Easy deletion of user data, and ways for users to configure the device securely.

Each of these maps directly onto techniques in Part IV.


European Union

RED cybersecurity requirements. Since 1 August 2025, internet-connected radio equipment sold in the EU must meet cybersecurity, privacy and anti-fraud requirements under a delegated act of the Radio Equipment Directive. The harmonized standards EN 18031-1, -2 and -3 describe how to meet them.
The Cyber Resilience Act (CRA) (Regulation (EU) 2024/2847 of the European Parliament and of the Council on horizontal cybersecurity requirements for products with digital elements (Cyber Resilience Act) 2024) covers almost all hardware and software “products with digital elements”. It entered into force in December 2024 with a staged timeline:

From 11 September 2026, manufacturers must report actively exploited vulnerabilities and severe security incidents to authorities (through ENISA’s single reporting platform) within strict deadlines.
From 11 December 2027, the full requirements apply: security by design and by default, a vulnerability-handling process, security updates for a defined support period (generally at least five years, or the expected product lifetime if shorter), an SBOM, conformity assessment and CE marking. Products deemed “important” or “critical” face stricter assessment.

The EU Data Act, applying from September 2025, gives users of connected products rights to access and share the data their devices generate.



United Kingdom
The Product Security and Telecommunications Infrastructure (PSTI) regime, in force since 29 April 2024, requires consumer connectable products sold in the UK to have no universal default passwords, to publish a way to report vulnerabilities, and to state the minimum period for which security updates will be provided.


United States
The US has no single federal IoT security law for consumer products. Instead:

California’s SB-327 (in force since 2020), and a similar Oregon law, require connected devices to have “reasonable security features”, including unique passwords or a forced password change on first use.
The IoT Cybersecurity Improvement Act of 2020 sets security requirements for IoT devices bought by federal agencies, based on NIST guidance.
The US Cyber Trust Mark is a voluntary FCC labeling program for consumer IoT products, based on NIST criteria. After its first lead administrator withdrew, the FCC selected the ioXt Alliance in April 2026; as of late October 2026 the FCC was still finalizing testing procedures, and no labeled products had yet reached store shelves (Nextgov/FCW 2026).
Sector regulators add their own rules (below).




Privacy and data protection
IoT devices often collect personal data, which data-protection laws regulate regardless of the product’s security:

The EU’s General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) requires a lawful basis for processing, data minimization, purpose limitation, security, and rights for individuals to access, correct and delete their data. Its principle of data protection by design and by default is effectively an engineering requirement.
In the US, state laws such as California’s CCPA (as amended by the CPRA) give consumers rights over personal information, and the FTC acts against companies whose security or privacy practices are deceptive or unfair.
Data that crosses borders may face transfer restrictions.

The design principles in Chapter 14 (minimization, local processing, retention limits, transparency) are the practical way to meet these obligations.


Sector-specific rules
Some domains add their own requirements on top of the general ones:

Medical devices. In the US, the FDA regulates connected medical devices; since 2023, manufacturers of “cyber devices” must submit cybersecurity plans, an SBOM and evidence of secure design with their applications. The EU Medical Device Regulation includes similar requirements. Health data may also fall under HIPAA.
Automotive. UN Regulations No. 155 (cybersecurity management) and No. 156 (software updates) apply to new vehicles in many markets.
Industrial systems. The IEC 62443 series defines security levels and processes for industrial automation and control systems.
Critical infrastructure and government procurement often add their own lists of approved or prohibited components and suppliers.



From regulation to engineering tasks
Regulatory requirements become concrete work items:



Table 17.1: Turning regulation into engineering work.









Requirement
Engineering task




No default passwords
Per-device credentials from provisioning (Chapter 15); first-use setup flow


Secure updates for a support period
Signed OTA with rollback (Chapter 16); budget for maintenance


Vulnerability handling and reporting
A security.txt or disclosure page; an internal triage process; ability to ship fixes quickly


SBOM
Generate a component list at build time


Secure storage and communication
Secure element or flash encryption; TLS with verification


Minimal attack surface
Disable debug interfaces and unused services in production builds


Data protection
Data inventory; minimization; deletion and export features


Radio compliance
Pre-certified modules; correct regional frequency plans; respect duty cycles












TipTry it on your kit: does it ship in the EU?



This exercise corresponds to the compliance discussion in lecture.

Assume your course project will be sold as a consumer product in the EU and the UK. Go through the ETSI EN 303 645 baseline above and mark each provision as met, partly met or not met by your current design.
List the three changes that would close the biggest gaps, and estimate the effort for each.
Your kit’s LoRa radio is a US 915 MHz part. What would have to change to sell the product in Europe?
Write a one-paragraph “security support statement” for your product, stating how long it will receive security updates and how people can report vulnerabilities.

title: 17  Compliance and Regulation
text:
17.3 In depth (optional)






Optional, in-depth explanation. This section goes beyond the rest of the chapter into the math and physics behind it. Nothing later in the book depends on it; skip it on a first reading.




Decibels, power limits and duty cycles
Radio rules are written in units that are easy to misread, and a factor of 10 is easy to miss.
Decibels relative to a milliwatt. Power in dBm is
\[
P_\text{dBm} = 10 \log_{10}\frac{P}{1\ \text{mW}} ,
\]
so 1 mW = 0 dBm, 25 mW ≈ 14 dBm, 100 mW = 20 dBm and 1 W = 30 dBm. Each 3 dB doubles the power; each 10 dB multiplies it by ten. Gains and losses then simply add.
EIRP and ERP. Limits usually apply to the power that leaves the antenna in its strongest direction, not to the transmitter’s output. EIRP (equivalent isotropically radiated power) is transmitter power plus antenna gain in dBi, minus cable loss. ERP uses a half-wave dipole as the reference instead of an ideal isotropic antenna, and a dipole has 2.15 dBi of gain:
\[
\text{EIRP} = \text{ERP} + 2.15\ \text{dB}.
\]
A rule of “25 mW ERP” is therefore 14 dBm ERP, or about 16.15 dBm EIRP. Swapping the kit’s spring antenna for a 6 dBi directional antenna adds 6 dB of EIRP without touching the radio, and can turn a compliant device into a non-compliant one.
Duty cycle. Where a band limits transmit time to a fraction \(\delta\), a device may transmit \(3600\,\delta\) seconds per hour; at 1%, 36 s. Chapter 10’s time-on-air formula converts that into packets per hour. Compliance is per device, so a firmware bug that retries forever is a regulatory problem as well as a battery problem.
Certification is about the whole product. A pre-certified radio module simplifies compliance only if it is used within the conditions of its grant: the listed antennas, power settings and host constraints. Changing any of them can require new testing.
Exercise. A module transmits at 20 dBm into a cable with 1.5 dB loss and a 3 dBi antenna. What is its EIRP in dBm and in milliwatts? What is its ERP?
Sources for this section: (ETSI EN 303 645: Cyber Security for Consumer Internet of Things: Baseline Requirements 2020).

text:
17.5 Common pitfalls

Treating compliance as a final step. Many requirements, such as unique credentials and updatability, cannot be added at the end.
Modifying a pre-certified module’s antenna and assuming the certification still applies.
Using the wrong regional radio frequencies.
Shipping without a vulnerability disclosure contact.
Promising updates without budgeting for them.
Collecting personal data “just in case”.

title: 18  AI on IoT and Edge ML
text:
18.1 Why it matters
IoT devices produce enormous volumes of raw data: accelerations sampled hundreds of times a second, audio, images, vibration spectra. The first generation of IoT systems sent all of it to the cloud for analysis. That works for a few devices with good connections, but it breaks down at scale, for battery-powered devices, and whenever a decision is needed immediately or the data is too sensitive to leave the device.
Advances in algorithms, model compression and microcontroller hardware now make it possible to run machine-learning models directly on devices like the ESP32. A smart doorbell can tell a person from a package without contacting a server; a wearable can detect a fall in milliseconds; a vibration sensor can flag a failing bearing and send one alert instead of streaming data all day. This chapter explains how.
crumbs: Part V — Intelligence at the Edge
18  AI on IoT and Edge ML

title: 18  AI on IoT and Edge ML
text:
18.2 Concepts

The limits of cloud-only processing
Sending all raw data to the cloud has four costs:

Latency. A round trip to the cloud takes tens to hundreds of milliseconds, and much longer on poor networks, too slow for emergency stops, fall detection or control loops.
Bandwidth. Streaming audio or video from many devices consumes network capacity and, on cellular links, money.
Energy. Transmitting data usually costs far more energy than processing it locally (Chapter 10).
Privacy. Raw data, such as audio from a living room, must leave the device, increasing the risk of leaks and misuse (Chapter 14).

There is also availability: a device that depends on the cloud to make every decision stops working when the network does.


The device–edge–cloud continuum
Computation can happen at several places between the sensor and the data center:



Table 18.1: The device–edge–cloud continuum.











Tier
Examples
Strengths
Limits




Device (extreme edge)
Microcontroller in a sensor or wearable
Lowest latency, works offline, raw data never leaves
Kilobytes of RAM, tight energy budget


Edge / fog
Gateway, router, phone, on-premises server
More compute, sees many devices, still local
Must be deployed and managed; shared by many devices


Cloud
Data-center servers
Effectively unlimited compute and storage; fleet-wide view
Latency, bandwidth, connectivity and privacy costs






Fog computing describes the middle tier: computing, storage and networking resources between devices and the cloud, often virtualized and shared, close to where the data is produced. Real systems split work across tiers. A camera might detect motion on the device, identify objects at the edge, and train improved models in the cloud.


Edge AI and TinyML
Edge AI means running machine-learning models on devices or edge nodes instead of only in the cloud. Only the result (“person detected”, “fall”, “abnormal vibration”) needs to be sent. Its benefits are real-time response, offline operation, lower bandwidth and energy, and privacy.
TinyML is the part of Edge AI that runs on the smallest devices: microcontrollers with kilobytes of memory and milliwatts of power. It sits at the overlap of machine learning and embedded systems, and applies when rule-based logic is not enough but the device is too small for conventional ML.
Typical applications include:

keyword spotting (“Hey…”) in smart speakers, running continuously at very low power;
activity recognition and fall detection in wearables;
anomaly detection in industrial machines (predictive maintenance);
visual wake words (is there a person in the image?) in cameras and doorbells;
gesture recognition from IMUs.



A machine-learning refresher
Machine learning teaches a computer rules from data instead of hard-coding them. Instead of writing “if acceleration > X then running”, you collect labeled acceleration data and train a model that learns the boundary.

Supervised learning uses labeled examples. Classification predicts a category (walking or running); regression predicts a number (the temperature in an hour, a motor’s speed from its sound).
Unsupervised learning finds structure without labels, for example clustering, or anomaly detection: learning what “normal” looks like and flagging what is not.
Training adjusts the model’s parameters to reduce errors on labeled examples. Testing evaluates it on data it has never seen, to check that it generalizes rather than memorizing.

Common supervised models for edge IoT include:








Model
Idea
Edge suitability




k-nearest neighbors
Predict from the labels of the most similar stored examples
Simple, but must store training data


Decision trees and small forests
A sequence of threshold tests
Tiny, fast, interpretable; easy to export as code


Linear and logistic regression
Weighted sum of features
Tiny and fast


Neural networks (MLPs, 1D/2D CNNs, small RNNs)
Layers of learned weights; CNNs capture spatial or temporal patterns
Most powerful; need compression to fit





Features from sensor data
Raw sensor streams are usually turned into features before (or inside) a model. For time series, a common pipeline is:

Windowing: split the stream into fixed-length windows, for example 2 s of accelerometer data at 50 Hz (100 samples), often overlapping.
Feature extraction: compute summary statistics for each window and axis, such as mean, standard deviation, minimum, maximum, energy, zero crossings or the magnitudes of frequency components.
Classification of each window.

Neural networks can learn their own features from raw windows, at the cost of more computation and data.


Why model size matters
A model that works in a notebook may be far too large for a microcontroller:









Cloud server
ESP32




Memory
Hundreds of GB of RAM
520 KB of SRAM (part used by Wi-Fi and the RTOS)


Storage
Terabytes
4 MB of flash, shared with the firmware


Compute
GPUs, TFLOPS
Two 240 MHz cores, single-precision FPU


Power
Hundreds of watts
Tens to hundreds of milliwatts



Edge models must therefore be tiny and efficient, trading some accuracy for size and speed. The main compression techniques are:

Quantization: storing weights and activations as 8-bit integers instead of 32-bit floats. This makes models about four times smaller and much faster on hardware without a strong floating-point unit, usually with only a small loss of accuracy. Post-training quantization converts a trained model; quantization-aware training simulates quantization during training for better accuracy.
Pruning: removing weights or whole neurons that contribute little.
Knowledge distillation: training a small “student” model to imitate a large “teacher”.
Architecture choice: using small, efficient model families designed for embedded devices.



The TinyML toolchain







Tool
Role




LiteRT for Microcontrollers (formerly TensorFlow Lite for Microcontrollers)
The most widely used inference runtime for MCUs; runs quantized models converted from TensorFlow, Keras, PyTorch or JAX


Edge Impulse
End-to-end platform: collect data from a device, label, train, optimize and generate firmware


ExecuTorch
PyTorch’s lightweight runtime for edge and embedded devices


Vendor libraries
Espressif ESP-DL, esp-tflite-micro and ESP-DSP; Arm CMSIS-NN; ST X-CUBE-AI; NXP eIQ. These use each chip’s accelerators and special instructions.



The typical workflow is:

Collect and label data on the real device, in realistic conditions.
Train a model on a PC, often in a Jupyter notebook.
Optimize: quantize, prune, and check accuracy after each step.
Convert to the runtime’s format (for LiteRT, a .tflite flat buffer, embedded in firmware as a C array).
Deploy to the device and run inference on live data.
Evaluate on the device: accuracy, latency, memory and energy, then iterate.



A tiny example: classifying motion with a decision tree
Not every edge model needs a neural network. A decision tree trained in Python (for example with scikit-learn) can be exported as plain C code. This one classifies 2-second accelerometer windows from the MPU-6050 (Chapter 6) as still, walking or running, using two features:
// Features computed over a 2 s window of acceleration magnitude (in g)
struct Features { float meanMag; float stdMag; };

Features extract(const float* mag, int n) {
  float sum = 0, sq = 0;
  for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) { sum += mag[i]; sq += mag[i] * mag[i]; }
  float mean = sum / n;
  return { mean, sqrtf(fmaxf(sq / n - mean * mean, 0.0f)) };
}

// Exported from a depth-2 decision tree (thresholds learned from labeled data)
const char* classify(const Features& f) {
  if (f.stdMag < 0.05f) return "still";
  if (f.stdMag < 0.45f) return "walking";
  return "running";
}
The whole model is a few comparisons and takes microseconds. The thresholds above are illustrative; yours must come from your own labeled data, collected on your kit and with the sensor mounted the way it will be used.


Evaluating an edge model
Accuracy alone does not decide whether a model is suitable for a device. Measure, on the device:

accuracy on held-out data collected separately from the training data, preferably from different people or machines; also precision and recall when classes are imbalanced;
latency per inference;
memory: flash for the model and code, RAM for activations (“tensor arena” in LiteRT);
energy per inference and per day, given how often inference runs.

Two practical risks recur:

Distribution shift. Models trained in the lab fail in the field when conditions differ: a different user, a different mounting position, a noisier machine.
Silent failure. A model always returns some answer. Monitoring confidence and occasionally sending samples for review helps detect when it has stopped working.



Larger models at the edge
More capable edge hardware runs much larger models. Camera boards such as the ESP-EYE run face and object detection with Espressif’s ESP-WHO framework. Gateways and single-board computers with neural accelerators run real-time vision, and even small language models, on premises. The same principles apply: move computation toward the data when latency, bandwidth, energy or privacy demand it.






TipTry it on your kit: from rules to a learned classifier




Record 2-second windows of MPU-6050 data while standing still, walking and running, at least 30 windows of each. Stream them over the serial port to a CSV file.
In a notebook, compute the mean and standard deviation of the acceleration magnitude per window, and train a small decision tree. Report its accuracy on windows recorded by a different team member.
Export the tree as C code and run it on the kit, showing the predicted activity on the OLED.
Measure the classification time with micros(), and the RAM used by your window buffer.
Optional: train a small neural network on the same data, quantize it to int8, and run it with LiteRT for Microcontrollers. Compare accuracy, size and latency with the tree.

title: 18  AI on IoT and Edge ML
text:
18.3 In depth (optional)






Optional, in-depth explanation. This section goes beyond the rest of the chapter into the math and physics behind it. Nothing later in the book depends on it; skip it on a first reading.




Fitting a model into a microcontroller
Sampling first. To capture motion up to frequency \(f_\text{max}\), the Nyquist criterion requires sampling at \(f_s > 2 f_\text{max}\). Human walking has most of its energy below about 3 Hz, and arm gestures below about 10–15 Hz, so 50 Hz accelerometer sampling is ample; sampling slower lets faster movements alias into false low-frequency patterns.
Features from raw axes. The acceleration magnitude
\[
|a| = \sqrt{a_x^2 + a_y^2 + a_z^2}
\]
does not depend on how the device is oriented, which makes it a robust input for step counting. Over a window of \(W\) samples, simple features such as the mean, standard deviation and number of threshold crossings summarize the motion into a few numbers a small model can use.
Counting the work. A fully connected layer with \(n_\text{in}\) inputs and \(n_\text{out}\) outputs performs \(n_\text{in} \times n_\text{out}\) multiply-accumulate operations (MACs) and stores the same number of weights. A 2-D convolution producing an \(H \times W \times C_\text{out}\) output with \(K \times K\) kernels over \(C_\text{in}\) input channels performs
\[
\text{MACs} = H\,W\,C_\text{out}\,K^2\,C_\text{in} .
\]
A gesture model with layers 300→32→16→4 needs \(9600 + 512 + 64 \approx 10\,200\) MACs and as many weights. At a few cycles per MAC on a 240 MHz core, inference takes well under a millisecond.
Quantization. Storing weights as 8-bit integers instead of 32-bit floats cuts memory four times and allows faster integer arithmetic. The common affine scheme maps a real value \(x\) to an integer \(q\) with a scale \(s\) and zero point \(z\):
\[
q = \operatorname{round}\left(\frac{x}{s}\right) + z, \qquad x \approx s\,(q - z),
\]
with \(s = (x_\text{max} - x_\text{min})/255\) for int8. The rounding error is at most \(s/2\) per value; accuracy usually drops by around a percentage point or less if the model was trained or calibrated with quantization in mind, and can drop much more if it was not.
Energy per inference. Energy is power times time: a core at 30 mA and 3.3 V running a 1 ms inference uses about 0.1 mJ. Sending the raw 300-sample window over Wi-Fi instead (hundreds of bytes plus connection overhead) costs far more. That ratio, compute is cheap and radio is expensive, is the main argument for edge intelligence.
Exercise. Your model has 25 000 float32 weights. How much flash does it need before and after int8 quantization? Would it fit alongside a 1.2 MB application in one 1.9 MB OTA partition?
Sources for this section: (Jacob et al. 2018; Warden and Situnayake 2019).

18.5 Common pitfalls

Testing on the training data, or on windows from the same recording, which overstates accuracy.
Collecting data in only one condition. Models fail on other users, placements or environments.
Ignoring RAM for activations. A model that fits in flash can still run out of RAM at inference time.
Measuring latency on a PC instead of on the device.
Using ML where a threshold would do. Start with the simplest model that meets the requirement.
Shipping without monitoring. Model accuracy degrades silently.







NoteAdvanced track





Federated learning. Instead of sending raw data to the cloud, devices can train locally and send only model updates, which a server aggregates. Read about federated averaging and explain what it protects and what it does not (model updates can still leak information).
Energy-aware inference. Design a cascade: a tiny, always-on model (such as a motion threshold) wakes a larger model only when needed. Estimate the energy saved compared with running the larger model continuously.
Benchmarks. MLPerf Tiny defines standard tasks (keyword spotting, visual wake words, image classification, anomaly detection) and reports accuracy, latency and energy on microcontrollers. Compare published results for two microcontroller families.

title: 19  Where IoT Is Heading
text:
19.1 Why it matters
The technologies in this book will change. The ESP32 will be replaced by newer chips; today’s protocol versions will be superseded; regulations will tighten. What lasts are the questions and trade-offs: how to sense and act reliably, how to move data at the right cost, how to keep devices trustworthy for years, and where computation should happen.
This chapter looks back at the whole stack, then looks forward at directions that are shaping the next generation of IoT systems, and offers a way to evaluate new technologies as they appear.
crumbs: Part V — Intelligence at the Edge

title: 19  Where IoT Is Heading
text:
19.2 Concepts

Looking back: one connected picture
Every chapter in this book addressed part of a single system:

The things (Parts I and II): microcontrollers, embedded software, buses, sensors and actuators, tied together by the Observe–Decide–Act loop.
The connections (Part III): a layered stack, from radios that trade range for power, through IPv6 adapted to small networks, to application protocols and the shared semantics that make devices interoperate.
Trust (Part IV): security requirements, threat modeling, device identity, secure updates and the regulations that now require them.
Intelligence and systems (Parts V and VI): where computation should run, and how to build, test and review a complete system.

The recurring theme is trade-offs under constraints: energy, memory, bandwidth, latency, cost, security and time to market. A good IoT engineer makes those trade-offs explicitly and can defend them.


Scalable deployment: CI/CD for firmware
Web services are often updated many times a day, thanks to continuous integration (CI) and continuous deployment (CD). The same practices increasingly apply to device firmware:

Continuous integration: every change to the repository triggers an automated build for every supported board, unit tests on the host, static analysis, and, ideally, tests on real hardware in a test rack (“hardware in the loop”).
Continuous deployment: successful builds are signed and stored as release candidates. They flow first to internal test devices, then to a staging group, and only then, in stages, to customer devices, using the OTA mechanisms and rollout safeguards from Chapter 16.

CI/CD shortens the time to deliver features and fixes, reduces risk by making each change small and quick to reverse, improves code quality through automation, and produces the build records (including SBOMs) that regulators increasingly expect.


Directions to watch

Connectivity everywhere

Cellular IoT keeps evolving. LTE-M and NB-IoT continue to replace 2G and 3G, and 5G RedCap (“reduced capability”) brings 5G to wearables and industrial sensors at lower cost and power.
Satellite IoT. Standards for non-terrestrial networks let small devices send messages directly to satellites, extending coverage to oceans, deserts and farms with no terrestrial network.
Wi-Fi and Bluetooth add features aimed at IoT: target wake time, longer range, and precise distance measurement.



Batteryless and ambient IoT
Batteries limit device lifetime and create waste. Energy harvesting from light, vibration, heat differences or radio waves can power devices that use very little energy. Backscatter communication lets a device send data by reflecting an existing radio signal instead of generating its own, as passive RFID tags do. Cellular standards bodies are defining “ambient IoT” devices that work this way, aiming at billions of very low-cost tags for logistics and retail.


Digital twins
A digital twin is a continuously updated software model of a physical asset (a machine, a building, a city) fed by IoT data. Engineers use it to monitor the asset, test changes in simulation before applying them, and predict failures. Digital twins depend on good sensing, reliable data pipelines and shared semantics, so they build directly on Parts II and III.


AI agents and natural-language control
Language models are beginning to act as interfaces to devices: “make the house comfortable before I get home” is translated into commands for thermostats, blinds and lights. This raises new questions in the spirit of Part IV: what an AI agent is authorized to do, how its actions are logged and reversed, how it handles ambiguous or malicious instructions, and how fail-safe defaults (Chapter 7) still apply when the “decide” step is a model rather than code you wrote.


Interoperable homes and buildings
Matter and Thread (Chapter 11, Chapter 13) are pushing the smart home toward devices that work across ecosystems. Similar efforts in buildings and industry, using shared semantic models, aim to make data from different vendors usable together.


Regulation and long-term support
The EU Cyber Resilience Act and similar laws (Chapter 17) make security, vulnerability handling and multi-year support mandatory. This changes product economics: maintenance becomes a planned cost from day one, and devices that cannot be updated become hard to sell.


Sustainability
Billions of devices consume energy and materials, and become electronic waste. Sustainable IoT design means low-power operation, repairability, long support periods, recyclable materials and graceful end-of-life, and asking honestly whether a product needs to be connected at all.



Evaluating emerging technologies: the case of blockchain
New technologies are often proposed as the solution to IoT’s problems. A useful way to evaluate them is to compare their properties with the requirements and constraints in this book.
Blockchain has been widely proposed for IoT. A blockchain is a ledger, replicated across many parties, to which records can be appended but not changed, with agreement among parties reached without a central authority. Proposed uses include:

tamper-evident logs of sensor data, for example in supply chains (where was this shipment, and was it kept cold?);
device identity and ownership records that no single company controls;
automated payments between devices (“machine-to-machine micropayments”) using smart contracts.

Measured against IoT requirements, the picture is mixed:







Requirement
Blockchain’s fit




Constrained devices
Poor: devices cannot store a ledger or run consensus; they must rely on gateways


Throughput and latency
Public blockchains confirm transactions in seconds to minutes, with limited throughput


Energy
Proof-of-work chains are very energy-intensive; proof-of-stake chains much less so


Privacy
Public ledgers are permanent and visible to all, which conflicts with data minimization and deletion rights


Data integrity
Good for records once written, but cannot verify that the sensor reading was true in the first place


Trust among parties
Useful when several organizations must share records and none is trusted to run a central database



The honest conclusion is that blockchain helps in a narrow set of cases: multi-party settings without a trusted operator, where tamper-evidence matters more than speed or privacy. For most IoT systems, a conventional database with signed records (Chapter 14) and good access control meets the same needs more cheaply. The same method of evaluation applies to the next technology to be proposed.






TipTry it on your kit: a CI pipeline for your project




Add a GitHub Actions (or similar) workflow to your project repository that builds your firmware with PlatformIO on every push.
Make the build fail if the code does not compile for the kit’s board, or if a simple unit test of your non-hardware logic (for example, your debounce or classification function) fails.
Have the workflow publish the compiled firmware.bin as a build artifact, named with the commit hash.
Describe the additional steps needed to turn this into continuous deployment to a fleet of kits, safely.

title: 19  Where IoT Is Heading
text:
19.3 In depth (optional)






Optional, in-depth explanation. This section goes beyond the rest of the chapter into the math and physics behind it. Nothing later in the book depends on it; skip it on a first reading.




Can a device run on harvested energy?
A recurring vision for the future of IoT is the battery-free device. Whether it works is an energy-balance question.
The balance. Over a long period, the energy harvested must at least equal the energy used:
\[
\bar P_\text{harvest} \ge \bar P_\text{device} = D\,P_\text{active} + (1 - D)\,P_\text{sleep}.
\]
A storage element (a supercapacitor or small rechargeable cell) covers the gap between moments of plenty and moments of need, but it cannot fix a negative average.
What sources offer. Orders of magnitude, which vary widely with conditions:

Approximate harvesting power densities (orders of magnitude).






Source
Typical harvested power density




Outdoor sunlight on a small solar cell
~10 mW/cm²


Indoor office lighting on a solar cell
~10–100 µW/cm²


Body heat (thermoelectric, small ΔT)
~10–50 µW/cm²


Vibration (machinery)
~10–100 µW/cm³


Ambient radio signals
~0.1–1 µW/cm² near transmitters, far less elsewhere



An example. An indoor sensor with a 10 cm² solar cell harvesting 20 µW/cm² gets 200 µW on average while the lights are on, say 10 hours a day: a daily average of about 83 µW. A BLE beacon that sleeps at 3 µW (≈10 µW with its regulator) and spends 30 µJ per advertising event can afford
\[
\frac{(83 - 10)\ \mu\text{W}}{30\ \mu\text{J}} \approx 2.4\ \text{events per second},
\]
comfortably above one advertisement per second. A Wi-Fi device that spends tens of millijoules per connection could afford roughly one report every few minutes, and only if its sleep current is in the microamperes. The radio, again, decides what is possible.
Why the trend helps. For decades, the energy needed per computation fell by roughly half every year and a half to two and a half years (an observation often called Koomey’s law). Radios and sensors improve more slowly, but each halving moves another class of application into the range of harvested energy.
Exercise. Using the table, what solar-cell area would a device that averages 1 mW need indoors? Outdoors? What does that suggest about where battery-free Wi-Fi devices make sense?
Sources for this section: (Koomey et al. 2011).

title: 20  From Idea to Vertical Slice
text:
20.1 Why it matters
Most failed student IoT projects do not fail because a sensor was too hard. They fail because the team spent weeks perfecting one part (a beautiful dashboard, an elaborate enclosure, a complex sensor driver) and discovered in the last week that the parts did not fit together: the radio could not reach the gateway, the battery lasted four hours, or the broker rejected the device’s messages.
The remedy is a disciplined path from idea to a thin, working, end-to-end system, followed by deliberate improvement. This chapter describes that path. It applies equally to a ten-week course project and to the first months of a real product.
crumbs: Part VI — Building an IoT System
20  From Idea to Vertical Slice

title: 20  From Idea to Vertical Slice
text:
20.2 Concepts

From idea to problem statement
Start with a problem, not a technology. A good problem statement says who has the problem, what it is, and why current solutions fall short:

Weak: “A LoRa-based smart garden.”
Better: “Community-garden volunteers water every plot daily because they cannot tell which plots are dry, wasting water and time. A low-cost soil-moisture monitor visible from a phone would let them water only plots that need it.”

From the problem statement, identify:

Users and stakeholders: who uses the system, who installs and maintains it, and who else is affected (neighbors, building managers, people whose data is collected).
Use scenarios: short stories of the system in use, including what goes wrong (the network is down; a sensor is stolen; the battery is low).



Requirements
Turn scenarios into requirements: statements that can be checked.

Functional requirements say what the system does: “The dashboard shows each plot’s moisture, updated at least every 30 minutes.”
Non-functional requirements say how well: battery life, range, latency, reliability, security, cost, size, privacy. They drive most IoT design decisions.

Make requirements measurable. “Long battery life” cannot be tested; “runs at least 30 days on two AA cells” can. Mark each requirement must, should or could, so that you know what to cut if time runs short.


Architecture
Sketch the system architecture on the four levels of Chapter 1: devices, network, services platform and applications. For each element, choose technologies using the trade-offs from earlier chapters:







Question
See




Which sensors and actuators, and how are they connected?
Chapter 5, Chapter 6, Chapter 7


Which link technology meets the range, power and data-rate needs?
Chapter 10


Which application protocol and message format?
Chapter 12, Chapter 13


Where does processing happen: device, edge or cloud?
Chapter 18


What are the threats, and how are devices identified and updated?
Chapter 14, Chapter 15, Chapter 16



Include a data-flow diagram showing every message, its topic or endpoint, its format and how often it is sent. It will be the basis of your threat model and of your testing.


Risks
List what could stop the project from working, and rank each risk by likelihood and impact. Typical IoT risks include:

a sensor that is less accurate or noisier than its datasheet suggests;
radio range or reliability that is worse than expected indoors;
power consumption that is far higher than estimated;
parts that arrive late or not at all;
a cloud service or library that does not do what you assumed;
integration problems between team members’ parts.

For each major risk, plan a spike: a quick, throwaway experiment that answers the question early. Measure the range with two kits before designing the network; measure the current before promising battery life.


The proposal
A project proposal brings these together. A useful structure is:

Problem statement and users
Proposed solution and how it will be used
Requirements, with priorities and measurable targets
System architecture and data-flow diagram
Hardware and software: parts (from the kit and any extras), libraries, services
Risks and how you will reduce them
Plan: milestones and who does what
Evaluation: how you will show that the requirements are met

A proposal is a starting point, not a contract. Feedback on a proposal is usually about making the project achievable and testable, not replacing it.


The vertical slice
A vertical slice is a thin version of the whole system that works end to end, through every layer of the architecture:

one real sensor reading → over the real network → through the real broker or server → stored → shown on the real dashboard, and one real command flowing back to one real actuator.

It does not need to be pretty, complete or efficient. It needs to be real: the actual hardware, protocols and services you intend to use, not stand-ins.
Building the vertical slice first has three benefits:

It retires integration risk early. Most surprises in IoT appear at the boundaries between layers, so you meet them while there is time to change course.
It gives everyone something to build on. Team members can improve their layer while the rest of the system keeps working.
It is always demonstrable. From then on, the project works at every moment, and progress means adding features to a working system.

The alternative, building each layer completely before connecting them (“horizontal” development), postpones integration to the end, where it is most expensive.


Milestones
Plan milestones that build on the vertical slice:







Milestone
Typical content




Proposal
Problem, requirements, architecture, risks, plan


Spikes
Answers to the riskiest questions (range, power, sensor quality)


Vertical slice
One end-to-end path working on real hardware and services


Progress report
Status against the plan; what changed and why; updated risks


Feature complete
All must requirements implemented


Security review
Threat model, review by another team, fixes (Chapter 22)


Reliability and field testing
Long-duration and real-environment tests (Chapter 21)


Final demonstration and report
Evidence that requirements are met; lessons learned





Working as a team
A team of three can easily lose a week to coordination problems. A few practices prevent most of them:

Clear ownership. Assign an owner to each part of the architecture (for example device firmware, networking and back end, application and data), plus shared responsibility for integration and testing.
Version control. Keep all code, configuration and documentation in one repository. Use branches and pull requests, and review each other’s code. Never commit secrets: keep them in an ignored secrets.h and provide a secrets.example.h.
Interfaces first. Agree early on message formats and topics, written down in the repository (a Thing Description, Chapter 13, works well). Then each member can work against the agreement.
Short, regular check-ins. Ten minutes, twice a week: what was done, what is next, what is blocking.
A shared hardware log. Note wiring changes, pin assignments and anything that was damaged.
Working agreements. How quickly to answer messages, how decisions are made, and what happens when someone falls behind.







TipTry it on your kit: your first vertical slice




Write your project’s problem statement and five measurable requirements.
Draw the architecture and data-flow diagram.
Build a vertical slice: one sensor reading from your kit reaches your dashboard or app through your chosen protocol and services, and one command from the dashboard changes an actuator on the kit.
Record a short video of the slice working, and list the three things that surprised you while building it.

title: 20  From Idea to Vertical Slice
text:
20.3 In depth (optional)






Optional, in-depth explanation. This section goes beyond the rest of the chapter into the math and physics behind it. Nothing later in the book depends on it; skip it on a first reading.




Sizing and reliability of a whole system
A vertical slice crosses several components: device, network, broker, database, dashboard. Two simple models let you reason about the whole chain before it exists.
Little’s law. In any stable system, the average number of items inside, \(L\), equals the arrival rate \(\lambda\) times the average time each spends inside, \(W\):
\[
L = \lambda\,W .
\]
If 500 devices each publish once every 10 s, the broker receives \(\lambda = 50\) messages per second. If the database writer takes \(W = 40\) ms per message on average, about \(L = 2\) messages are in the pipeline at any time. If a slow query raises \(W\) to 400 ms, 20 messages queue up; if \(W\) exceeds \(1/\lambda\) per writer for long, the queue grows without bound. The law holds regardless of the arrival pattern, which makes it a quick sanity check for any queue in your design.
Peaks, not averages. If every device reports on the minute, the arrival rate in that second is \(N\), not \(N/60\). Adding a random offset to each device’s schedule spreads the load; this is called jitter, and it is one of the cheapest scalability fixes.
Reliability multiplies along a chain. If a reading must pass through \(k\) components in series, each available with probability \(A_i\), the end-to-end availability is
\[
A_\text{chain} = \prod_{i=1}^{k} A_i .
\]
Five components at 99% each give \(0.99^5 \approx 95\%\): more than a day of outage per month. Each component’s availability can be estimated as \(A = \text{MTBF}/(\text{MTBF} + \text{MTTR})\), mean time between failures over that plus mean time to repair.
Redundancy adds in parallel. Two independent components in parallel, either of which suffices, fail only if both do: \(A_\text{par} = 1 - (1 - A_1)(1 - A_2)\). Two 99% gateways give 99.99%. Buffering readings on the device until the network returns has a similar effect: it turns a network outage from data loss into delay.
Exercise. Your slice is device (99.5%), Wi-Fi (98%), broker (99.9%), database (99.9%), dashboard (99%). What is the end-to-end availability? Which single change would help most?
Sources for this section: (Little 1961; Nygard 2018).

title: 21  Testing in the Field
text:
21.1 Why it matters
A device that works for five minutes on a desk has proven very little. In the field it will meet weak signals, crowded radio bands, power glitches, network outages, memory leaks that only appear after two days, sensors that drift, and users who press buttons in the wrong order. Many IoT failures appear only after hours or days, or only in a particular place.
Testing in IoT therefore has two dimensions that ordinary software testing often lacks: time and environment. This chapter explains how to test along both.
crumbs: Part VI — Building an IoT System

title: 21  Testing in the Field
text:
21.2 Concepts

Levels of testing



Table 21.1: Levels of testing for an IoT system.










Level
What it checks
How




Unit tests
Logic that does not need hardware: parsing, state machines, filters, classifiers
Run on a laptop or in CI (PlatformIO’s native environment and Unity test framework)


Hardware-in-the-loop
Drivers and firmware on the real board
Automated tests on a board connected to a test machine


Integration tests
End-to-end paths: device → network → broker → back end → app
Scripted scenarios against the vertical slice


Fault-injection tests
Behavior when things go wrong
Disconnect Wi-Fi, stop the broker, unplug a sensor, cut power mid-operation


Long-duration (reliability) tests
Behavior over days: leaks, drift, reconnection, uptime
Run unattended for 24–72 hours or more, with logging


Field tests
Behavior in the real environment with real users
Deploy where the system will actually be used






Each level catches problems the others miss. Unit tests are fast and cheap but know nothing about radios; field tests are realistic but slow and hard to repeat.


Designing for testability
Testing is much easier if the firmware is designed for it:

Separate logic from hardware. Put decision logic (state machines, thresholds, message formatting) in functions that take values and return results, so they can be tested on a laptop.
Log meaningfully. Every important event (boot, reset reason, connect, disconnect, error, command received) should be logged with a timestamp and enough context to diagnose it later (Chapter 4).
Report health. Publish a periodic heartbeat with uptime, free heap, firmware version, signal strength (RSSI), reconnect counts and last error. A missing heartbeat is itself a signal.
Record why the device restarted. esp_reset_reason() distinguishes power-on, software reset, watchdog timeouts, brownouts and crashes.

#include <esp_system.h>

const char* resetReasonText() {
  switch (esp_reset_reason()) {
    case ESP_RST_POWERON:  return "power-on";
    case ESP_RST_SW:       return "software";
    case ESP_RST_PANIC:    return "crash";
    case ESP_RST_INT_WDT:
    case ESP_RST_TASK_WDT:
    case ESP_RST_WDT:      return "watchdog";
    case ESP_RST_BROWNOUT: return "brownout";
    case ESP_RST_DEEPSLEEP:return "deep-sleep wake";
    default:               return "other";
  }
}

void publishHeartbeat() {
  char msg[160];
  snprintf(msg, sizeof msg,
           "{\"up_s\":%lu,\"heap\":%u,\"rssi\":%d,\"fw\":\"%s\",\"reset\":\"%s\",\"reconnects\":%u}",
           millis() / 1000, ESP.getFreeHeap(), WiFi.RSSI(), FIRMWARE_VERSION,
           resetReasonText(), reconnectCount);
  mqtt.publish(HEARTBEAT_TOPIC, msg);
}


Fault injection
Deliberately break things and watch what happens:







Fault
Expected behavior to verify




Wi-Fi access point switched off for 10 minutes
Device keeps sensing and acting locally; buffers or drops data as designed; reconnects automatically


Broker or server unreachable
Back-off between retries; no crash; no battery drain from tight retry loops


Sensor unplugged or returning nonsense
Plausibility checks reject bad data; actuator goes to its fail-safe state (Chapter 7)


Power cut during a write or an update
Settings and firmware remain valid (Chapter 16)


Burst of commands or malformed messages
Device rejects invalid input without crashing


Clock not yet synchronized
Timestamps and certificate checks behave sensibly





Long-duration reliability testing
A reliability test runs the complete system, unattended, for an extended period, typically 24 to 72 hours, and measures how well it keeps working.
Plan it like an experiment:

Define the configuration: firmware version, hardware, location, network, power source.
Define the metrics and how each is measured:

uptime and the number and causes of resets;
message delivery ratio: messages received ÷ messages sent, using sequence numbers to count gaps;
latency distribution (median and 95th percentile), using timestamps;
reconnections and how long each outage lasted;
free heap over time (a steady decline indicates a memory leak);
power or battery voltage over time, if battery-powered;
application-specific correctness, such as sensor values within plausible ranges.

Log everything to a place that survives the device: the broker and a back-end database, not just the serial port.
Run it without touching it. Intervening invalidates the result; if you must, record what you did and when.
Analyze and report: plots of each metric over time, a list of every incident with its cause, and what you changed as a result.

A simple sequence-number scheme makes message loss measurable:
RTC_DATA_ATTR uint32_t seq = 0;      // survives deep sleep; resets on power loss

void publishReading(float value) {
  char msg[96];
  snprintf(msg, sizeof msg, "{\"seq\":%lu,\"t_ms\":%lu,\"v\":%.2f}", ++seq, millis(), value);
  mqtt.publish(DATA_TOPIC, msg);
}
// On the server: delivery ratio = received / (max_seq - min_seq + 1), per boot
Expect the first long test to find problems. That is its purpose. Typical findings include memory leaks from repeated String concatenation, connections that never recover after a router restart, watchdog resets from blocking network calls, and TLS sessions that fail after the device’s clock drifts.


Field testing
A field test places the system where it will actually be used, with the people who will actually use it. It reveals problems no lab can: a wall that blocks the signal, a sensor that reads differently in sunlight, a user who misunderstands the display.
A useful field-test plan includes:

objectives: which requirements and risks the test addresses;
site and setup: where devices are placed, with photos and a map;
procedure: what testers and users do, and for how long;
data collected: logs, measurements, observations, user feedback;
safety and permissions: permission to install devices, electrical and physical safety, and the privacy of anyone whose data is collected (Chapter 14, Chapter 17).

Report the results honestly. A field test that shows the range is half what you expected is valuable, provided you explain what you learned and what you would change.


Preparing the final demonstration
A live demo is a small field test under pressure. Reduce the risk:

Have a rehearsed script with a clear story: the problem, the system, the evidence that it works.
Bring your own network if possible (a travel router), or confirm the venue’s network in advance.
Keep a backup: a recorded video of the system working and screenshots of dashboards and long-test results.
Charge everything, and bring spare cables.
Show evidence, not just features: the reliability plots and field-test results are often more convincing than the live demo.







TipTry it on your kit: a 72-hour reliability test




Add a heartbeat and sequence-numbered data messages to your project firmware.
Write a small script on a laptop or server that subscribes to your topics and stores every message with its arrival time.
Run the complete system unattended for 72 hours.
Produce plots of message delivery ratio per hour, latency, free heap and RSSI, and a table of every reset and disconnection with its cause.
Write one page on what failed, why, and what you changed.

title: 21  Testing in the Field
text:
21.3 In depth (optional)






Optional, in-depth explanation. This section goes beyond the rest of the chapter into the math and physics behind it. Nothing later in the book depends on it; skip it on a first reading.




How much testing is enough?
Field tests produce numbers such as “no failures in 72 hours” or “997 of 1000 packets delivered”. Statistics tells you how much those numbers actually prove.
Zero failures is not zero failure rate. If a test of \(n\) independent trials sees no failures, the 95% upper confidence bound on the failure probability is approximately
\[
p_\text{upper} \approx \frac{3}{n} \qquad \text{(the "rule of three")},
\]
because \((1 - p)^n = 0.05\) gives \(p \approx -\ln(0.05)/n \approx 3/n\). 1000 successful packets show, with 95% confidence, a loss rate below 0.3%, not a loss rate of zero.
Mean time between failures from a short test. For failures that occur at a constant rate, a test of total duration \(T\) with no failures supports, at confidence \(C\),
\[
\text{MTBF} \ge \frac{T}{-\ln(1 - C)} .
\]
A 72-hour run with no failures shows MTBF ≥ 72/3.0 ≈ 24 hours at 95% confidence. To claim a month, you would need about three months of failure-free device-hours, which is why teams test many devices in parallel: 30 kits for 72 hours give 2160 device-hours.
Estimating a rate with an interval. For \(x\) successes in \(n\) trials, the observed rate is \(\hat p = x/n\), and a simple 95% interval is
\[
\hat p \pm 1.96\sqrt{\frac{\hat p (1 - \hat p)}{n}} .
\]
997 of 1000 gives 99.7% ± 0.34%. The approximation is poor near 0% and 100%, where the Wilson interval is better, but it shows the key point: to halve the uncertainty, you need four times the trials.
Comparing before and after. If a fix raises delivery from 96% to 98%, is that real? With 200 packets each, the intervals (about ±2.7% and ±1.9%) overlap; with 2000 each they do not. Decide the sample size before the test, not after seeing the result.
Exercise. Your team’s device must deliver at least 99% of readings. How many consecutive successful readings, with no failures, would let you claim that with 95% confidence?
Sources for this section: (Hanley and Lippman-Hand 1983).

text:
21.4 Design trade-offs







Decision
Considerations




Test duration
Longer tests find rarer problems but delay feedback


Logging detail
More detail aids diagnosis but costs bandwidth, storage, energy and possibly privacy


Automated vs. manual testing
Automation is repeatable and runs in CI; some field behavior can only be observed by people


Lab vs. field
Labs are controlled and repeatable; the field is realistic

title: 21  Testing in the Field
text:
21.5 Common pitfalls

Testing only the happy path.
Logging only to the serial monitor, so the record disappears when the laptop sleeps.
No sequence numbers or timestamps, so loss and latency cannot be measured.
Changing firmware during a long test without restarting the clock.
Ignoring resets because “it came back”.
A demo that depends on unfamiliar Wi-Fi.







NoteAdvanced track





Statistics of rare failures. If your device runs 72 hours with no failures, what can you say about its mean time between failures? Using the “rule of three”, estimate a 95% upper bound on the failure rate, and discuss how many device-hours you would need to claim a mean time between failures of one year.
Chaos testing. Write a script that randomly disconnects the broker, delays messages and restarts the access point during a long test, and compare the system’s behavior with an undisturbed run.
