title: 22  Reviewing Someone Else’s System
text:
22.1 Why it matters
Builders test their systems the way they expect them to be used. They know which button not to press, which order to power things up in, and which warning to ignore. Attackers and real users know none of this. An independent reviewer, with fresh eyes and a different set of assumptions, finds failures and vulnerabilities that the builders cannot see.
Professional teams build review into their process: code review on every change, design reviews before major decisions, and penetration tests or security audits before release. Many regulations now expect evidence of such reviews (Chapter 17). This chapter describes two forms of review you can apply to a peer team’s project: a device review, where you receive and probe their device, and a security code review (Advanced track), where you examine their source code and design.
crumbs: Part VI — Building an IoT System

title: 22  Reviewing Someone Else’s System
text:
22.2 Concepts

Ground rules
Reviews work only when both sides trust the process:

Scope and permission. Review only the systems you have been given, within the agreed scope. Do not attack shared infrastructure (the course broker, campus Wi-Fi) or other teams’ systems. This is the same rule that separates professional security testing from attacks.
Do no harm. Do not damage hardware, delete data or leave changes behind. Report what you could have done instead of doing it.
Critique the system, not the people. Findings describe behavior and code, with evidence, not judgments about the builders.
Confidentiality. Findings go to the team (and the teaching staff), not to everyone, until they are fixed.



Preparing for a review
The team being reviewed provides a short review package:

a one-page description of the system and its intended use;
the architecture and data-flow diagram, with trust boundaries (Chapter 14);
instructions to set up and use the device;
the repository (for a code review), with build instructions;
the team’s own threat model and any known issues.

The reviewers read the package first, then plan their review around the most valuable targets: where trust boundaries are crossed, where commands reach actuators, and where secrets are stored.


The device review
In a device review, reviewers receive the other team’s working device, use it as intended, then try to make it fail. A useful structure follows the STRIDE categories (Table 14.2) and the reliability concerns from Chapter 21:







Area
Questions to investigate




First use
Can you set it up from the instructions alone? Are there default credentials?


Normal use
Does it meet its stated requirements? Is feedback clear?


Physical access
Are secrets readable over the serial console? Is a debug menu exposed? What happens if you press buttons during boot?


Network observation
Using a desktop MQTT client or packet capture on a network you control: are messages encrypted? Do they reveal personal or sensitive information?


Spoofing and tampering
Can you send commands that the device accepts without authorization? Can you replay a captured command?


Denial of service
What happens with a flood of messages, malformed payloads, a disconnected network or a removed sensor?


Recovery
After power loss or network loss, does it recover on its own, and into a safe state?



Record every test, including the ones where the device behaved well. A finding of “replay rejected” is useful evidence.


The security code review (Advanced track)
In a security code review, reviewers read another team’s repository with an attacker’s eye. Work through it systematically rather than skimming:

Build and run it. Confirm that the instructions work. Many problems surface here.
Map the attack surface. Find every place where external input enters: network callbacks, serial input, configuration pages, BLE characteristics, sensor readings.
Trace each input to where it is used. Is it validated? Can it overflow a buffer, change a command, or reach an actuator without authorization?
Check secrets. Search the repository and its history for passwords, keys and tokens (git log -p, or a secret-scanning tool). Check that secrets.h is ignored.
Check cryptography and TLS. Is certificate verification disabled (setInsecure())? Are standard libraries used correctly? Is there replay protection on commands (Chapter 14)?
Check the update path. Can firmware be replaced over the network? Is it authenticated (Chapter 16)?
Check failure handling. Do network calls have timeouts? Are fail-safe states defined?
Check privacy. What personal data is collected, logged or retained, and is all of it needed?

A checklist of common findings in student IoT code:

Wi-Fi passwords, broker credentials or API keys committed to the repository, sometimes later “removed” but still in the history;
setInsecure() or disabled certificate checks;
one MQTT topic for everything, with any client able to send commands;
commands accepted without authentication, or authenticated without replay protection;
strcpy, sprintf and fixed-size buffers fed with network input;
String concatenation in loops, causing heap fragmentation over days;
blocking calls without timeouts, triggering watchdog resets;
verbose debug output in production builds, including secrets.



Writing findings
Each finding should let the receiving team understand, reproduce and fix the problem:







Field
Content




Title
A short description: “Unlock command can be replayed”


Severity
Critical, high, medium or low, based on impact and likelihood


Category
STRIDE category, or reliability, privacy, usability


Evidence
Steps to reproduce, captured messages, file and line references, screenshots


Impact
What an attacker or a failure could cause in the real use case


Recommendation
A concrete fix, with references to standard practices



A simple severity guide:

Critical: remote control of actuators or full device compromise without credentials.
High: exposure of credentials or sensitive personal data; reliable denial of service.
Medium: weaknesses that need special access or conditions to exploit.
Low: hardening and best-practice improvements.

End the report with a short summary: the most important findings, what the team did well, and the overall risk.


Responding to a review
Receiving a review is part of the exercise. The team should:

Acknowledge each finding, and ask clarifying questions if needed.
Triage: agree or disagree with each severity, with reasons.
Fix the important findings, and verify each fix, ideally with the reviewers.
Document what was fixed, what was accepted as a known risk and why, and what was deferred.

The response is evidence of engineering maturity, and is often worth as much as the fixes themselves.






TipTry it on your kit: review a peer team




Prepare your team’s review package and exchange it with your assigned peer team.
Perform a device review of their kit (or, on the Advanced track, a security code review of their repository) using the structure above, within the agreed scope.
Write a findings report with at least five findings, each with severity, evidence and a recommendation.
When you receive your own report, write a response that triages every finding and documents your fixes.

title: 22  Reviewing Someone Else’s System
text:
22.3 In depth (optional)






Optional, in-depth explanation. This section goes beyond the rest of the chapter into the math and physics behind it. Nothing later in the book depends on it; skip it on a first reading.




How many defects are left?
A review finds some defects. The question a team really wants answered is how many it did not find.
Independent reviewers find more. If each reviewer independently finds a given defect with probability \(p\), then \(k\) reviewers find it with probability
\[
P_\text{found} = 1 - (1-p)^k .
\]
With \(p = 0.4\), one reviewer finds 40% of defects, two find 64%, three 78%. Each extra reviewer adds less; and in practice reviewers are not independent (they share blind spots), so real gains are smaller. Checklists and different review roles (one reviewer per STRIDE category, for instance) make reviewers less alike.
Estimating what remains: capture–recapture. Ecologists estimate a population by catching animals, marking them, and seeing how many marked ones are caught again. The same idea estimates the number of defects. If reviewer A finds \(n_A\) defects, reviewer B finds \(n_B\), and \(m\) of them are the same, then an estimate of the total number of defects is
\[
\hat N = \frac{n_A\,n_B}{m} .
\]
If A finds 12 issues in a peer team’s device, B finds 10, and 6 are common, \(\hat N = 120/6 = 20\). Together they found \(12 + 10 - 6 = 16\), so about 4 are probably still there. A small overlap is a warning: it means the reviewers are sampling a large population of defects.
The estimate assumes both reviewers look at the same scope and that every defect is equally easy to find; easy defects are found by both, so it tends to underestimate. It is still far better than assuming the count of found defects is the count of defects.
Severity, not just count. Scoring systems such as CVSS combine how a weakness is exploited (network or physical access, complexity, privileges needed) with its impact on confidentiality, integrity and availability. Whatever the scale, rank findings so that the team fixes the few that matter before the many that do not.
Exercise. Two reviewers of the same repository report 8 and 5 findings with 1 in common. Estimate the total. What would you tell the team about the review’s coverage?
Sources for this section: (Eick et al. 1992; OWASP Foundation, n.d.).

title: 22  Reviewing Someone Else’s System
text:
22.4 Design trade-offs







Decision
Considerations




Device review vs. code review
A device review tests what is actually built and deployed; a code review finds issues that are hard to trigger from outside


Breadth vs. depth
A broad checklist finds common issues; depth on the riskiest path finds serious ones


Fixing everything vs. accepting risk
Not every finding is worth fixing before release; document accepted risks explicitly

title: 22  Reviewing Someone Else’s System
text:
22.5 Common pitfalls

Reviewing outside the agreed scope, or disrupting shared systems.
Vague findings (“security is weak”) without evidence or a fix.
Severity inflation, which hides the findings that matter.
Checking only the current code, not the repository history, for secrets.
Defensive responses instead of triage and fixes.







NoteAdvanced track





Coordinated disclosure. In industry, researchers who find vulnerabilities in products they do not own follow coordinated disclosure: report privately to the vendor, give a reasonable time to fix, then publish. Read ISO/IEC 29147 (vulnerability disclosure) or a vendor’s published policy, and write a disclosure policy for your project as if it were a product.
Automated analysis. Run a static analyzer (such as cppcheck or clang-tidy) and a secret scanner (such as gitleaks) on the repository you reviewed. Which of your manual findings did the tools catch, which did they miss, and what did they find that you missed?

title: Lab 0: Bench Safety and Soldering
text: Goals

title: Lab 0: Bench Safety and Soldering
text:
Work safely at an electronics bench.
Make reliable through-hole solder joints on header pins.
Recognize and fix common soldering defects.

title: Lab 0: Bench Safety and Soldering
text:
Safety first







Hazard
Precaution




Burns (iron tips reach 300–450 °C)
Always return the iron to its stand. Never touch the tip or the metal shaft. Assume every iron is hot.


Fumes from flux
Use the fume extractor or work in a well-ventilated area; keep your face out of the plume.


Lead (in leaded solder)
Prefer lead-free solder. Do not eat or drink at the bench. Wash your hands afterwards.


Eye injury from flying solder or clipped leads
Wear safety glasses. Hold leads when clipping and point them down.


Electrical
Check the iron’s cord before use. Keep liquids away. Never solder a powered circuit.


Fire
Work on a heat-resistant mat. Turn the iron off when you leave the bench, even briefly.



Always unplug the USB cable before changing any wiring on the kit.

title: Lab 0: Bench Safety and Soldering
text:
Background
Soldering joins metal parts with a low-melting alloy (solder), making a joint that is both an electrical connection and a mechanical one. Electronics uses soft soldering, at roughly 180–450 °C. You will do through-hole soldering: component leads or header pins pass through holes in a circuit board and are soldered to the copper pads around them. (Surface-mount soldering, where parts sit on pads on the surface, needs finer technique and is not required.)

Tools and materials

Soldering iron or station, ideally temperature-controlled (25–40 W is typical). Around 330–370 °C suits most lead-free work on small pads.
Tips: a conical tip for precise work, a chisel tip for general use (headers and wires), bevel and knife tips for drag soldering.
Solder: lead-free (such as SAC305) or leaded (60/40, 63/37); thin (0.5–0.8 mm) wire is easiest for headers. Most solder wire has a rosin flux core; a flux pen helps when solder will not flow.
Tip cleaner: brass wool or a damp (not wet) sponge.
Workholding: helping hands or a board holder; a spare breadboard holds header pins straight.
Corrections: desoldering braid (wick) and a solder sucker.

title: Lab 0: Bench Safety and Soldering
text:
Procedure: soldering header pins
The breakout boards in the kit (the OLED, BMP280, MPU-6050, ATECC608A and LoRa radio) come with loose header pins.

Set up. Heat the iron, clean the tip, and tin it: melt a small amount of solder onto the tip so it is shiny.
Hold the pins straight. Push the long ends of the header into a breadboard, then place the breakout board on top, with the pins through its holes and the board level.
Tack one pin. Touch the iron to both the pad and the pin for 1–2 seconds, then feed solder into the joint (not onto the iron). Remove the solder, then the iron.
Check alignment. If the board is tilted, reheat the single joint and straighten it. This is much easier with one pin soldered than with all of them.
Solder the rest. Heat the pad and pin together for 2–3 seconds, feed solder until it flows around the pin and covers the pad, then remove solder and iron. Move steadily; do not hold the iron on the board for long.
Inspect. Each joint should be shiny (or slightly satin for lead-free), smooth and cone- or volcano-shaped, fully covering the pad.
Clean up. Return the iron to its stand, clean and re-tin the tip, and switch off the iron when done.

title: Lab 0: Bench Safety and Soldering
text:
Recognizing good and bad joints









Joint
Appearance
Cause
Fix




Good
Shiny, smooth, concave cone covering the pad
—
—


Cold
Dull, grainy or lumpy; may not wet the pad
Not enough heat, or movement while cooling
Reheat with a touch of flux until it flows


Bridge
Solder joining two adjacent pins
Too much solder
Drag the iron between pins, or use desoldering braid


Insufficient
Pad only partly covered; gap around pin
Too little solder or heat
Add a little solder while heating


Excess
Large ball hiding the pin
Too much solder
Remove some with braid


Lifted pad
Copper pad detached from board
Too much heat or force
Ask a TA; may need a wire repair



After soldering, run the kit check from Lab 1 or an I²C scan (5  Serial Communication: UART, SPI and I²C). A device that does not appear often has a cold joint or a bridge on its SDA or SCL pin.

A breakout board with all header pins soldered, straight, and passing visual inspection by a TA.
The board working in a quick test (for example, appearing in an I²C scan).

title: Lab 1: Build the Kit in Stages
text:
The layout
The kit uses two 830-point breadboards side by side along their long edges, with the ESP32 DevKit V1 at the bottom end, bridging the seam so that each row of pins lands on a different board.

Left board: LEDs, buttons, potentiometer and buzzer; at the top, the servo and its 470 µF capacitor on a short, separate 5 V rail.
Right board: from top to bottom, the ATECC608A, the OLED, the MPU-6050 and the BMP280.
A printed holder at the top (download link in Appendix A — Kit Reference) carries the servo and, in some kits, the LoRa radio and its antenna; otherwise the radio sits on the right board.

Figure A.1 in Appendix A shows the finished layout, and Figure A.3 to Figure A.6 show the wiring for each stage.
Run the ESP32’s 3V3 and GND pins to the power rails of both boards. Keep wires short, flat and color-coded: red for 3.3 V, black for ground, a different color for each signal type.






Warning



The servo’s 5 V rail (fed from the ESP32’s VIN pin) must never be connected to the 3.3 V rails. The ESP32’s pins are not 5 V tolerant.

Stage 1: basic I/O and the display (this lab)

Part
Connection
Notes




Red LED (LED 1)
GPIO 2 → 220 Ω → LED → GND
Longer leg (anode) toward the resistor

Green LED (LED 3)

title: Lab 1: Build the Kit in Stages
text:
Procedure

Inventory your parts against the kit list in Appendix A — Kit Reference. Report anything missing or damaged.
Solder headers on the breakout boards (Lab 0).
Place the breadboards and ESP32, and wire the power rails. With the USB cable connected and nothing else wired, measure 3.3 V between the rails (a TA can help with the multimeter). Unplug again.
Wire Stage 1 one part at a time, following Table 1. After each part, check the wiring against the table with a teammate.
Run the kit check: open the provided kit-check project in PlatformIO, build, upload and open the Serial Monitor at 115200 baud. It blinks each LED, reads each button and the potentiometer, beeps the buzzer, and writes to the OLED. Fix anything that fails before moving on.

title: Lab 2: Traffic Controller
text:
Goals
Uses: Stage 1 of the kit (Lab 1): LED 1 red (GPIO 2), LED 2 yellow (GPIO 4), LED 3 green (GPIO 15), button 1 (GPIO 32), buzzer (GPIO 27).

title: Lab 2: Traffic Controller
text:
Design and implement a finite-state machine on a microcontroller.
Use non-blocking timing with millis() so several behaviors run at once (3  Programming the Device).
Think about safe default states and accessibility (7  Actuators and the Observe–Decide–Act Loop).

title: Lab 2: Traffic Controller
text:
The problem
Build a simplified pedestrian traffic light for a road crossing:

The light cycles green → yellow → red → red-yellow → green.
Red lasts 10 seconds. Yellow and red-yellow each last 2 seconds.
The light stays green until a pedestrian presses the button. After the button is pressed, it stays green for at least 5 more seconds before changing to yellow.
A buzzer helps people with visual impairments: while green, it sounds 500 ms on, 1 500 ms off; while red, it sounds 250 ms on, 250 ms off. It is silent in the other states.

(A fingertip on top of the buzzer lowers the volume, which your lab neighbors will appreciate.)

title: Lab 2: Traffic Controller
text:
Design
Model the light as a state machine with four states: RED, RED_YELLOW, GREEN and YELLOW, as shown below.

Each state has:

outputs: which LEDs are on, and the buzzer pattern;
transitions: the conditions (timer expired, button pressed) that move to the next state.

Keep the buzzer as a second, independent state machine (on/off, with its own timer) that reads the current traffic-light state to choose its pattern. Neither machine may use delay(): the button must be noticed immediately, whatever the buzzer is doing.

title: Lab 2: Traffic Controller
Lab 2: Traffic Controller
text:
Testing
Write a short test plan before demonstrating:







Test
Expected result




Power on
The light starts in the state you chose as safest


No button press
Light cycles to green and stays green indefinitely


Press during green, more than 5 s after entering green
Green lasts 5 more seconds, then yellow (2 s), red (10 s), red-yellow (2 s), green


Press during red
Does the press carry over? Decide, document and justify


Hold the button down
No repeated or stuck requests


Buzzer
500/1500 ms pattern in green, 250/250 ms in red, silent otherwise, never blocking the button



Time each state with a stopwatch or by printing timestamps over the serial port.

title: Lab 2: Traffic Controller
text:
What to show and submit

A live demonstration of every requirement to a TA.
Your code, with the state machine clearly structured.
A text file answering the analysis questions.

title: Lab 2: Traffic Controller
text:
Analysis questions

Why does the light stay green if the button is never pressed? Is that a sensible design for a road crossing?
What is the safest initial state when the controller powers up or resets? Why?
What would you add to make the crossing safer for people with auditory or visual impairments?
What should the controller do if it detects that a lamp has failed?

Part 2: SPI, showing data on the OLED

Initialize the OLED over SPI (7  Actuators and the Observe–Decide–Act Loop) using the kit pins.
Show the temperature and pressure from Part 1, updated once per second, plus a counter of SPI frame updates.
Measure how long one full-screen update takes with micros(). Estimate the number of bytes sent per update (128 × 64 pixels at 1 bit each) and the effective data rate.

text:
Part 3: UART, talking to another device

On your laptop, open the Serial Monitor at 115200 baud and implement a small command interface: typing temp, pres or led 1 on should produce a reply or an action.
Make the parser robust: ignore case, reject unknown commands with an error message, and never block while waiting for input.
Optional: connect two kits with a second UART (Serial2) on free pins, crossing TX and RX and sharing ground, and send readings from one kit to the other’s display.

title: Lab 3: Serial Communication
text:
Stretch: hardware vs. software SPI
Drive the OLED with a software (bit-banged) SPI on different free pins, using the display library’s software-SPI constructor. Measure the update time again and compare it with hardware SPI. When is software SPI worth using anyway?

title: Lab 3: Serial Communication
text:
What to show and submit

Demonstrate Parts 1–3 to a TA, including the BMP280 values computed from your own compensation code.
Submit your code and a text file with the analysis answers and your measurements.

title: Lab 3: Serial Communication
text:
Analysis questions

Which oversampling and filter settings did you choose for the BMP280, and why?
Why must the temperature be computed before the pressure in the BMP280’s compensation?
How many bytes does one OLED update send, and what effective rate did you measure? How does this compare with what I²C at 400 kHz could achieve?
When is it reasonable to use a communication method that is not native to your hardware, such as software SPI?





BMP280 Digital Pressure Sensor Datasheet. n.d. Bosch Sensortec. https://www.bosch-sensortec.com/products/environmental-sensors/pressure-sensors/bmp280/.

title: Lab 4: BLE Step Counter
text:
Goals
Uses: the MPU-6050 (Stage 2) and the OLED (Stage 1). You also need a phone with a BLE explorer app, such as nRF Connect.

title: Lab 4: BLE Step Counter
text:
Turn raw accelerometer data into a meaningful event: a step.
Expose the result over Bluetooth Low Energy using GATT services and characteristics (10  The Link Layer: Short and Long Range).
Evaluate a detector’s accuracy with real walking data.

title: Lab 4: BLE Step Counter
Lab 4: BLE Step Counter
text:
Part 2: publishing over BLE

Create a BLE peripheral named after your team (for example IoT-Team-07) with a custom Step Counter service.
Add a step-count characteristic (read and notify) that sends the count as a 32-bit unsigned integer, and notify connected clients whenever the count changes.
Add a reset characteristic (write): writing 1 resets the count to zero.
Connect with the phone app, enable notifications, and watch the count update as you walk.

The BLE stack uses a lot of flash. If the build reports that the program is too large, select a larger application partition in platformio.ini:
board_build.partitions = huge_app.csv

title: Lab 4: BLE Step Counter
text:
Part 3: evaluating accuracy

Walk exactly 100 steps (have a teammate count) at a normal pace, three times. Record the counts.
Repeat walking slowly, walking quickly and climbing stairs.
Shake the kit by hand for 10 seconds without walking. How many false steps are counted?
Report the error for each condition as \((\text{counted} - \text{actual}) / \text{actual}\).

title: Lab 4: BLE Step Counter
text:
What to show and submit

A live demonstration: walk 20 steps while the count updates on both the OLED and the phone, then reset it from the phone.
Your code, your tuned thresholds and how you chose them, and your accuracy table.

title: Lab 4: BLE Step Counter
text:
Analysis questions

Why does the detector use the magnitude of acceleration rather than one axis?
What do the hysteresis and the refractory period each prevent?
Where was your detector least accurate, and why?
How would you reduce the energy this device uses, if it had to run on a coin cell for a month? Consider sampling rate, BLE advertising and connection intervals, and the sensor’s own features.
How could you replace the hand-tuned thresholds with a learned model (18  AI on IoT and Edge ML)?

title: Lab 5: Cloud Communication
text:
Goals
This pipeline is the backbone of the team project: the reliability test (21  Testing in the Field) reuses the same broker, status topic and dashboard, and the lab is a natural point to build your project’s vertical slice (20  From Idea to Vertical Slice).

title: Lab 5: Cloud Communication
text:
Publish sensor data to a cloud MQTT broker over TLS (12  Application Protocols: HTTP, CoAP, MQTT and More).
Keep secrets out of the source code: store credentials in the board’s flash and enter them over Serial.
Choose a publish rate on purpose and defend it.
Use MQTT’s Last Will so that the broker announces when the device disappears.
Build a dashboard and an offline alert in Node-RED.

BMP280 + knob → ESP32 ──(Wi-Fi, TLS, MQTT, port 8883)──→ cloud broker (EMQX Serverless)
                                                              │
                         Node-RED on a team laptop  ←─────────┘
                         dashboard + offline alert

title: Lab 5: Cloud Communication
text:
What you need

The kit as wired for Lab 3; nothing new. The lab uses the BMP280 (I²C, 0x76), the potentiometer (GPIO 34) and the OLED.
A laptop with VS Code and PlatformIO, and Node.js 18 or newer (or Docker) for Node-RED.
A 2.4 GHz WPA2-Personal network. Enterprise networks such as eduroam need a username and certificate that a plain WiFi.begin(ssid, password) cannot provide, and campus networks may block port 8883. A phone hotspot (on an iPhone, turn on Maximize Compatibility) or the lab’s travel router works (Appendix B — Toolchain Setup).
The term’s starter project, which compiles before you start.

title: Lab 5: Cloud Communication
text:
Part A: the cloud side

A1. Create a broker
In Fall 2026 the lab uses EMQX Serverless, which has a free plan with no credit card. (The free serverless plan used earlier, HiveMQ Cloud, was closed to new clusters in November 2026; existing clusters could be kept until the end of the year. Any broker that offers MQTT over TLS with username and password authentication works the same way.)

Sign up at the EMQX Cloud site (one account per team) and create a Serverless deployment on the free plan. Check the current free-tier limits on the provider’s site; they are far above what this lab needs.
From the deployment’s overview page, copy its address (the MQTT host, of the form xxxxxxxx.ala.us-east-1.emqxsl.com). The port for MQTT over TLS is 8883.
Under Access Control › Authentication, add a credential: a username and a long password. Better: create two, one for the device and one for Node-RED, so either can be revoked without breaking the other. Keep them in a password manager, never in a file in your repository.
Optional check: connect a desktop client such as MQTTX to the address on port 8883 with TLS on, subscribe to iot/#, and leave it open.



A2. Node-RED and the dashboard
Install Node-RED with npm (npm install -g --unsafe-perm node-red, then node-red) or Docker (docker run -it -p 1880:1880 -v node_red_data:/data nodered/node-red), open http://localhost:1880, and install @flowfuse/node-red-dashboard (Dashboard 2.0) from Manage palette.
Import the starter flow, replace the team ID, and edit the MQTT broker node: your EMQX address, port 8883, Use TLS ticked with broker verification left on, and the Node-RED credential on the Security tab. Deploy; each MQTT-in node should show connected.
Node-RED stores the password separately in flows_cred.json in its own folder, so an exported flow does not contain it. Never commit that file.

title: Lab 5: Cloud Communication
section: Part B: credentials in flash, not in code
text:
Part B: credentials in flash, not in code
A secrets.h file ends up in Git, in zip files and on course sites. In this lab the board instead asks for its credentials once over Serial and keeps them in NVS (non-volatile storage, a key-value area of the flash) with the Preferences library. The source code contains no secrets at all.

loadCredentials(): open the namespace read-only, read the Wi-Fi SSID and password, MQTT host, username and password with getString(), and close it. Return true only if the SSID, host and username are present.
saveCredentials(): open it read-write and putString() the same keys.
On first boot the board prompts for each value and echoes passwords only as ********. After a reset it prints Credentials loaded from NVS and asks nothing; the values survive power cycles and new uploads.
Type PROVISION within 3 seconds of a reset to change the values, or FORGET to erase them. Erase them before the kit is returned: kits are reused.

title: Lab 5: Cloud Communication
section: Part C: TLS, Last Will, back-off and telemetry
text:
Part C: TLS, Last Will, back-off and telemetry

TLS client. Configure WiFiClientSecure and PubSubClient: server and port 8883, a keepalive of about 15 s, a short socket timeout and a buffer of about 512 bytes. In this lab the client may call setInsecure(). Put a comment above it, in your own words, saying that the connection is encrypted but the broker is not verified, so a fake hotspot could impersonate the broker and collect the MQTT password. Lab 6 fixes this; do not fix it here.
Connect with a Last Will. Use the seven-argument connect(): client ID, username, password, will topic (iot/T07/status), will QoS 1, will retained true, will message offline. On success, publish online to the same topic, retained, so that a dashboard started later still sees the current state.
Reconnect with back-off. loop() calls maintainWiFi(), maintainMqtt() and mqtt.loop() on every pass, and never uses delay(). In maintainMqtt(), retry only when the back-off interval has passed; on failure, print the client’s state, double the interval up to 30 s and add a little random jitter, so that 40 boards do not all retry at the same instant after a router reboot.
Telemetry at a rate you can defend. Set PERIOD_MS and justify it in a comment: how fast does room temperature change, how many messages per day is 86400000 / PERIOD_MS, and what does that add up to over a 72-hour test? Then publish, not retained:

{"seq":42,"temp_c":23.41,"press_hpa":1012.60,"pot_pct":37,"rssi":-61,"uptime_s":420}
seq increases by one per message, so a gap reveals a lost message.






TipWhy does offline take about 20 seconds?



The broker cannot see a pulled cable. It waits for a message or a keepalive ping and gives up after 1.5 × keepalive of silence (about 22 s with a 15 s keepalive), then publishes the Will. A shorter keepalive detects failures faster but costs more pings, and therefore more traffic and energy. The telemetry rate does not change detection time; the keepalive does. A clean disconnect() tells the broker the device left on purpose, so no Will is sent; publish offline yourself before a planned disconnect.

title: Lab 5: Cloud Communication
text:
Part D: dashboard and alert

Dashboard. Feed the parsed telemetry to a gauge and a chart of the temperature, plus at least one more value (pressure or the knob).
Alert. Complete the offline detector function so that it outputs an alert message (with the time) only when the status changes to offline, remembering the previous state in the node’s context. It drives a dashboard notification.
Test. Unplug the board: within about 25 s the status changes to offline and the notification appears. Plug it back in and the status returns to online.

title: Lab 5: Cloud Communication
text:
Part E: project analysis
Where is the weakest point in this pipeline, and what would it cost to fix? Follow the data from the sensor to the alert on the screen: sensor, ESP32, Wi-Fi, the local network, TLS, the free cloud broker, the laptop running Node-RED, the browser. Pick the link most likely to fail first or easiest to attack, give your evidence, and estimate the cost of fixing it in money, time, power and complexity. Candidates include setInsecure(), a laptop that must stay awake, one shared password, a free tier with no service-level agreement, flaky Wi-Fi and QoS 0 telemetry.

title: Lab 5: Cloud Communication
text:
What to show and submit

A live demonstration: data reaching the broker, the dashboard updating, the Last Will marking the device offline when unplugged, and the alert. Any team member should be able to explain the NVS, Last Will, back-off and mqtt.loop() code.
Your source code with the PERIOD_MS justification, and the written analysis. No passwords anywhere: search your repository (git grep -i part of the password) before pushing. If a password ever reaches Git, change it in the broker console; deleting the commit is not enough.

title: Lab 5: Cloud Communication
text:
Stretch goal
Add a stale-data watchdog in Node-RED: if no telemetry arrives for 3 × PERIOD_MS, show a warning even while the status says online. A frozen sensor loop still looks online to the broker.

title: Lab 5: Cloud Communication
text:
Analysis questions

Why does the device connect out to the broker instead of the dashboard connecting to the device?
Which QoS and retain settings did you use for each topic, and why?
What does the Last Will give you that a heartbeat alone does not?
What is the risk of setInsecure()? Describe an attack it allows.
How would your topic design change for 1000 devices owned by different customers?

title: Lab 6: Harden Your Device
text:
Goals
Uses: your Lab 5 system.

title: Lab 6: Harden Your Device
text:
Apply the security practices from Part IV to your own device and system.
Remove credentials from source code and authenticate the broker properly.
Protect commands against tampering and replay.
Reduce the device’s attack surface.
Understand, without burning anything, how the ESP32’s eFuses protect production devices.

title: Lab 6: Harden Your Device
text:
Part 1: threat model
Draw the data-flow diagram of your Lab 5 system with its trust boundaries, and apply STRIDE (14  Security and Privacy). List your top five threats with likelihood and impact. Keep this list: each part below should address one or more of them.

title: Lab 6: Harden Your Device
text:
Part 2: verify the broker
Replace setInsecure() with real certificate verification:

Find the root CA certificate that issued your broker’s certificate (your broker’s documentation names it; for example, many services use Let’s Encrypt’s ISRG Root X1).
Store it in the firmware as a PEM string and pass it to setCACert().
Make sure the device has the correct time (with configTime() and NTP) before connecting, since certificate validity depends on it.
Show that connecting to a different host with the same code now fails.

title: Lab 6: Harden Your Device
section: Part 3: get secrets out of the source code
text:
Part 3: get secrets out of the source code

Remove Wi-Fi and broker credentials from secrets.h in the firmware.
Implement serial provisioning: at first boot (or when both buttons are held at start-up), the device asks for its credentials over the Serial Monitor and stores them in NVS (non-volatile storage) using the Preferences library. Normal boots read them from NVS.
Check your repository’s history for secrets that were ever committed (git log -p | grep -i pass), and rotate (change) any you find.

NVS on this ESP32 is not encrypted unless flash encryption is enabled. Note in your report what an attacker with physical access could still read, and what a production device would do instead (16  Over-the-Air Updates and the Device Lifecycle).

title: Lab 6: Harden Your Device
text:
Part 4: authenticate commands
Protect your command topic against spoofing, tampering and replay, using either:

an HMAC with a per-device shared key and a monotonically increasing counter (14  Security and Privacy), with the counter stored in NVS so that a reboot does not reset it; or
ECDSA signatures verified on the device, if your kit’s ATECC608A has been provisioned with a key by the staff (read-only use; 15  Device Identity and Secure Elements).

Show that a modified command and a replayed command are both rejected, and that a valid one is accepted.

title: Lab 6: Harden Your Device
text:
Part 5: reduce the attack surface

Add a PRODUCTION build flag that removes debug output containing secrets or internal state.
Validate every field of every incoming message: types, ranges and lengths. Reject anything else.
Rate-limit commands, so a flood cannot keep the buzzer on or the CPU busy.
Use per-device broker credentials with permissions limited to your own topics, if your broker supports access control.

title: Lab 6: Harden Your Device
text:
Part 6: eFuses, read-only
Run the read-only summary command from the ESP-IDF tools, with the kit connected:
espefuse.py --port /dev/ttyUSB0 summary
(On Windows the port is COM3 or similar; on macOS, /dev/cu.usbserial-… or /dev/cu.SLAB_USBtoUART.)
Identify the eFuses for flash encryption, secure boot, JTAG and UART download mode. Are any of them set on your board? Then watch the staff demonstration of flash encryption on a dedicated board.

title: Lab 6: Harden Your Device
text:
What to show and submit

A demonstration: provisioning over serial, a verified TLS connection, and rejection of tampered and replayed commands.
Your threat model, showing which threats each change addresses and which remain.
Your code (with no secrets in it or in its history).
Answers to the analysis questions.

title: Lab 6: Harden Your Device
text:
Analysis questions

Which of your top five threats did this lab address, and which remain? What would you do next?
Why does certificate verification depend on the device knowing the correct time?
What could an attacker with physical access to your kit still extract, and how would secure boot and flash encryption change that?
Why must the replay counter survive a reboot?
Explain, from your eFuse summary, why enabling these protections on a production device is irreversible, and why that is a feature rather than a flaw.

title: About the Activities
text:
How each activity works
The eight activities in this part are short, hands-on exercises designed for a lecture session. Each one takes 15 to 45 minutes and turns one idea from a chapter into something that runs on a board.

title: About the Activities
text:
Starter code with TODOs. Each kit activity starts from a small PlatformIO project in which the interesting lines are left as numbered TODOs. The handout gives a hint for each one. The activities in this book describe the TODOs; the starter projects are distributed by the course and will be published alongside the book.
Required part and extension. The TODOs are the required part. The Extension at the end is optional, for teams that finish early.
Roles. Kit activities work best in teams of two or three with rotating roles: a Driver at the keyboard and board, a Navigator who reads the handout and hints aloud, and a Recorder who keeps notes for the questions.
Questions. Each activity ends with four short questions. They are meant to be answered in a sentence or two, and they check understanding rather than code.
Grading. In IoT@UCI, activities are graded on participation, not correctness. Solutions are not published.

title: About the Activities
section: Helpers used by the starter projects
text:
Helpers used by the starter projects
The starter projects share a small support library, so that activity code stays short:



Table 2: Support helpers used in the activities.









Helper
What it does




IoTPins::…
Pin names from iot_pins.h (Appendix A — Kit Reference)


iotInitI2C()
Starts the I²C bus on SDA 21 / SCL 22


iotInitSPI()
Starts the SPI bus on SCK 18 / MOSI 23 / MISO 19


iotInitDisplay()
Initializes the OLED; returns true on success


iotDisplayLines(a, b, c, d)
Writes up to four lines to the OLED


iotConnectWiFi()
Joins the network in secrets.h; returns true on success












NoteFor instructors





The network activities (5 and 7) need a 2.4 GHz WPA2-Personal network that every board can join, such as a travel router (Appendix E — Setting Up a Teaching Lab), and a server or broker on the instructor’s laptop. Activity 6 needs one receiving radio at the front of the room. Activity 8 needs ATECC608A chips that were provisioned before the term: students must never configure or lock the chips themselves.

title: Activity 1: Blink and Basic Circuits
text:
Goal
Time: about 15 minutes · Format: individual · Hardware: none, the free Wokwi ESP32 simulator in a web browser · Chapter: 2  Development Boards and the IoT Kit
Build the simplest useful embedded circuit, an LED with a current-limiting resistor, and make it blink from software. The code runs unchanged on a real ESP32 later.
After this activity you should be able to:

title: Activity 1: Blink and Basic Circuits
Activity 1: Blink and Basic Circuits
text:
Set up the simulator

Open wokwi.com (an optional free account lets you save and share projects).
Start a new ESP32 project from the Arduino template. The editor is on the left, the simulated board on the right.
Add parts with the + button; make a wire by clicking one pin and then another; click a part to change its settings.
Press ▶ Start to run. Serial output appears below the board.

title: Activity 1: Blink and Basic Circuits

Expected result
The LED is on for about half a second, off for about half a second, and repeats; the Serial Monitor shows the title line once.

title: Activity 1: Blink and Basic Circuits
text:
Extension (optional)
Add a second LED with its own 220 Ω resistor on GPIO 27 and make the two LEDs alternate, or blink SOS (three short, three long, three short). The simulator may light an LED wired without a resistor: what would happen on a real board? (7  Actuators and the Observe–Decide–Act Loop has the arithmetic.)

title: Activity 1: Blink and Basic Circuits
text:
Troubleshooting

LED never lights: the anode must face the GPIO pin, the cathode GND.
Nothing happens: the circuit must be on the same pin as LED_PIN.
Compile error: read the first error line; a missing semicolon is the usual cause.
LED stays on or off: check that both delays are present and that TODO 1 is inside setup().

title: Activity 1: Blink and Basic Circuits
text:
Questions

Why does the circuit need a resistor in series with the LED?
Why must a GPIO pin be configured with pinMode() before it is used?
What would you observe if both delay() calls were removed? Why?
What would you change to make the LED blink twice as fast?

title: Activity 2: Buttons, Debouncing and Interrupts
text:
Goal
Time: about 15 minutes · Format: individual · Hardware: none, the Wokwi ESP32 simulator · Chapter: 3  Programming the Device
Count button presses with an interrupt service routine (ISR) instead of polling, and add a software debounce so that one press counts once. Wokwi’s pushbutton imitates the contact bounce of a real button, so you will see the problem before you fix it.
After this activity you should be able to:

title: Activity 2: Buttons, Debouncing and Interrupts
Activity 2: Buttons, Debouncing and Interrupts
text:
Build the circuit
Add one pushbutton: one side to D27 (GPIO 27), the other to GND. No resistor is needed: the internal pull-up holds the pin HIGH until the button pulls it LOW. In the simulator, click and hold the button to press it.

title: Activity 2: Buttons, Debouncing and Interrupts
Activity 2: Buttons, Debouncing and Interrupts
text:
Hints







TODO
Hint




1
Read millis(); accept the press only if more than 150 ms have passed since lastInterruptMs, and then update lastInterruptMs.


2
Increment inside the accepted branch only.


3
pinMode() with INPUT_PULLUP.


4
attachInterrupt(digitalPinToInterrupt(pin), handler, FALLING).


5
Serial.print() then Serial.println().



Keep the ISR short: never call Serial or delay() inside it (4  Embedded Systems and Operating Systems).

title: Activity 2: Buttons, Debouncing and Interrupts
text:
Expected result
Each press prints one new line, such as Button count: 3.

title: Activity 2: Buttons, Debouncing and Interrupts
text:
Extension (optional)
Set the debounce window to 0 ms and press several times: how often does one press count more than once? Then add an LED (with a 220 Ω resistor) that toggles on every valid press.

title: Activity 2: Buttons, Debouncing and Interrupts
text:
Troubleshooting

Count jumps by several per press: the debounce check is missing or the window is too small.
Count never changes: check the wiring and INPUT_PULLUP.
Counts on release: use FALLING, not RISING.
Simulation crashes when pressing: something slow is inside the ISR.

title: Activity 2: Buttons, Debouncing and Interrupts
text:
Questions

What is an interrupt, and why is it useful compared with checking the button in loop()?
What problem does debouncing solve? What did you see with a 0 ms window?
Why does INPUT_PULLUP let you wire the button without an external resistor?
Why is the falling edge used here?

title: Activity 3: Scan the I²C Bus, Report on SPI

Troubleshooting

0 devices found: TODO 1 must run before the scan; check the four bus wires (3V3, GND, SDA 21, SCL 22).
0x60 missing although wired: the ATECC608A sleeps until woken and can miss a scan. Press EN to scan again.

What would happen if two devices on one bus had the same address? How do some sensors avoid this?

title: Activity 4: The Observe–Decide–Act Loop
text:
Goal
Time: about 45 minutes · Format: team of 2–3 with the kit · Hardware: kit Stage 3 (servo on its 5 V rail) · Chapters: 6  Sensors and 7  Actuators and the Observe–Decide–Act Loop
Make the servo follow the potentiometer. Every 100 ms the program will:

title: Activity 4: The Observe–Decide–Act Loop
Activity 4: The Observe–Decide–Act Loop
text:
Before you start
Check the Stage 3 wiring (Lab 1): servo signal on GPIO 13, red wire on the 5 V rail from VIN, brown or black on GND, and the 470 µF capacitor across the rail with its stripe to GND. Do not power the servo from 3V3: its current spikes reset the ESP32.

title: Activity 4: The Observe–Decide–Act Loop
text:
TODOs

Activity 4 TODOs.







TODO
Task
Hint




1
Make the potentiometer pin an input
pinMode(IoTPins::POT_ADC, INPUT)


2
Set up a 50 Hz, 16-bit PWM channel on the servo pin
ledcSetup(SERVO_CH, 50, 16) and ledcAttachPin(...); the starter uses channel 2 because tone() uses channel 0


3
Observe: read the ADC
analogRead() returns 0–4095


4
Decide: map to 600–2400 µs, then to a duty value
map(), then the provided usToDuty()


5
Act: write the duty value
ledcWrite(SERVO_CH, duty)









NoteThe duty arithmetic



At 50 Hz one period is 20 ms. With 16-bit resolution the period is divided into \(2^{16} = 65\,536\) counts, so a pulse of \(t\) microseconds needs a duty of \[\text{duty} = \frac{t}{20\,000\ \mu\text{s}} \times 65\,536 .\] A centred servo (1500 µs) is therefore about 4915 counts.

title: Activity 4: The Observe–Decide–Act Loop
text:
Expected result
Pot  328 ->  744 us -> duty 2437
Pot 2048 -> 1500 us -> duty 4915
Pot 4095 -> 2400 us -> duty 7864
The OLED shows the reading, the pulse width and the approximate angle, and the servo follows the knob.

title: Activity 4: The Observe–Decide–Act Loop
text:
Extension (optional)
Add a dead band: only write a new duty when the pulse width differs from the last one sent by more than 20 µs. Does the servo stop buzzing when you let go of the knob? Why would a battery-powered product want this?

title: Activity 4: The Observe–Decide–Act Loop
text:
Troubleshooting

Servo does not move: signal on GPIO 13; servo ground shared with the ESP32; ledcAttachPin() in setup().
Board resets (“Brownout detector was triggered”): the servo is on 3V3 or the capacitor is missing.
Servo buzzes at the ends: it is pushing against its end stops; narrow the range to about 700–2300 µs.
ledcSetup does not compile: the project needs Arduino core 2.x (espressif32@6.9.0); core 3.x renamed these functions.

title: Activity 4: The Observe–Decide–Act Loop
text:
Questions

Which lines of your code are Observe, which Decide, and which Act?
What duty value gives a 1.5 ms pulse? Why does the servo never use most of the 0–65 535 range?
What would change if the loop ran once per second instead of every 100 ms?
Why is the servo powered from the 5 V rail with a capacitor instead of the 3V3 pin?

title: Activity 5: A Classroom Poll over HTTP
text:
Goal
Time: about 35 minutes · Format: team of 2–3 with the kit · Hardware: kit Stage 1 and a classroom Wi-Fi network · Chapter: 8  Communication Models: OSI and TCP/IP
Turn the ESP32 into an HTTP client. It joins the room’s Wi-Fi network, reads the potentiometer as a percentage, and, when Button 1 is pressed, sends the team’s answer to a poll server on the instructor’s laptop. A dashboard at the front of the room shows every team’s answer and the class average.
Every layer of the TCP/IP model is at work:

title: Activity 5: A Classroom Poll over HTTP
text:
The layers in the poll.






Layer
In this activity




Application
HTTP: GET for the question, POST for the answer, and a status code back


Transport
TCP connection to port 8080, reliable byte delivery


Internet
IP routing to the server’s private address on the room router


Link
Wi-Fi (802.11) frames between the board and the router
crumbs: Activity 5: A Classroom Poll over HTTP

No new wiring. The network name, password and server address are shown in the room. Use the class router, not the campus enterprise network, which blocks unregistered devices (Appendix B — Toolchain Setup).

Status codes you may see

Status codes in the poll.






Code
Meaning here

Answer accepted

title: Activity 6: A LoRa Emergency Beacon
text:
Class signal test
Transmit once with the kit in its normal orientation (round A), then rotate it about 90° without moving and transmit again (round B). Record RSSI and SNR for both. RSSI closer to 0 dBm is stronger: −65 dBm is stronger than −90 dBm.

title: Activity 6: A LoRa Emergency Beacon

Extension (optional)
Use the time-on-air formula in the chapter’s in-depth section (In depth (optional)) to estimate how long your 23-byte packet occupies the channel at the starter’s spreading factor. How many such packets per hour fit within a 1% duty cycle?

title: Activity 6: A LoRa Emergency Beacon
text:
Troubleshooting

Radio fails to start: check the antenna and Stage 4 wiring, power-cycle and upload again.
Packet does not appear at the receiver: wait for other teams, transmit once more, and check that the team ID is not 00.
Different RSSI each time: expected. Orientation, people, furniture and multipath all change it.

title: Activity 6: A LoRa Emergency Beacon
text:
Questions

Which orientation gave the stronger signal, and what is one plausible reason?
Why is the payload a short text string rather than JSON with long field names?
Your packet reached the receiver with no router and no Internet. What did you give up compared with Wi-Fi?
Give one IoT application for which LoRa is a better choice than BLE, and one for which it is worse.

title: Activity 7: MQTT Command Center and Picking the QoS
text:
Goal
Time: about 30 minutes · Format: team of 2–3 with the kit · Hardware: kit Stage 1 and a classroom Wi-Fi network with an MQTT broker · Chapter: 12  Application Protocols: HTTP, CoAP, MQTT and More
Connect the board to a classroom MQTT broker. It publishes potentiometer telemetry to a team topic and subscribes to a class-wide command topic, so that one message from the instructor changes every kit in the room. Then decide which QoS, retain and Last Will settings fit four real situations.
crumbs: Activity 7: MQTT Command Center and Picking the QoS

title: Activity 7: MQTT Command Center and Picking the QoS
text:
MQTT delivery options.






Term
Meaning




QoS 0
At most once: no acknowledgment; may be lost


QoS 1
At least once: resent until acknowledged; may be duplicated


QoS 2
Exactly once: a four-step handshake, at extra cost


Retained
The broker keeps the last message on a topic and gives it to new subscribers


Last Will (LWT)
A message the broker publishes for a client that disconnects unexpectedly
crumbs: Activity 7: MQTT Command Center and Picking the QoS

title: Activity 7: MQTT Command Center and Picking the QoS
text:
Part B: pick the QoS
The starter’s library publishes at QoS 0, so this part is a design exercise. For each situation choose a QoS level, decide whether the message is retained, and justify it in one sentence. Then choose one situation where a Last Will helps and write its topic and payload.

A greenhouse sensor publishes temperature every 10 seconds to a live dashboard.
A phone app sends an “unlock” command to a smart door lock.
A smart electricity meter reports a daily billing reading that must be counted exactly once.
A dashboard must show whether each device is online, including devices that just lost power.

title: Activity 8: Signed Messages and STRIDE
text:
Goal
Time: about 20 minutes · Format: team of 2–3 with the kit · Hardware: kit Stage 2 with a pre-provisioned ATECC608A · Chapters: 14  Security and Privacy and 15  Device Identity and Secure Elements
Protect a sensor message with a digital signature made by the kit’s ATECC608A secure element, whose private key never leaves the chip. Then show two things: changing a signed message makes verification fail (tampering), and resending an old, valid message is only caught by a freshness check (replay). Finally, map what you saw to STRIDE.

title: Activity 8: Signed Messages and STRIDE
text:
Important



The code only uses the chip. It never configures or locks it and never reads private keys. If the chip reports that it is not provisioned, stop and ask the teaching staff.

title: Activity 8: Signed Messages and STRIDE
text:
TODOs

Activity 8 TODOs.







TODO
Task
Hint




1
Convert the ADC reading to 0–100 %
map()


2
Build the message
Exactly DEVICE=<chip serial>;SEQ=<seq>;SENSOR=<percent>; the serial is cryptoContext.serialNumber


3
Sign it in hardware
IoTCrypto::signMessage(packet.message, packet.signature), a 64-byte ECDSA P-256 signature from key slot 0


4
Verify the authentic message
IoTCrypto::verifyMessage(message, signature, cryptoContext.publicKey)


5
Tamper test
Verify the modified message with the original signature; do not re-sign


6
Replay test
(A) the old message still verifies; (B) accept it only if sequence > lastAcceptedSequence

title: Activity 8: Signed Messages and STRIDE
text:
Running it
Turn the knob, press Button 1 to create, sign and verify a message. Press Button 2 once for the tamper test, and again for the replay test.

Expected results.






Test
Expected OLED




Authentic
AUTHENTIC MESSAGE · Signature: VALID


Tamper
TAMPER DETECTED · Signature: INVALID


Replay
REPLAY DETECTED · Signature: VALID · Freshness: REJECT



The replay row is the key lesson: a valid signature proves the message is authentic and unmodified, but only the sequence check shows it is new.

title: Activity 8: Signed Messages and STRIDE
text:
Extension (optional)
Reset the board and press Button 1. The sequence number starts over. Would a receiver that remembered the last accepted sequence now reject every new message? Propose one way a real device keeps freshness working across reboots (15  Device Identity and Secure Elements).

title: Activity 8: Signed Messages and STRIDE
text:
Questions

Which STRIDE category does the tamper test demonstrate, and which part of your code defends against it?
A signature does not hide the sensor value. Which STRIDE category is still open, and what would close it?
Why does a valid signature not stop a replay? Besides a sequence number, name another way to prove freshness.
What does keeping the private key inside the ATECC608A protect against, compared with storing it in the ESP32’s flash?

title: Appendix A — Kit Reference
text:
A.1 What the finished kit looks like
The layout follows a few deliberate rules:

title: Appendix A — Kit Reference
text:
Figure A.1: The team kit, top view. The ESP32 bridges the two breadboards at the bottom; I/O parts are on the left board, bus-connected modules on the right, and a printed holder at the top carries the servo and the radio.





Two 830-point breadboards, joined along their long edges, give every module its own rows and leave space for project additions.
The ESP32 straddles the seam between the boards, at the end nearest the edge of the desk, so the USB cable does not cross the circuit.
Left board, top to bottom: the 5 V servo rail and its capacitor, three LEDs, the potentiometer, two buttons and the buzzer. These are the parts students touch.
Right board, top to bottom: ATECC608A, OLED, MPU-6050, BMP280. All four sit on shared buses, so their header pins line up with the bus wiring.
The holder at the top keeps the servo and radio from pulling on their wires.

TipWhy a quarter-wave antenna is 78 mm



A simple wire antenna works best at a quarter of the wavelength. At 915 MHz the wavelength is \(\lambda = c / f = 3\times10^8 / 9.15\times10^8 \approx 0.328\) m, so \(\lambda/4 \approx 82\) mm. A real wire is made slightly shorter (about 95%) because the signal travels a little slower along a conductor than in free space, which gives the familiar ≈78 mm.

title: Appendix A — Kit Reference
text:
A.3 The printed holder
The holder is a single printed part that clips over the outer edges of the two breadboards and carries the servo and the radio, so that they do not pull on their wires.






NoteGet the holder file from its designer



The holder is the Breadboard Snap-On Component Tray (830-point), designed by Alvin Ma and shared as a free download on Cults3D: https://cults3d.com/en/3d-model/gadget/breadboard-snap-on-component-tray-830-point. Download the STL there rather than from a copy: the designer keeps it up to date based on feedback from users, and instructors who need a variation for their own kits can find his other designs on the same page. This book does not redistribute the file.








Figure A.2: Functional dimensions of the holder used in Fall 2026, measured from the printed part. Download the part itself from its designer (link above); the dimensions are given to check a print and to plan compatible parts.

title: Appendix A — Kit Reference
Appendix A — Kit Reference
text:
A.7 Power

The board is powered from USB (5 V), regulated to 3.3 V for the ESP32 and the 3V3 rails.
VIN carries the USB 5 V (minus a diode drop on some boards) and feeds only the servo rail.
Budget: the 3.3 V regulator on a typical DevKit supplies several hundred milliamperes, and Wi-Fi transmission alone can draw up to about 250 mA in bursts. Do not power motors or additional radios from 3V3.

title: Appendix A — Kit Reference
text:
A.8 Kit care

Unplug USB before changing wiring.
Keep the antenna attached to the LoRa radio.
Store the kit with wires pressed flat and parts seated; loose parts are the most common cause of “it worked yesterday”.
Report damaged parts to the teaching staff rather than swapping in parts from elsewhere.

title: Appendix B — Toolchain Setup
text: B.1 What you need

title: Appendix B — Toolchain Setup
text:
A laptop running macOS, Windows or Linux, with a free USB port (USB-A or USB-C, matching your cable).
Visual Studio Code and the PlatformIO IDE extension.
Git, and a GitHub (or similar) account for your team repository.
Optionally: Wokwi (browser-based ESP32 simulator), an MQTT client such as MQTT Explorer, Node-RED, and Python 3 with Jupyter for data analysis.

title: Appendix B — Toolchain Setup
text:
B.2 Installing PlatformIO

Install VS Code from code.visualstudio.com.
In VS Code, open the Extensions view and install PlatformIO IDE. The first installation downloads its own Python environment and tools; this can take several minutes.
Restart VS Code. The PlatformIO (alien-head) icon appears in the left sidebar.

title: Appendix B — Toolchain Setup
text:
B.3 USB drivers
The DevKit’s USB-to-UART bridge is usually a Silicon Labs CP210x or a WCH CH340 chip. macOS and Linux usually recognize both; Windows may need the vendor’s driver.
To check that the board is detected:

macOS: ls /dev/cu.* should show cu.usbserial-…, cu.SLAB_USBtoUART or cu.wchusbserial….
Linux: ls /dev/ttyUSB*; add yourself to the dialout (or uucp) group if uploads fail with a permission error.
Windows: Device Manager → Ports (COM & LPT) should list a new COM port.

If nothing appears, try a different cable: many USB cables carry power only.

title: Appendix B — Toolchain Setup
text:
B.4 Opening a project
Starter projects are complete PlatformIO projects.

Unzip the starter.
In VS Code: PlatformIO → Open Project, and select the folder that contains platformio.ini. Do not open a single .cpp file.
Wait for PlatformIO to install the platform and libraries listed in platformio.ini.

A typical project looks like this:
my-project/
├── platformio.ini       build configuration: board, platform version, libraries
├── include/
│   ├── iot_pins.h       kit pin map
│   ├── secrets.h        your credentials (git-ignored)
│   └── secrets.example.h
├── lib/                 project-specific libraries
├── src/
│   └── main.cpp         your code
└── test/                unit tests

Use the buttons in the blue status bar at the bottom of VS Code:

title: Appendix B — Toolchain Setup
text:
B.6 Secrets
Never commit passwords or keys.

Keep credentials in include/secrets.h, and list that file in .gitignore.
Commit a secrets.example.h with placeholder values so teammates know what to fill in.

// secrets.example.h — copy to secrets.h and fill in
#pragma once
#define WIFI_SSID      "your-network"
#define WIFI_PASSWORD  "your-password"
#define MQTT_HOST      "xxxxxxxx.ala.us-east-1.emqxsl.com"
#define MQTT_USER      "device-user"
#define MQTT_PASS      "device-password"

title: Appendix B — Toolchain Setup
text:
B.7 Wokwi
Wokwi simulates an ESP32 with LEDs, buttons, displays and many sensors in the browser, and can also run inside VS Code. It is useful for the early activities, before the kit is built, and for testing logic without hardware. Simulated timing and radios are not identical to real hardware, so always confirm on the kit.

title: Appendix B — Toolchain Setup
text:
B.8 Networks
Campus enterprise Wi-Fi (WPA2-Enterprise) and networks with captive portals generally do not work with small devices. Use the course IoT network, a phone hotspot (2.4 GHz), or a travel router.

title: Appendix C — Troubleshooting
text:
C.1 Power and upload
Work from the bottom of the stack up: power and wiring first, then the bus, then the code, then the network. Change one thing at a time, and write down what you changed.

What to try

title: Appendix C — Troubleshooting
text:
C.7 Wi-Fi and MQTT








Symptom
Likely causes
What to try




Never connects to Wi-Fi
5 GHz-only network; WPA2-Enterprise; captive portal; typo
Use a 2.4 GHz WPA2-Personal network (Appendix B)


TLS connection fails
Wrong CA certificate; clock not set; wrong port
Set time with NTP; check the CA; use 8883


MQTT connects then drops repeatedly
Two clients with the same client ID; mqtt.loop() not called
Unique IDs; call loop() every pass


Messages not received
Topic typo; subscribed before connecting; payload larger than the buffer
Watch with a desktop client subscribed to #; setBufferSize()

Memory leak; no reconnection logic; watchdog
Log free heap and reset reasons (Chapter 21)

title: Appendix C — Troubleshooting
text:
C.8 When you are stuck

Write down exactly what you expected and what happened.
Reduce the problem to the smallest program that shows it.
Swap one component with a known-good one (another team’s sensor, another cable).
Ask for help with the evidence from steps 1–3: the error message, the minimal program, a photo of the wiring.

title: Appendix D — Glossary
text:
6LoWPAN

IPv6 over Low-Power Wireless Personal Area Networks; an adaptation layer that compresses and fragments IPv6 packets for small radio frames (Chapter 11).

ACK / NACK

Acknowledgment / negative acknowledgment, confirming whether data was received.

Actuator

A device that converts a control signal into a physical effect such as motion, light or sound (Chapter 7).

ADC

Analog-to-digital converter; measures a voltage and converts it to a number (Chapter 3).

AEAD

Authenticated encryption with associated data; encryption that also guarantees integrity, such as AES-GCM (Chapter 14).

BLE

Bluetooth Low Energy (Chapter 10).

Border router

A router connecting a low-power network such as 6LoWPAN or Thread to the wider IP network (Chapter 11).

Broker

In publish/subscribe systems such as MQTT, the server that receives messages and forwards them to subscribers (Chapter 12).

Certificate (X.509)

A signed statement binding a public key to an identity (Chapter 15).

CoAP

Constrained Application Protocol; a REST protocol over UDP for constrained devices (Chapter 12).

Constrained device

A device with limited memory, processing and energy (Chapter 9).

Debouncing

Filtering the rapid on/off transitions of a mechanical switch (Chapter 3).

Deep sleep

An ESP32 low-power mode in which only the RTC domain stays powered (Chapter 10).

DODAG

Destination-oriented directed acyclic graph; the routing structure built by RPL (Chapter 11).

Duty cycle

The fraction of time a signal is on (PWM), or that a device or radio is active.

eFuse

One-time-programmable memory bits inside a chip, used for keys and security configuration (Chapter 16).

Edge / fog computing

Processing close to where data is produced, between devices and the cloud (Chapter 18).

Encapsulation

Wrapping data with each protocol layer’s header as it moves down the stack (Chapter 8).

Fail-safe state

The state that causes the least harm when something fails (Chapter 7).

Flash encryption

Transparent encryption of a device’s external flash memory (Chapter 16).

GATT

Generic Attribute Profile; the BLE data model of services and characteristics (Chapter 10).

GPIO

General-purpose input/output pin.

HMAC

Hash-based message authentication code; proves integrity and authenticity with a shared key (Chapter 14).

Hysteresis

Using separate on and off thresholds to prevent rapid switching near a set point (Chapter 7).

I²C

Inter-Integrated Circuit; a two-wire, addressed serial bus (Chapter 5).

IMU

Inertial measurement unit; an accelerometer and gyroscope, sometimes with a magnetometer (Chapter 6).

Interrupt / ISR

A hardware signal that pauses normal execution to run an interrupt service routine (Chapter 3).

Interoperability

The ability of systems to exchange information and use it (Chapter 13).

LLN

Low-power and lossy network (Chapter 11).

LoRa / LoRaWAN

A long-range, low-power radio modulation, and the network protocol built on it (Chapter 10).

LPWAN

Low-power wide-area network.

Matter

A smart-home interoperability standard running over IP on Wi-Fi, Ethernet and Thread (Chapter 13).

MEMS

Micro-electro-mechanical systems; microscopic mechanical structures in silicon, used in most motion and pressure sensors.

MQTT

A lightweight publish/subscribe messaging protocol (Chapter 12).

mTLS

Mutual TLS, in which both client and server present certificates (Chapter 15).

NAT

Network address translation, which maps private addresses to a public one (Chapter 8).

ODA loop

Observe–Decide–Act, the cycle connecting sensing to actuation (Chapter 7).

OTA update

Over-the-air update: delivering new firmware through the network (Chapter 16).

PKI

Public-key infrastructure; the certificate authorities, certificates and policies that establish trust (Chapter 15).

Provisioning

Giving a device its identity, credentials and configuration (Chapter 15).

Pull-up / pull-down resistor

A resistor that holds an input at a defined level when nothing else drives it (Chapter 3).

PWM

Pulse-width modulation; switching a signal rapidly to control average power or encode a value (Chapter 3).

QoS

Quality of service; in MQTT, the delivery guarantee level (Chapter 12).

Real-time system

A system that must respond within a specified time (Chapter 4).

Replay attack

Resending a captured valid message to repeat its effect (Chapter 14).

RPL

IPv6 Routing Protocol for Low-Power and Lossy Networks (Chapter 11).

RSSI / SNR

Received signal strength indicator / signal-to-noise ratio.

RTOS

Real-time operating system (Chapter 4).

SBOM

Software bill of materials; a list of all software components in a product (Chapter 16).

Secure boot

Verifying the signature of each piece of software before running it (Chapter 16).

Secure element

A tamper-resistant chip that stores keys and performs cryptography without exposing keys (Chapter 15).

SoC

System on a chip; a microcontroller or processor integrated with larger subsystems such as radios.

SPI

Serial Peripheral Interface; a fast synchronous bus with a chip-select line per device (Chapter 5).

STRIDE

Spoofing, Tampering, Repudiation, Information disclosure, Denial of service, Elevation of privilege; a threat-modeling mnemonic (Chapter 14).

Thing Description

A W3C JSON-LD document describing a device’s properties, actions and events (Chapter 13).

Thread

An IPv6 mesh networking protocol on 802.15.4 radios (Chapter 11).

TinyML

Machine learning on microcontrollers (Chapter 18).

TLS / DTLS

Transport Layer Security, and its datagram (UDP) variant.

TSN

Time-Sensitive Networking; IEEE standards for deterministic Ethernet (Chapter 10).

UART

Universal asynchronous receiver/transmitter; point-to-point serial communication without a clock wire (Chapter 5).

Vertical slice

A thin, end-to-end working version of a whole system (Chapter 20).

Watchdog timer

A timer that resets the processor unless software services it regularly (Chapter 4).

title: Appendix E — Setting Up a Teaching Lab
text:
E.1 The room
This appendix is for instructors and lab managers who want to run the course, or a course like it. It describes what a room needs so that every team can build, solder, program and test its kit safely. Quantities assume a section of about 30 students working in teams of two or three, with up to 10 people soldering at once.
crumbs: E  Setting Up a Teaching Lab

title: Appendix E — Setting Up a Teaching Lab
text:
Table E.1: Room requirements.










Need
Recommendation
Why




Layout
A dedicated soldering bench along one wall; separate tables for pair work with laptops; an instrument shelf; lockable storage; a visible safety station
Keeps hot irons away from laptops, paper and foot traffic


Power
Hard-wired or properly rated outlets at each bench; no daisy-chained power strips; cords routed off the floor
Every station draws power at once, and crossing cords are a trip and burn hazard


Ventilation
A fume extractor at each soldering station, and confirmation from your environmental health and safety office that room ventilation is adequate
Rosin flux fumes are a respiratory irritant


Surfaces
Heat-resistant, wipeable bench tops or silicone mats at the soldering bench
Solder spatter and dropped irons


Seating
Fixed, wipeable stools at the soldering bench
Fabric chairs on casters collect spatter, build static, and roll over cords


Lighting
Task lighting at the soldering bench
Small pads and fine pitch need good light


Network
A 2.4 GHz WPA2-Personal network able to handle about 30 devices, or a dedicated travel router
Enterprise and captive-portal networks block small devices (Appendix B)


Safety station
First-aid kit including burn dressings, fire extinguisher, eyewash if required, posted soldering procedure and emergency contacts
Required by most institutions; makes the rules visible

title: Appendix E — Setting Up a Teaching Lab
text:
E.3 Before the first lab

Kits: count, label and test every kit; flash a kit-check sketch; pre-solder or pre-provision anything students should not do themselves (for example, locking secure elements).
Network: test that 30 boards can join the room network and reach your broker or server at the same time.
Safety briefing: present the soldering procedure, show the safety station and require safety glasses.
Staffing: plan at least one teaching assistant per 10 students during soldering.
Kit policy: decide whether kits are returned at the end of the term or can be bought, and how damaged parts are replaced.
crumbs: E  Setting Up a Teaching Lab

title: Appendix E — Setting Up a Teaching Lab
text:
E.4 Running costs
Budget each term for consumables (solder, flux, wire, resistors and LEDs), replacement parts (an ESP32 or a sensor per few kits is typical), and spare tips for the soldering stations.
